EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Thu, 05 Nov 2026 08:33:56 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 Two fatal train disasters in less than a year: I never thought I would see this happen in my native Spain https://euobserver.com/246831/two-fatal-train-disasters-in-less-than-a-year-i-never-thought-i-would-see-this-happen-in-my-native-spain/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 19:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246831 As Spain’s transport minister resigns and politicians trade accusations over budgets and responsibility, many ordinary Spaniards are left wondering why the safety systems failed - and how the country could suffer 115 railway deaths in a single year.]]> As recent headlines have made clear, at least 115 people have been killed in two major high-speed train accidents in Spain in 2026 – so far.

Such events are, as many have said, inexplicable in a country such as Spain.

A double-tragedy of this magnitude, which resulted in the resignation of the country’s transport minister earlier this week, is likely to turn into a political blow to the PSOE-led government ahead of key snap elections. And polls suggest the opposition is set to win these elections.

Read more

Why Spain’s Left missed the chance to unite ahead of November’s snap election

The images of the 28 October high-speed collision near Urda, Toledo, which killed 69 people and injured around 200, have left the country in shock — again. People didn’t have time to recover from the images in January, when a high-speed train derailed near Córdoba, killing 46 people.

“It’s inexplicable. I don’t know whether I feel angrier or sadder about it,” my mum told me yesterday as we discussed the events, just a few minutes before the country’s transport minister, Oscar Puentes, announced his resignation (something very uncommon in the country I know best).

Once is an accident, twice is a pattern, goes the saying. 

And while this is far from a pattern, two fatal accidents of this scale in a year make last week’s crash even harder to understand, raising serious questions about protocol and maintenance, leaving aside accountability.

Spain has the largest high-speed rail network in Europe and the second-largest in the world, after China.

I admit I didn’t know this before, despite my nationality.

But I wonder whether a country like Spain can actually afford such infrastructure.

Critics have pointed to underinvestment, arguing that spending on maintenance has failed to keep pace with needs (as high-speed services have increased by 52 percent since 2019).

Spain is also still operating under its 2023 budget, which has been rolled over for three consecutive years and may have affected spending in areas such as transport.

The Spanish government, however, rejects these claims.

Read more

Spain’s 54-day sprint to the polls: can Sánchez’s housing gamble stop the far-right from entering into government?

The railway line (Madrid-Seville) where last week’s accident happened is undergoing a major modernisation plan, but it still mainly uses an older German safety system (LZB) dating back to 1992. 

When LZB is disrupted, trains rely on trackside signals and automatic braking systems to regulate traffic and stop trains passing red signals. In this case, all these safety measures failed.

The LZB is being replaced by ERTMS, a newer EU system designed to improve and standardise railway safety across Europe. 

But the €93.8m EU-funded contract to replace the system, awarded in 2021, that should have been completed by January 2026, still hasn’t been.

It is clear that railway safety cannot depend on a single technology. Safety systems are designed not to fail, and therefore are not expected to do so, but when they do, human control should step in.

]]> Afghan pushback survivor fights ‘impossible’ evidence rules in European courts with new UN case against Greece https://euobserver.com/246932/afghan-pushback-survivor-fights-impossible-evidence-rules-in-european-courts-with-new-un-case-against-greece/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 17:34:16 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246932 The EU's human rights court rejected a case from an Afghan pushback survivor who was just 15 years old when he was turned back to Turkey by the Hellenic coast guard. The impossibility of achieving justice on the systematic practice against migrants of all ages was highlighted by the European court's inadmission, as the young survivor was forced to appeal to the UN's human rights courts instead. ]]> The survivor of a brutal pushback in Greece was forced to take action at UN level, in a display of the impossibly high standard of evidence required in European courts to prevent victims of pushbacks from accessing justice.  

A Hazara teenager’s flight from Afghanistan in 2018 during an uptick in Taliban violence against the minority, ended in a rubber dinghy ride from Turkey to Samos, a Greek island. 

The 13 year-old had unsuccessfully attempted to obtain international protection in Iran, Turkey, and later in a refugee camp in Samos upon arriving in 2020, now aged 15. His requests to initiate an asylum procedure were ignored, and he was promptly hoisted onto a coast guard boat to Turkey. 

The boy was handcuffed to another young traveller, and both had their phones and money stolen by Greek coast guards. 

Despite providing photos, videos, locations shared in real time, Turkish Coast Guard and Frontex database records, the European Court of human rights (ECHR) rejected the case for lack of evidence in 2025. 

Now granted refugee status in Europe, the young man tried overcoming the maze of obstacles which have so far prevented anyone from successfully pursued legal action against a pushback on Friday (30 October), submitting a claim to the UN’s Human Rights Committee against Greece.

Read more

Von der Leyen’s State of the Union speech risks making border pushbacks ‘normal’ EU migration policy

The case represents an extraordinary mishandling of basic human rights, since pushback cases usually fail to see justice because there is usually no evidence of their arrival on European soil.

Yet here, the Afghan boy had made it all the way to the camp where they met asylum seekers that were known to them.

]]> Moldova seen as ‘best performer’ on EU-accession reforms, despite onslaught of Russian sabotage https://euobserver.com/246966/moldova-seen-as-best-performer-on-eu-accession-reforms-despite-onslaught-of-russian-sabotage/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 17:14:55 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246966 Chișinău's progress took place against a backdrop of growing hybrid attacks from Russia, such as drones entering the country’s airspace, cyberattacks, and Moldovan citizens recruited to perform sabotage.]]> The European Commission has held up Moldova as an example for other EU-aspirant states to follow, both in terms of internal reforms and resilience to Russian interference, while also praising Albania, Montenegro, and Ukraine.

Enlargement commissioner Marta Kos told press in Brussels, on Wednesday (4 November) that, out of the four frontrunners, Albania, Moldova, and Montenegro were “on track” for EU accession by 2030, despite anti-government riots in Tirana this year.

But she added that Moldova was “the best performer” showing “strong determination” to implement reforms.

Albania started EU accession talks in 2022, Montenegro in 2012, while Moldova and Ukraine began theirs in 2024.

The EU has long praised Kyiv for advancing reforms while at the same time fighting off Russia’s war machine.

But Chișinău’s progress also took place against a backdrop of growing hybrid attacks from Russia, such as drones entering the country’s airspace, cyberattacks, and Moldovan citizens recruited to perform sabotage.

It has also been forced to deal with disinformation campaigns originating from Moscow and the buying of an estimated 100,000 votes in its 2024 presidential elections in favour of an anti-EU candidate.

“For the first time, we have opponents who are interfering in our accession process,” said Kaja Kallas, the EU foreign affairs chief, speaking alongside Kos on Wednesday.

Moldova has collaborated with EU countries to push back against Russian interference and its experiences also helped “refine the EU’s toolbox for countering hybrid threats,” according to a commission progress report on its enlargement progress out on Wednesday.

But despite these efforts, hackers still gained access to citizens’ personal data from government databases on Tuesday (3 November).

The prime minister, Vasile Tofan, suspects the attack was run by a state actor.

Russian military forces have also controlled the Transnistria region in eastern Moldova since 1992, but this would “not become an obstacle” to the country’s EU admission, Kallas told Moldova’s prime minister in May.

Read more

[Interview] ‘It’s now or never’ for enlargement, Montenegro’s former EU ambassador warns

For its part, Ukraine also hopes to join the EU by 2028, but the commission said this was an “ambitious” target, given the size of the country.

Michael Gahler, a German centre-right MEP dealing with Ukraine, told EUobserver the 2028 was “achievable”, if “necessary reforms continue at pace”.

But he added that it was yet to open EU talks on integrating its massive agricultural sector into the single market, which would be “one of the most complex chapters in Ukraine’s accession negotiations.”

Meanwhile, accession talks with Georgia, Serbia, and Turkey had been de facto frozen due to democratic backsliding, the commission reports noted.

But in Serbia, where the opposition won parliamentary elections on 25 October, it was “time for a fresh start,” Kos said.

Talks with Bosnia and North Macedonia were also limping along due to internal political divisions in Sarajevo and North Macedonia’s bilateral dispute with Bulgaria over languages and history, with little sign of progress in either file.

When candidate countries wrap up their EU negotiations, each of the 27 member states still need to ratify their accession, in a final hurdle.

And in France, where anti-immigrant and anti-enlargement feeling was on the rise, this meant either a referendum or a three-fifths supermajority in a parliament vote.

]]> Russia fails in bid to reverse ban on its ships using Europe’s docks and locks https://euobserver.com/246925/russia-fails-in-bid-to-reverse-ban-on-its-ships-using-europes-docks-and-locks/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 16:55:06 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246925 Russian authorities challenged restrictive measures imposed by EU ministers against ships approved by the St Petersburg ship-certifying body. The EU's General Court rejected a bid to overturn the ban, but left the door open for future recognition of the authority.]]> An attempt by the Russian Maritime Register of Shipping to overturn an EU ban on its ships from docks and locks has failed.

The EU’s General Court’s ruling on Wednesday (4 November) means that sanctions barring Russian-certified ships from using maritime docks and canal locks will stay in place, for now.

But in a partial victory for the Russian authority, the Luxembourg-based court said a suspension of Russian Maritime Register of Shipping (RMRS) recognition would be more appropriate than withdrawal.

Sanctions agreed by ministers from EU member states had proposed a permanent measure against recognition of the body, but this was found to be too stringent.

According to the General Court, the RMRS has classified 4,207 ships of which 3,772 fly the flag of Russia.

The ship-certifying body approves ice-breakers, oil tankers, cargo ships and fishing vessels.

The ruling comes as Russia is suspected of being implicated in the cutting of cables near Svalbard, a Norwegian archipelago, and also in the Baltic sea.

And in October, reports emerged of Russian fishing trawlers hovering above vital infrastructure connecting Europe and the US.

Brussels is worried by the intensifying hybrid attacks across the European continent. These can come in the form of cyberattacks, spreading misinformation, or sending drones to attack grain shipments in the Black Sea.

]]> Energy tax and carbon emissions law on chopping block as EU Commission doubles down on ‘simplification’ drive https://euobserver.com/246919/energy-tax-and-carbon-emissions-law-on-chopping-block-as-eu-commission-doubles-down-on-simplification-drive/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 16:31:51 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246919 More than 30 laws will be mothballed or repealed, the EU Commission announced on Wednesday, as its deregulation agenda continues to gather pace.]]> Curbing energy prices, defence and cutting red tape as part of its so-called “simplification” are at the heart of a slimmed down 2027 work programme published by the EU Commission on Wednesday (4 November).  

Among the 23 policy initiatives to be put on the table is a promise to create a clean heat market mechanism which, the commission says, should ““support the deployment of heat pumps, reduce up-front costs for households and lower exposure to high fossil fuel prices.” 

Other proposals will include a housing simplification package to make it easier to build and renovate homes and reduce costs. 

The commission will create a European Corporation on Critical Raw Materials as part of the bloc’s efforts to reduce its reliance on China. 

On defence, however, the work programme warns that Europe’s ambition to be militarily ready by 2030 is “at risk” despite what it describes as “unprecedented decisions and funding.” 

“Our external borders, critical infrastructure and the values underpinning our ‘European way’ are increasingly coming under threat,” the paper says, citing hybrid threats as an example. 

The commission says that it will “explore the possibility” of establishing a European Security Council with the EU’s allies. 

But the agenda’s main focus is on scaling back existing regulation.

]]> Lame duck or angry duck? Europe’s leadership largely silent on Trump’s election disaster, fearing backlash https://euobserver.com/246872/lame-duck-or-angry-duck-europes-leadership-largely-silent-on-trumps-election-disaster-fearing-backlash/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 15:19:42 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246872 Sweeping US mid-term election wins by the Democrats have earned only muted or scattered responses and reactions from Europe's leadership.]]> Hours before the US election mid-results cemented Democrats as king-makers in Congress, Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelensky said Washington’s role on world affairs may be diminishing.

Zelensky then threw his weight behind Germany – and Europe as a whole – following years of chaotic foreign policy under Donald Trump.

“US voters have made their choice clear,” said Kaja Kallas, the EU’s foreign policy chief, later on Wednesday (4 November).

“I hope that the new Congress and the new Senate will continue supporting Ukraine and and also putting more pressure on Russia,” she told reporters in Brussels.

Democrats are likely to use their new-found powers over spending and hold hearings, but Congress won’t have much sway over Trump’s foreign policy instincts.

Read more

Trump likely to lash out in foreign policy if Democrats take Congress, warns ex-US ambassador to EU

The win is nevertheless a significant rebuttal of Trump’s MAGA coalition that has so far defined his presidency.

Democrats took 54 seats in the Senate (out of 100) and 228 in the House (out of 435). According to the New York Times, the Democrat congressional take-over is the largest for either party since 1976.

Trump had told voters ahead of the election to pretend he was on the ballot. Once the results were announced, he posted on Truth Social that he wasn’t on the ballot.

Trump is still pro-Putin, anti-EU, pro-tariffs, and is struggling to find an exit ramp on the Iran war that has embroiled his administration in a possible never-ending war.

]]> [Interview] ‘It’s now or never’ for enlargement, Montenegro’s former EU ambassador warns https://euobserver.com/246762/interview-its-now-or-never-for-enlargement-montenegros-former-eu-ambassador-warns/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 13:52:40 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246762 "With the Russian intervention in Ukraine, the geopolitical situation changed dramatically ... the EU understood they have to fortify 'their territory' in south-eastern Europe, and now you have, again, full energy [in the enlargement process]," Bojan Šarkić said.]]> If internal EU politics were to block Montenegro’s accession in 2028, it would risk killing Western Balkans enlargement and leaving a “black hole” in Europe, a veteran diplomat from Podgorica told EUobserver.

“I’m afraid it’s now or never,” said Bojan Šarkić, Montenegro’s former ambassador to the EU from 2016 to 2020.

“If it doesn’t happen, that would be a very bad signal to everyone in the region. The reaction would be: ‘Look at these Montenegrins. They did everything they were asked to do by the EU and what did they get? Nothing’,” he added.

“It would confirm what eurosceptics in the region have been saying – and there are quite a few of them. Just switch on Serbian TV, every day you hear: ‘The EU is falling apart. Look at the demonstrations in France’,” he said.

“And all this creates fertile soil for interference by other countries,” Šarkić said, referring to Russia.

The 67-year-old diplomat, who retired last year, spoke to EUobserver as the European Commission prepared to publish its annual reports on the 10 candidate countries in line to join the 27-nation bloc one day – the six Western Balkan states, Georgia, Moldova, Turkey, and Ukraine.

Šarkić began his diplomatic career in the former Yugoslavia in 1987, spent four years in Moscow in what was then the Soviet Union, before being sent to London and Brussels.

Croatia was the last country to join the EU, in 2013.

Following the EU’s migration crisis in 2015, enlargement appetite waned, while Turkey’s post-coup crackdown in 2016 saw its talks put on hold.

In the past two years, democratic backsliding in Georgia and Serbia also saw their talks frozen.

But at the same time, Russia’s full invasion of Ukraine in 2022 created a new geopolitical imperative to save the Western Balkans and post-Soviet states from becoming what Šarkić called a “black hole” of instability and Russian meddling in Europe.

The EU fast-tracked Moldova and Ukraine’s accession bids, while Armenia also peeled away from Russia and now aimed to formally apply for membership, in 2027 or 2028.

“In my time in Brussels, I had top politicians in the EU, in the Council, in the European Commission, telling me to forget about becoming a member of the EU in the forthcoming future,” said Šarkić.

“And while the EU was slow and lazy on enlargement, Russia was not lazy at all in trying to build its influence in the region,” he said.

]]> Roma ‘intimidation’ in Bulgarian presidentials as Iliana Iotova’s win raises alarm bells for press freedom https://euobserver.com/246567/roma-intimidation-in-bulgarian-presidentials-as-iliana-iotovas-win-raises-alarm-bells-for-press-freedom/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 12:28:43 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246567 Iliana Iotova's election win in Bulgaria's presidential run-off has analysts worried about her relationship with Russia and attitude towards democratic freedoms. She is expected to align with prime minister Rumen Radev.]]> Bulgaria’s Iliana Iotova’s presidential run-off win came after an election fraught with heavy policing of Roma voters and warning signs for the country’s media ecosystem.

Her victory in Sunday’s poll has strengthened Bulgaria’s pro-Russian stance, building on the success of Rumen Radev’s Progressive Bulgaria party in the April 2026 parliamentary elections, analysts say.

Bulgarian Socialist Party candidate Iotova won 57.6 percent of votes against pro-European independent Andrey Gyurov’s 39.5 percent in Bulgaria’s presidential election run-off.

She first became president in January when her predecessor Radev successfully ran for prime minister in a snap election.

Roma ‘intimidation’ amid low turn-out

Iotova won the Bulgarian presidency with the lowest number of votes of a presidential election winner in decades. 

“There are many voters who abstain from voting, because they don’t see any of the promises of Progressive Bulgaria being fulfilled,” Vesselin Zhelev, the foreign desk editor of media outlet Club Z, told EUobserver.

“Many Radev supporters have become disappointed that he didn’t do good on his promises to fight inflation or to take meaningful steps against corruption and oligarchy or for judicial reform,” he added. 

Read more

[Interview] Bulgaria’s presidential election becomes a test of Rumen Radev’s grip on power

And turnout among Roma people, an ethnic minority of up to 10 percent of Bulgaria’s population, also hit record lows amid reports of police intimidation of the community at polling stations.

Adela Militaru, programme director at the Barcelona-based political foundation Roma for Democracy, said candidates’ lack of an agenda for Roma people is “politically dumb”. As a result, she said, Roma voters have “unseen” abstention rates.

Militaru’s organisation described police being stationed outside polling stations in Roma neighbourhoods, and counted 175 to 180 police raids in voting locations during the first round of the presidential election.

The reports come amid a history of vote-buying in the country and antigypsyism across Europe.

Militaru said the police raids “intimidate voters” and “stigmatise the Roma rather than dismantling broker networks operating on the ground”.

She added that Bulgarian politicians have not made visible attempts to garner support from the Roma community: “The Roma vote can actually be won by anyone who wants to compete for it.”

“The current political offer remains extremely limited towards Roma voters. Future political offers should include housing and land, education and employment, support for Roma entrepreneurship, culture and identity,” Militaru also said.

‘Alarm bells’ raised for media

Iotova was a TV news chief before entering politics, serving a seven-year stint as a member of the European Parliament. Her vice-president Kiril Valchev is stepping down as head of the National Telegraph Agency.

Teodora Yovcheva, a political scholar at Sofia University, told EUobserver she is worried that ties between the government and media could be influencing press freedom.

]]> Listen: What is Europe’s military exercise in Poland really for? https://euobserver.com/246745/listen-what-is-europes-military-exercise-in-poland-really-for/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 09:19:56 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246745 A large-scale military exercise is about to begin in Poland, starting Monday, 9 October. The coalition of the willing is testing how their forces work together and sending a political message supporting Ukraine.]]>

Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

Find the full transcript below: 

A large-scale military exercise is about to begin in Poland, starting next week. It will last more than ten days and bring together 11 countries.

So what is this exercise really for? The exercise is an initiative of the “coalition of the willing”, a group of around thirty countries. This is not NATO and this is important. It’s a group of countries that have volunteered to act, outside of any binding framework.

Only eleven of them are taking part in the exercise because of time constraints. France is providing the bulk of the contingent, alongside the United Kingdom, Belgium and Poland, among others.

Read more

THIS WEEK: EU enlargement report tops Brussels agenda as ‘coalition of the willing’ faces Trump’s midterm test

So what will these 2,800 troops actually be doing for more than ten days? Its goal is to test, and to show, what Europeans are actually able to do as part of security guarantees for Ukraine.

Let’s maybe remember what we mean by “security guarantees”. These are the commitments some European countries are ready to make once the war is over, or at least after a genuine ceasefire, to make sure Ukraine is not invaded again.

Ukraine insists on this for a simple reason: the Minsk agreements of 2015, meant to bring peace to the Donbas, were never respected by Russia.

Back to the exercise. Troops will be testing command structures, logistics and, above all, coordination between air, naval and land forces. The ground exercise takes place in Poland, the aircraft are expected to fly in from Romania, and Turkey should lead a simulated maritime exercise.

According to Tom Bateman, the commander of this exercise, the aim is to show that this contingent can be deployed quickly. And of course, it’s also a signal to Kyiv: the volunteer countries are serious when they promise security guarantees.

Read more

[Interview] There are still more American soldiers than Western ones on Nato’s eastern border, says defence expert Robert Pszczel

But there is another message, aimed at Washington. The American contribution to these guarantees is, for now, completely uncertain, just like the US support for Ukraine’s war effort more broadly.

So Europeans are playing on two fronts. First, setting an example, and perhaps encouraging the Americans to join in, or at least to provide a safety net. And second, simply getting ready to manage without them. A full-scale exercise helps with that.

Now, is it already settled that Ukraine can count on European troops on its soil once the war is over? Yes and no. At the EU level, there are commitments in that regard, but the term “security guarantees” is broad and could cover different things: It could be men, but it could also be material support only. All of this is not clear.

France and the United Kingdom, however, have gone further. In a declaration of intent signed in January, they committed to sending forces to Ukraine if a peace deal is reached. Emmanuel Macron has even spoken of “several thousand soldiers”.

Read more

Russia faces a strategic crisis and record losses, but thanks to Trump it sees things positively (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,713)

But France is far from having unanimous support, whether within the EU or within NATO. And for good reason: European troops potentially facing Russian soldiers would risk opening a new conflict.

That’s why the ideas on the table always refer to preventive forces, deployed far from the front line.

Finally, as far as the peace negotiations are concerned, a trilateral meeting between Russia, Ukraine and the United States is planned next week in Abu Dhabi.

Ahead of that, an American delegation is in Brussels this week to prepare the ground with the Europeans, who are not part of the talks in Abu Dhabi.

Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky was in Berlin yesterday.
In his own words, it was about diplomatic coordination, strengthening Ukraine’s air defence and supporting its energy sector.

Let’s see whether this show of force in Poland is enough to make European guarantees credible, in Kyiv, in Moscow and in Washington.

]]> It’s not a coup: Tusk is right to reclaim Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal, but wrong in how he is doing it https://euobserver.com/246515/its-not-a-coup-tusk-is-right-to-reclaim-polands-constitutional-tribunal-but-wrong-in-how-he-does-it/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 06:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246515 Donald Tusk has a legal duty to rebuild Poland’s captured Constitutional Tribunal. But the government’s handling of the latest confrontation and its own appointments risks turning a victory for the rule of law into a political defeat, writes Alberto Alemanno.]]> Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal is at the centre of an unprecedented rule-of-law confrontation.

Last Friday (30 October), seven judges elected by parliament entered the court in a highly-contentious operation, escorted by the state protection service.

After more than six months of president Karol Nawrocki refusing to accept their oaths, one of them, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, announced she was assuming leadership of the tribunal.

Nawrocki cut short his official visit to Senegal and rushed back to Warsaw. Cameras filmed the scuffles at the entrance.

The images prompted two opposing interpretations: a legitimate effort to restore the rule of law, or a coup?

Whatever the images suggested, Friday’s operation was not a coup. It aimed to restore a lawful court, not to capture it.

Read more

[Explainer] Polish right turns court dispute into election battleground, dragging in the EU

Far-right seizes on spectacle

Yet the circumstances surrounding Friday’s intervention made that accusation easier to spread, as hard-right leaders from Marine Le Pen to Nigel Farage quickly showed.

The crisis began in December 2015, when Poland’s then-governing Law and Justice party (PiS) appointed three judges to seats that had already been filled.

What followed was a sustained effort to bring the country’s constitutional watchdog under political control. Its leadership became increasingly aligned with the political interests of the former ruling party, with its president, Julia Przyłębska, described as an ally of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński. Its rulings helped dismantle constitutional safeguards, most consequentially through its October 2020 decision restricting access to abortion.

European courts have also ruled on the Tribunal’s compromised composition and lack of independence.

Courts judge Tribunal

In December 2025, the European Union’s highest court ruled that Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal could not be considered an independent and impartial court established by law, citing irregularities in the appointment of some of its judges and its president.

The European Court of Human Rights had reached a similar conclusion in 2021. In May this year, it ordered Poland not to obstruct judges elected by parliament. The Council of Europe’s legal experts also made clear in October that the president cannot simply refuse to swear in judges chosen by the legislature.

On Saturday, the European Commission confirmed that the appointment of constitutional judges falls within parliament’s powers.

The law is clear: Poland must have an independent Constitutional Tribunal. By refusing to swear in judges elected by parliament, the country’s president is abusing his office to block their appointments and effectively claiming a veto power he does not have.

This constitutes a breach of – not a defence – of the rule of law. Yet the president’s obstruction does not give the government unlimited discretion in how it restores the tribunal. Its response must also comply with the law.

Friday’s operation raises legitimate questions.

No, EU backing for Morocco is conditional, and Spanish election will be pivotal https://euobserver.com/246595/is-the-western-sahara-now-friendless-no-eu-backing-for-morocco-is-conditional-and-spanish-election-will-be-pivotal/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246595 Spain's general election could be, in part, a referendum on the country's partnership with Morocco, with the opposition promising tougher border control measures and closer ties with Rabat's neighbour and enemy, Algeria.]]> The collapse of the United Nations peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara, after a 35 year mandate, is the latest diplomatic win for Morocco, but Rabat’s European support may prove to be less conclusive than it thinks. 

The end came at a UN Security Council last week, when the United States and Russia effectively cancelled each other out by vetoing rival resolutions on extending the mandate of the UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara. 

Russia vetoed a US-drafted resolution on Western Sahara at the Security Council on Friday (30 October), leaving the UN peacekeeping mission without a renewed mandate just a day before it expired. 

The US resolution would have extended the mission for another year but enshrining a plan to give Western Sahara limited autonomy under Morocco’s sovereignty as the only basis ‌for talks to settle the dispute that dates back to the end of Spanish colonialism in the 1970s. The US text also proposed to remove any reference to a referendum among the Sahrawi people on their future. 

The security council then rejected a rival Russian resolution to extend the mission for a year. France and the UK — the two other permanent Security Council members — along with eight non-permanent members, backed the US resolution. 

The end of the UN mission is undeniably better for Morocco than the Polisario Front, the political wing of the Sahrawi independence movement.

Thousands of protesters gathered in Prague, Brno and Ostrava demonstrations supported by media, students, theatres and more than 300 Czech athletes.

“An unprecedented day in the history of Czech public service media has begun”, said Michal Kubal, Czech Television’s news chief, at 00:00 on 3 November 2026 marking a start to an all-day strike by the broadcasting workers.

TV management had concluded a memorandum with the strike organisers under which media staff would provide essential news coverage in the event of extraordinary developments.

With wildfires growing bigger and more often due to climate change, there needs to be more professional firefighters, with modern equipment, to face them, argues the European Federation of Public Service Unions (EPSU), who organised the protest together with various Belgian workers’ organisations.

As of 7 October, 692 419 hectares burnt in wildfires across the EU this year – an area almost as big as the Greek island of Crete – burning some 30 million tonnes of CO2. Southern countries, Portugal, Greece, Italy, and Spain, suffered most. According to the World Health Organisation, wildfires in Europe have increased by 57 percent since 2022.

Read more

Europe’s summer of wildfires puts spotlight on economic cost of climate inaction

On average, wildfires cause some €2.5bn losses across the EU each year.

The protest gathered in front of a conference on civil protection organised by the EU Commission, where crisis management commissioner Hadja Lahbib presented new guidelines on what citizens should prepare for the first days of an emergency.

The firefighters and unions were there to protest the cuts to the next EU budget for disaster management: from over €10bn requested by the commission to just under €7bn proposed by the Irish presidency last month. Yet that would still be double what the 2021-2027 budget had room for.

“I believe that the risk is getting bigger. So yes, it’s necessary to also increase the support,” Tiago da Cunha, president of a municipality in northern Portugal, where the most summer wildfires hit in 2026, told EUobserver.

Read more

Europe’s 2026 wildfires show the cost of ignoring prevention

Stalo Yostili, 43, has been a firefighter in Cyprus for a decade. She said her country does not recognise how dangerous the profession is. She complained of too few staff, which means for an operation that would normally need 15 firefighters, only six are sent, making it more potentially dangerous.

Profession-specific healthcare is also a big topic, Ireneusz Kierzkowski from the Polish firefighter union, told EUobserver. Retired firefighters often have PTSD, and they also develop cancers more often.

Al Munasseq, meaning ‘The Coordinator’ in Arabic, is an app launched by Israel’s Coordination of Government Activities in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (COGAT) unit in 2019 to manage the movement of Palestinians for work, healthcare, prayer, and everyday tasks.

A report published on Tuesday (3 November) by global consumer group Ekō found Microsoft to be hosting key components of Al Munasseq in data centres in Ireland, effectively enabling what is feared to be mass surveillance.

A cancer patient who needs radiotherapy in Jerusalem, a worker who needs to feed his family, a daughter who wants to sit beside her mother in hospital – all of them must ask Israel’s military for a permit to move across their own stolen land, and that permission runs through the Al Munasseq app,” said Ekō senior campaign director, Rewan Al-Haddad.

This is inspirational.]]> The ink had hardly dried under articles explaining lessons learned from Péter Magyar’s electoral overthrow of Hungary’s government, when Serbia’s Student List managed to overthrow the semi-authoritarian Aleksandar Vučić.

    Both cases had similarities: long-standing rulers that lied and flaunted their corruption ever more openly; they were ripe for defeat.

    In both cases the opposition avoided strongly partisan positioning and instead focused on state functioning and anti-corruption. 

    Intriguingly, they had almost identical results: 53 percent of the vote for the opposition, 39 percent for the incumbent party. In both cases the opposition showed unity and campaigned across the country and on social media; a well-known ingredient of any campaign to overthrow entrenched authoritarians. 

    Read more

    Serbia’s student protestors win parliamentary majority – setting scene for showdown with Vučić in December’s presidential poll

    In other ways the two cases are strikingly different.

    The Hungarian campaign was focused on Magyar, a consummate politician and former Fidesz member, who knew the incumbent party from the inside.

    In Serbia a collective of students from different universities turned massive mobilisation against the corrupt government into an electoral platform. 

    In Hungary, Magyar dominated his party, in Serbia, the student collective reached decisions democratically, voting on all major points; an extreme contrast between a one-man show and a movement that hardly had any individual faces. 

    What can we learn from these elections?

    First, we should not get fixated on silver bullets. One success story does not mean that the same recipe works elsewhere. Social movements and electoral campaigns are highly complex and contingent on circumstances. No leader like Magyar appeared in Serbia, no massive student initiative developed in Hungary, although both had similar problems of political repression by the ruling party.

Search-and-rescue ships have been hampered by legal hurdles and funding cuts, while the central Mediterranean has become a grave for tens of thousands of people.]]> Search-and-rescue NGO efforts to conduct life-saving work in the Mediterranean face continuous derailment by European authorities hoping to stop migrants reaching EU soil – and drowning thousands in the process.

    Since Friedrich Merz took over as German chancellor in May 2025, all funding to national search-and-rescue organisations has stopped. 

    The conservative leader has faced accusations from other EU leaders that the German NGO vessels prevalent across the central Mediterranean’s deadly zone of migrant crossings have acted as a ‘pull factor’, attracting migration to the EU. 

    Current foreign affairs minister Johann Wadephul went so far as to allege that sea rescue organisations are “enabling people-smuggling gangs to carry out their business” in 2023.

    “Of course we know that people don’t travel into the Mediterranean because there are NGOs [there]. They are escaping famine, conflict, violence, some people are even trapped in Libya,” said Sofia [the charity’s workers use first names only], communications coordinator on board German charity SOS Humanity’s mothership.

    Read more

    How the rescue of 28 people from a makeshift dinghy in a stormy Mediterranean unfolded – exposing the lethal reality of EU border policy

    After rescuing 28 people adrift in an overcrowded dinghy last week, the humanitarian NGO has now in total rescued 5,213 people since August 2022. A third of those were children. 

    SOS Humanity were part of a former funding pool that split an annual €2m from Germany’s federal budget for humanitarian aid between search-and-rescue organisations. Despite growing fuel costs, and increasing legal costs from administrative barriers and port detentions by the Italian government, search-and-rescue groups are now dealing with an astronomical gap in their budget. 

    This has also been compounded since Giorgia Meloni’s far-right Italian government came into power in 2022. 

    Rescue charities operating in the central Mediterranean have subsequently been subject to decree 1/2023, requiring them to navigate directly towards the assigned port of safety following a rescue at sea – in other words, preventing more than one rescue operation at a time.

    ]]>         When adults take over youth protests, EU children’s own demands vanish https://euobserver.com/246292/when-adults-take-over-youth-protests-eu-childrens-own-demands-vanish/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 12:25:18 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=246292 As youth protests spread from France to Belgium, Spain, Italy, Greece and Albania, Europe is confronting a stark test of whether under‑18s are treated as political actors in their own right, or merely as props in adult power struggles.]]> France’s lycée students have taken to the streets over shortages of teachers, crumbling buildings, and inequalities that determine educational opportunities and university admissions.

    Yet, as political parties and trade unions joined the protests and students found themselves confronted by riot police, the debate shifted from their demands to their inability to act for themselves.

    In France, adultism has deep roots, reflected in negative stereotypes of young people, their gradual exclusion from public spaces, and the persistent assumption that children are politically innocent and therefore easily manipulated by adults.

    Here lies a democratic paradox: children are expected to develop into politically responsible citizens, but when they start behaving like them, their political agency suddenly becomes questionable.

    Lost in this debate, however, is the fact that students are making political claims of their own, challenging not only their school conditions, but also the political decisions and budgetary priorities that perpetuate these inequalities and jeopardise their future.

    Read more

    Generation Z in France, Spain and Albania is trapped: study hard, stay poor, live with your parents. No wonder they’re protesting

    A right to speak, but who will listen?

    Beyond the political controversy, children are already political citizens, even without voting rights.

    The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, ratified by every state except the United States, guarantees freedoms of expression, association and peaceful assembly, and requires children’s views to be given due weight in matters affecting them.

    The EU and France also have legal provisions recognising children’s participation rights, including in educational governance.

    However, political citizenship extends beyond a formal legal status to participation in public life, where children can actively exercise political agency through expression, collective action, and political claims.

    Their exclusion from electoral politics does not diminish their political legitimacy, nor relieve states of their obligation to take their voices seriously.

    But can blockades and protests bring about the change children demand? Faced with  hundreds of thousands of demonstrators taking to the streets across France in support of students, the French government appears to have rediscovered the virtues of listening to children, launching consultations and promising stronger student representation, more teachers, and funding for school renovations.

    Student representatives welcomed some of these commitments, but insisted on seeing actual renovations and additional teachers in classrooms.

    With the 2027 presidential election approaching in France, these commitments risk becoming entangled in campaigning, and potentially overshadowing children’s demands with competing political agendas.

    The question is what will come of the promises; and just as importantly, who will be held accountable, and how, if those promises are never delivered?

    Read more

    Europe’s youth asked for hope – but politicians just offer fear and hate

    Adults arrive, children disappear?

    The growing involvement of adults (teachers, parents, unions) in the protests also fuelled accusations of political instrumentalisation: the government was quick to accuse left-wing La France Insoumise (LFI) of manipulating the children.

    If there was any adult interference, it deserves scrutiny, but assuming that children must be manipulated whenever they organise politically is mere adultism disguised as paternalistic concern. 

    Concerns over the criminalisation of children’s protests have also grown. While incidents of vandalism and violence overshadowed students’ demands, the crackdown was striking: by 14 October, 6,773 minors had been taken into custody, with 2,190 of them facing prosecution.

    Children are apparently mature enough to face legal consequences, even as their political competence is questioned.

    Meanwhile, investigations into police violence against minors raise questions about the state’s duty to protect them.

    As the riots of 17 October erupted into violence and chaos, students’ demands seemed to have faded from sight amid an increasingly heated debate over public order and wider social and political tensions.

    Meanwhile, protests by young people have also taken place elsewhere in Europe, in Belgium, Spain, Italy, Greece, and Albania.

    Although grievances and political circumstances differ, these protests reveal an important distinction between schoolchildren and university students as political citizens.

    Most university students can vote, allowing them to turn collective mobilisation into electoral pressure, as Serbia’s student-backed movement showed when it won the parliamentary election on 25 October.

    But most secondary-school pupils have no equivalent leverage: their political citizenship depends on adults and institutions taking their demands seriously, without constantly calculating how many votes they could win or lose. 

    Beyond the diverse political interpretations of these protests lies another important question: what will children themselves take away from these experiences, and how might these impact their political citizenship?

    They may seek greater influence through consultations, intensify protests or create alternative forms of participation.

    But if their demands continue to fall on deaf ears, while protesting exposes them to the threat of police repression and to adultism, disillusionment may instead drive some away from political participation altogether.

    The promise of children’s rights to be heard was certainly more ambitious than that.

      <title>US stocks rise, dollar slides as investors digest Democrats’ midterm victories</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/04/us-dollar-slides-democrats-midterm-election-win-growth-fears</link>
      <description><p>Government bond yields fall while initial fears ease over impact of election results on world’s biggest economy</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2026/nov/04/midterm-elections-results-senate-house-michigan-maine-mississippi-latest-updates">US midterm elections – live updates</a></p></li><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/04/explainer-midterms-trump-us-global-economy-markets">After US midterms, what will lame-duck Trump mean for global economy?</a></p></li></ul><p>US stocks have surged as investors digest the Democrats’ victories in the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/us-midterm-elections-2026">midterm elections</a>, lifted by hopes that <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s turbulent policymaking would be restrained and shaking off initial fears about the impact on growth in the world’s largest economy.</p><p>The Dow Jones rose close to 3%, its best day in over a year, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq and the benchmark S&amp;P 500 gained about 1.5% each when markets closed on Wednesday afternoon, turning around overnight falls in US stock futures after the news that the Democratic party <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2026/nov/03/midterm-election-results-live-updates">won control</a> of the Senate and the House of Representatives.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/04/us-dollar-slides-democrats-midterm-election-win-growth-fears">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/04/trump-blames-fox-news-republican-losses</link>
      <description><p>Fox News pundits hardly criticized the US president in midterms coverage but Trump was still quick to cast blame</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2026/nov/05/midterm-elections-live-latest-updates-mississippi-senate-race">US midterms 2026 live – latest updates</a></p></li><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2026/nov/03/midterm-elections-full-results-senate-house-governor-races">Track live results from all 50 states</a></p></li><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/04/midterm-election-results-question-answer">Tell us: what do you want to know about the midterm election results?</a></p></li></ul><p>In the weeks leading up to Tuesday’s midterm elections, <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/28/trump-fox-news-truth-social">Donald Trump made clear that he would place some blame on his favorite cable channel</a>, Fox News, if his party did poorly.</p><p>On election day, he didn’t disappoint.</p><p>This article was amended on 4 November 2026; a previous version incorrectly stated that Karoline Leavitt is Donald Trump’s most recent press secretary, when it is in fact Katie Zacharia.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/04/trump-blames-fox-news-republican-losses">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>CVS Health to split pharmacy chain from health insurance</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/04/cvs-health-pharmacy-insurance</link>
      <description><p>CVS Pharmacy will be separate from CVS Health, housing major insurer Aetna and benefits manager Caremark</p><p>CVS Health, the largest US healthcare conglomerate valued at $117bn, has announced its plans split off its pharmacy chain from its <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/money/healthinsurance">health insurance</a> and benefits businesses, ending an era in which healthcare companies grew into vast conglomerates.</p><p>In their announcement on Wednesday, CVS Health said they will split off its 9,000 pharmacies, in-store clinics and mail order prescription business into a business named CVS Pharmacy.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/04/cvs-health-pharmacy-insurance">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Brent crude drops by more than 6% to $105.55 a barrel, the lowest level in more than two weeks</p><p>The oil price has fallen to its lowest level in more two weeks amid new hopes of a breakthrough to end the Iran war.</p><p>Brent crude, the international benchmark, dropped by more than 6.5% to as low as $105.55 a barrel on Monday, the lowest since 16 October, sending shares in airline companies higher and pushing down government borrowing costs.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/02/oil-price-falls-amid-hope-of-a-breakthrough-to-end-iran-war">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/01/us-china-trade-war-trump-xi</link>
      <description><p>A truce has cooled the trade conflict, but neither country has done anything to limit the outbreak of new hostilities</p><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s trade wars have largely fallen off the headlines. Fears of new tariffs flare up from time to time when the US president goes off the rails – for instance, threatening to end US trade with countries with which it has a deficit unless the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/federal-reserve">Federal Reserve</a> cuts interest rates. But the sense that the world’s two largest economies are plowing ahead into an overt economic conflagration has taken a back seat to other, more salient fears, about Trump ending American democracy, AI killing us all and stuff like that.</p><p>The sense of calm is misleading. Under the radar, the world is marching toward an economic war of potentially epic proportions, one that, history suggests, could well spill over into the real thing.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/01/us-china-trade-war-trump-xi">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Chains in seven countries say cooling unit temperatures rose overnight in incident similar to hack of French shops</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/02/europe-supermarket-fridges-freezers-who-hacking-why">Who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why?</a></p></li></ul><p>Supermarket chains in at least seven European countries have said the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in some of their shops soared overnight to as high as 50C (122F), echoing a cyber-attack last month that caused millions of euros of damage in France.</p><p>Retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems on Monday, and several companies confirmed they had been hacked.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/02/supermarket-freezers-across-europe-hit-by-second-suspected-cyber-attack">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>The survival of American democracy depends on taxing billionaires</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/27/democracy-tax-billionaires</link>
      <description><p>It is essential not just to fund the public goods the nation needs, it is indispensable to restore a sense of fairness</p><p>Money doesn’t buy happiness, we’re told. Even some economists agree. The Nobel prize-winning economists Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton once <a href="https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.1011492107">proposed that</a> rising income increased people’s emotional wellbeing only up to a ceiling of about $115,000 in today’s money.</p><p>They probably hadn’t met many billionaires. The ultra-rich may not pursue happiness in the joyful sense of the word. But they will try every trick in the book to hang on to their stash and woe betide the tax authority that tries to lay a finger on their treasure.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/27/democracy-tax-billionaires">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comThu, 05 Nov 2026 08:58:56 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Diageo posts unexpected rise in organic net sales]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/05/diageo-posts-unexpected-rise-in-organic-net-sales/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/05/diageo-posts-unexpected-rise-in-organic-net-sales/Thu, 05 Nov 2026 08:22:20 +0000Guinness maker Diageo posted an ‌unexpected rise in quarterly organic net sales ​after a slower-than-expected decline in its key North America market.

Guinness sales were weaker in Ireland and Great Britain during the quarter, with the company attributing the single-digit decline to hotter weather.

Chief executive ​Dave Lewis called the first-quarter results ⁠a small step in the ‌right ‌direction.

The ​drinks company, which also makes Johnnie Walker whisky, ⁠posted organic ​net sales growth ​of 0.6 per cent for the ‌three months ended September ​30th, compared with a 0.4 per cent ⁠decline expected ⁠by ​analysts in a company-compiled poll.

Organic net sales declined 3.6 per cent in North America, its largest market, compared with a 6.7 per cent drop expected ‌by analysts.

The group said organic net sales in its Europe, Middle East and Africa rose 2.4 per cent, with volumes up 4.4 per cent. Pricing was down 2 per cent on targeted price repositioning.

Growth in the region was led by Turkey, Africa and the Middle East, offsetting weakness in Italy and France.

Spirits and the ready-to-drink products were key drivers of growth. Johnnie Walker saw double-digit growth, while Baileys achieved mid-single-digit growth. That offset weakness in the Smirnoff and Tanqueray brands.

The beer sector, meanwhile, achieved low-single-digit growth, with Guinness growth in Africa and some central European countries offsetting a decline in Britain and Ireland sparked by hotter weather and increased competition.

The ⁠world’s largest spirits maker kept its organic net ‌sales outlook broadly flat for the year.

Lewis said making the company’s offer more competitive remained Diageo’s biggest challenge but clear actions were underway.

“Whilst the market remains challenging, and volatility continues given the geopolitical uncertainty and impact of the ongoing conflict in the Middle East on energy, supply and distribution, results in the first quarter represent a small step in the right direction,” he said.

Lewis, who took over at the start of the year, has been implementing a turnaround plan for the drinks group, aiming to save about $1 billion. That includes cutting jobs, with Diageo’s annual report in August showing the company already had 2,000 fewer staff than the previous year. - Additional reporting: Reuters

]]>Liam McBurney<![CDATA[After the SuperValu cyberattack, might your smart fridge be the next target? ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/11/04/after-the-supervalu-cyberattack-might-your-smart-fridge-be-the-next-target/https://www.irishtimes.com/technology/2026/11/04/after-the-supervalu-cyberattack-might-your-smart-fridge-be-the-next-target/Wed, 04 Nov 2026 12:41:50 +0000Do you feel differently about your smart fridge?

The high-tech home hub allows you to check what food you have in, suggest recipes, and manage the family calendar, should you be able to afford its not-insignificant price tag.

But this week’s cyberattack on Supervalu’s refrigeration systems might be forcing people to re-evaluate its position in their home.

Where could the next attack come from?

You might equally be eyeing your connected coffeemaker warily, worried about what it could be getting up to behind your back. You might consider unplugging the robot vacuum cleaner in case it goes rogue while you are out on the school run.

Jokes aside, the recent spate of attacks on seemingly harmless systems should give us pause for thought. The problem with many of these connected devices is that as soon as you hook anything up to the internet, it opens up a chink in your armour , no matter how hard we try to lock it down.

It is a trade-off that we might not be aware we are making at the time – but it is a common thread in the modern world. For the sake of convenience, we give up a little security. Even with the most diligent company in charge of maintaining the security of the appliances, there is always a risk that something will go wrong. And with the growth in artificial intelligence (AI), the chance of a previously undetected vulnerability rearing its head has suddenly been magnified.

You might wonder why hackers would want to attack a smart home device in the suburbs of Dublin. While we may not have thousands of euro of stock to destroy, or disposable income to pay out ransoms, we do have something that is valuable: our data. And that, as we know, is worth a lot of money in the right – or wrong – hands.

There is also the chance that our smart home devices, unpatched and open to exploitation, may be used as part of an attack on a high-value target.

Stop the bots: Six key steps to securing your smart home

In recent days, a joint operation between public and private partners in the tech industry took down a global botnet that had been hidden in set-top boxes across 200 countries. The botnet, which was placed on the devices before they were sold, surreptitiously used the set-top boxes and internet connections of those unlucky enough to have installed them in their homes.

This is not a new threat. Botnets have been carrying out large-scale attacks for years. One example: in 2016, the Mirai botnet took over up to 560,000 unsecured or weak cameras, printers, and DVR players and knocked out Twitter, Reddit, and Netflix, among others.

So what can we do to protect ourselves? Besides cutting off the connection, that is, although you could argue there is no compelling need to have an oven or coffee maker with an internet connection.

There is some help on the way from the bureaucrats, with various rules regarding security being implemented at an EU level, forcing manufacturers to adopt a secure-by-design approach. But we can’t rely on them to fully shield us from all the risks.

There are ways to protect ourselves: keeping up to date with software releases to patch up any security holes is a given;buying reputable brands rather than settling for cheap, unbranded technology from online marketplaces is another. Changing the default passwords on devices is another tip from security experts.

But we need to be aware of what could be coming down the line.

Anthropic recently warned of another threat: that AI models are becoming so smart and small in terms of storage requirements that they could copy themselves into places you might not suspect – such as your smart fridge.

That could create an army of smart botnets that could, in theory, be commanded to launch attacks without needing a data centre to run from. And, the experts argue, that would be one that is very difficult to battle, because there is no centralised point from where the attack has been launched.

Of course it is never as simple as it looks. The scenario proposed by Anthropic was a test rather than a real-world incident, and the end result – a model that replicates itself – is more of a ‘could’ than a ‘did’. The model didn’t have to break in as such, although we are often so lax about security on these connected devices that it wouldn’t have presented a huge barrier if that had been the case.

There are a few lessons to learn here.

Take the claims of AI companies about the power and potential of their technology with a grain of salt, for both good and bad.

But perhaps, to be safe, you might also consider limiting smart technology to the essentials. Sometimes the trade-off just isn’t worth it.

]]><![CDATA[Retirement saving cost almost doubles with each decade of delay, Goodbody says]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/05/retirement-saving-cost-almost-doubles-with-each-decade-of-delay-goodbody-says/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/05/retirement-saving-cost-almost-doubles-with-each-decade-of-delay-goodbody-says/Thu, 05 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000The cost of saving for retirement rises by more than 80 per cent with each decade a person waits to start contributing to their pension fund, new analysis from wealth management firm Goodbody indicates.

Beginning to invest in a pension fund at age 56 requires a monthly contribution nearly 10 times higher than starting at age 26 to reach the exact same target, according to Goodbody’s analysis, highlighting “how quickly the cost of delay builds”.

In order to accrue a retirement fund of €1,225,000, or €50,000 for nearly 25 years, a person beginning to invest at age 26 would require a €799 monthly contribution to the fund, Goodbody found.

However, this contribution rises to €1,466 and €2,968 every month if the person starts investing aged 36 and 46, respectively – an 83 and 271 per cent increase from beginning one or two decades beforehand.

Beginning to invest for a €50,000 annual pension payment at age 56 requires a €7,865 monthly contribution – a near-tenfold increase from having started saving aged 26, Goodbody found.

Michelle O’Keefe, head of wealth advisory at Goodbody, said: “Every decade brings new priorities, but a later start isn’t a reason to switch off. This is a reminder that it’s never too late to start, and that every year you act makes the goal easier to reach.”

Alongside its cost-of-retirement analysis, Goodbody commissioned research into the saving practices and sentiments of women in Ireland.

The research, conducted by Red C in September,is based on a survey of more than 600 women. It was published nearly a month after the official announcement of the personal investment account scheme in Budget 2027.

Accounts in the scheme are to become publicly available from July 1st next year, and “could transform investing in Ireland by making it simpler and more accessible, helping people to take that first step” in investing, Goodbody said.

Pension or the new investment account: where should your spare cash go?

Up to 77 per cent of women in their 20s reported an interest in investing “but do not know where to start”, according to the financial services firm, with 68 per cent of women in their 30s finding themselves equally in the dark on the topic.

Pointing to “a gap between intention and action”, Goodbody said financial advice can solve the issue. “Among women who had received professional advice, 68 per cent said they felt more reassured about their financial future”, with 83 per cent of women in their 50s who have done so agreeing as well.

Up to 56 per cent of women in their 40s, and 61 per cent of those in their 50s, pointed to “a realistic retirement plan” as an area of financial support they were lacking, although women in their 60s “show the strongest discipline of any age group surveyed”.

Goodbody found 75 per cent felt as though they “successfully stick to their financial goals” and 76 per cent “feel confident managing their own personal finances independently”, although only 46 per cent are confident in “assessing investment risks and potential returns”.

]]><![CDATA[Oil extends slide amid heightened hopes of end to Iran war]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/11/05/oil-extends-slide-amid-heightened-hopes-of-end-to-iran-war/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/11/05/oil-extends-slide-amid-heightened-hopes-of-end-to-iran-war/Thu, 05 Nov 2026 06:36:36 +0000Brent oil pushed lower after tumbling more than 8 per cent in the previous session as investors bet that a Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections could accelerate efforts to end the war in the Middle East.

The global benchmark traded near $94 a barrel, while West Texas Intermediate was around $87 after its biggest loss since May on Wednesday. Vice president JD Vance said voter frustration over the war and the US-Israel relationship doomed Republicans in the elections. Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer, a Democrat, pledged to end the conflict, now in its ninth month.

Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the midterms, dealing a major setback to US president Donald Trump and his Republican Party. The sweep gives them greater leverage over government spending, potentially constraining the administration’s ability to prosecute the Iran conflict.

Brent rallied to a six-month high in October as Trump threatened renewed strikes on Iran after the midterms. While polls were still open, Trump told the Financial Times that he had no immediate plans to ramp up attacks, and later conceded that it’s “largely true” Republicans lost because of the war.

Despite the conflict, there has been a revival of crude exports from the Persian Gulf, putting pressure on Middle East prices, although shipments of oil products remain constrained. Those disruptions, along with escalating Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, have helped drive gasoline and diesel prices higher.

“Larger crude oil exports out of the Middle East along with President Trump stating he has no immediate plans to strike Iran are keeping the pressure on crude oil prices for now,” said Dennis Kissler, senior vice president for trading at BOK Financial Securities. “Democratic control of Congress could also tighten US military spending” and bring an end to the war sooner, he added.

The election outcome and Trump’s restraint on further attacks against Iran reverberated across energy markets on Wednesday. North Sea crude prices slumped to fresh lows, while European natural gas tumbled.

Still, tightness persists in fuel markets. In the US, stockpiles of distillates — a category that includes diesel — dropped below 100 million barrels last week, the lowest level since 2003, according to government data. Nationwide crude inventories fell for a fifth week. - Bloomberg
