]]>Aidan Crawley<![CDATA[Why are the chief executives of Ireland’s big banks so coy about their strong growth?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/05/why-are-the-ceos-of-irelands-big-banks-so-coy-about-their-strong-growth/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/05/why-are-the-ceos-of-irelands-big-banks-so-coy-about-their-strong-growth/Thu, 05 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000Irish bank bosses don’t really engage in colourfully worded or gleeful commentary.

In the past week, Ireland’s three main banks each posted strong results, but their chief executives kept it coy.

AIB boss Colin Hunt said the bank notched up “another strong quarter”, which is probably an understatement given new lending rose by 17 per cent.

Bank of Ireland chief Myles O’Grady noted that it has “real momentum” after it again upgraded key financial targets, while PTSB boss Eamonn Crowley said its results reflected “strong momentum”.

Before the global financial crisis, Ireland had around a dozen banks. Between institutions collapsing and some consolidation, the country has been left with three main retail banks. Threatening to break their hold are a number of neobanks, seeking to challenge the status quo.

Monzo launched in Ireland in April with 100,000 on its waiting list. Revolut, with 3.4 million customers in Ireland, has made the biggest impression, while Bunq recently said its Irish saver numbers grew 74 per cent in 2025.

Zippay is the pillar banks’ answer to the convenient person-to-person mobile payments offered by the likes of Revolut, but is that enough to stave off rivals broadening their own offerings?

Avant Money has become an established mortgage challenger, offering competitive fixed and variable rates. Revolut is working on a mortgage product, although it has missed launch expectations and offered no firm timetable.

PTSB may itself pose a greater threat to AIB and Bank of Ireland if Austrian financial group Bawag’s €1.6 billion takeover deal, which is still subject to a court challenge, goes through.

PTSB income rises 7% as loan book grows ahead of Bawag sale

AIB and Bank of Ireland still have formidable advantages. Based on a recent consumer survey commissioned by the Department of Finance, AIB is the dominant banking provider, with 39 per cent using it as their main current account, followed by Bank of Ireland at 34 per cent. PTSB is a distant third at 13 per cent.

A not-so-dark horse, familiar to many, that may also pose a threat to the banks’ hold on the mortgage market is the credit union. In September, their mortgage lending topped €1 billion for the first time, according to the Irish League of Credit Unions.

Some customers may be more trusting of their local, bricks-and-mortar credit union as an alternative lender.

Hunt, O’Grady and Crowley are probably right to stick to their coy commentary. The good times won’t last forever.

]]>Paul Scott<![CDATA[Sales of second-hand homes fall as rate hikes weigh on demand]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/05/sales-of-second-hand-homes-fall-as-rate-hikes-weigh-on-demand/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/05/sales-of-second-hand-homes-fall-as-rate-hikes-weigh-on-demand/Thu, 05 Nov 2026 06:00:01 +0000Sales of existing homes fell by 2.2 per cent in the third quarter as higher mortgage costs and stretched affordability weighed on demand, according to property tech firm Geowox.

The group’s latest report on the property market also found that homebuyers are now paying a premium of close to €100,000 for more energy-efficient properties.

There were 14,787 homes sold (3,432 of them new) between July and the end of September this year, the report, which mines data from the State’s property price register said.

Total sales were up 0.3 per cent compared with the third quarter last year, driven by sales of new homes which rose by 9.4 per cent.

Sales of existing homes, which represent most of the market, were, however, down by 2.2 per cent.

This comes in the wake of two interest rate hikes from the European Central Bank (ECB) which have squeezed borrowing costs.

The surge in inflation and wider geopolitical uncertainty are also said to be weighing on demand.

The median or middle price paid for a home in the Republic in the third quarter was €406,000, up 5.2 per cent on the same quarter of 2025.

In Dublin, the median price was €550,000 (up 1.3 per cent). The median price paid for an apartment in the capital was €407,000 (up 2.8 per cent).

Outside Dublin, the median price was €360,000, up 5.6 per cent.

Among main towns with at least 30 sales, Dublin city and suburbs (€570,000) and Naas (€518,000) had the highest median house prices while Wexford was the most affordable at €270,000.

In Dublin, Dublin 6 (€815,000), Dublin 14 (€790,000) and Dublin 4 (€750,000) were the most expensive postcodes, and Dublin 10 the most affordable at €339,000.

Comparing the same kinds of home in the same areas a year apart, prices (nationally) were up 4.9 per cent. This compares to like-for-like growth of 7.2 per cent in the third quarter last year.

The report also found that homebuyers paid on average 26 per cent more for energy-efficient homes.

The median sales price achieved for homes with a top Ber (building energy rating) of between A and B was €466,000.

This represented a €96,000 or 25.9 per cent premium over the €370,000 paid for homes rated C-G. The comparison leaves out new homes.

Geowox’s report comes as one of Ireland’s biggest home builders, Cairn Homes, said Ireland had “little chance” of scaling up the State’s annual housing supply to 60,000 units, the target level, unless half of all units built each year are apartments.

Apartment schemes face the most planning difficulties.

The Government’s housing plan has a goal of 300,000 home completions by the end of 2030.

Meeting this target would require completions to rise from around 36,000 last year to 50,000-60,000 annually.

On the supply side, recent market data has underlined the acute shortage of second-hand homes for sale.

The situation for buyers at the more affordable end of the market is even tighter, according to estate agent Sherry Fitzgerald, with the number of homes available below €350,000 falling almost 10 per cent year-on-year to 5,676 entering the second half of 2026.

]]>Teamjackson<![CDATA[The pitfalls of hybrid working when managers are left on their own to deal with staff]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/05/the-pitfalls-of-hybrid-working-when-managers-are-left-on-their-own-to-deal-with-staff/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/05/the-pitfalls-of-hybrid-working-when-managers-are-left-on-their-own-to-deal-with-staff/Thu, 05 Nov 2026 05:49:00 +0000

Break-up songs like Prince’s Nothing Compares 2 U (a smash for Sinéad O’Connor), Dolly Parton’s I Will Always Love You (ditto Whitney Houston) and Miley Cyrus’s Flowers have long been popular culture staples. But who knew that breaking up with full-time office work would be so agonising for business culture – and especially for the line managers left to negotiate the wreckage?

Workplace tension continues between leaders who demand a return to the office and workers who want flexibility to help defray the cost of living, and to better cope with commuting times and care commitments.

The whole debate about whether or not hybrid, or remote, is actually workable, is the wrong question to ask, says Tatiana Andreeva, professor in organisational behaviour at Trinity Business School, who studies hybrid work and collaboration.

Instead, how can employers embrace hybrid in a way that creates sustainable value for the business, employees and society?

More than a third of the labour force now works either a hybrid arrangement or a fully remote one – accounting for an estimated 530,000 people – according to a forthcoming report from the National Economic and Social Council.

In 2026, about 35 per cent of the labour force worked from home either usually or sometimes, whereas before the Covid-19 pandemic, only about 14 per cent of employees worked from home to some extent.

Even though this is a relatively new way of working, those managing these arrangements may be largely left on their own – without training, support or even simple tips for communicating with hybrid workers.

New report on impact of hybrid working in Ireland to deliver its findings

The problem isn’t with remote work itself, but in how it’s managed, says Andreeva. “We can make it work if the people who are actually managing it on a daily basis – line managers – are better prepared. If we fix this group, the spillover effects for the organisation will be amazing.”

The resources already exist to make this possible too, she says. Grow Remote, for example, is a government-supported social enterprise that helps employers, managers and remote workers thrive through online training, resources and community connections.

New ways of working

In the past decade, line managers have taken on more HR responsibilities (onboarding, interviews, appraisals), but the power to manage hybrid work policies and team-oriented ways of working has been taken from them. Andreeva, Dr Jordi Trullen (ESADE Business School) and Jim Copeland (Maynooth University) interviewed 36 line managers across 32 organisations to understand their shifting responsibilities, their reaction to hybrid work policies and the obstacles they face.

Most of these qualitative in-depth interviews were with line managers working in US multinationals in Ireland. The study found that hybrid policies were mostly set centrally without consulting line managers, who then had to adapt them informally with little training or information on how to manage hybrid teams.

The interviews revealed some worrying trends. Line managers reported that their organisations gave them no say on remote policies, no insights into remote workers’ schedules, and no training or support on how to manage them. They’re flying blind while being expected to deliver the same or better levels of productivity.

Although line managers are expected to support or reinforce compliance, they were typically not given access to live or recent individual-level attendance data or monitoring tools. This limited their ability to intervene effectively or anticipate issues within the team.

Many managers also expressed concerns over the official reasons provided for returning to the office, as these were often not convincing. This, and getting little or no notice on policy-change announcements, limited managers’ ability to persuade their subordinates to follow the policy.

Managers identified persistent challenges with hybrid work co-ordination. Yet few received any structured training or support on how to manage these dynamics.

“The line managers feel that there’s an assumption in the organisation that if you were a manager during Covid that you know how to do it, and that is why training doesn’t come up,” says Andreeva.

Hybrid teams require complex co-ordination due to staggered schedules and individual exceptions. But, instead of reporting these difficulties to leadership, line managers operated from a place of fear, and often withheld details of these operational challenges to prevent a full return to working from the office for everyone.

Managing hybrid

Andreeva has been working on a book chapter with Prof N Sharon Hill of George Washington University School of Business to help address the information deficit in understanding hybrid work dynamics and best practices. Hill developed the CAARE framework (configuration, autonomy-alignment, relationships, equity) in 2023 and her work was published in MIT Sloan Management Review.

‘One of the managers in our study added 15 minutes with no work-related agenda to daily team meetups to allow the team to connect casually, compensating for lost in-person informal lunchtime chats’

Tatiana Andreeva, Trinity Business School

The CAARE framework helps organisations and managers think through and implement remote and hybrid ways of working with their team.

Configuration

Remote and hybrid teams have a different shape and rhythm compared to teams that work entirely from the office. Configuration is a strategic way to establish agreements on how members will work together.

What’s the real reason your boss wants you back in the office?

“Team agreements may, for example, specify core hours of availability, expected response times for communications, and procedures for providing updates on work status,” says Hill.

Atlassian and Dropbox designed tool kits for managers to help them co-develop these charters with their teams. Managers are encouraged to review these charters regularly with teams as employee preferences and situations may change.

Autonomy and alignment

To be effective, there needs to be a balance between individual autonomy and team alignment. Grow Remote found that some companies do this in a quick and clever way that works best for their team.

NearForm trained their managers to introduce asynchronous daily stand-ups. Each morning, team members answer four questions in Slack (How are you feeling? What have you done? What will you do today? Do you need help?). The manager scans responses for blockers instead of holding a daily call. The regularity of these check-ins ensures alignment, while also giving employees autonomy in where and when they work.

Relationships

“One of the managers in our study added 15 minutes with no work-related agenda to daily team meetups to allow the team to connect casually, compensating for lost in-person informal lunchtime chats; another added a five-minute fun fact slot in weekly meetings, inviting one of the team members to share something that you wouldn’t know about them,” Andreeva says.

In both cases, the manager’s aim was to provide space for informal connection and relationship-building.

Spotify developed “Talk it Through” training for their managers, as a part of their “Heart & Soul” mental health strategy. This training coached managers to include wellbeing check-ins in every one-to-one meeting with employees, to identify signs that colleagues might be struggling, and signpost appropriate support.

Equity

Managers can use several strategies to ensure they’re not unduly rewarding those they see in person more regularly, or proximity bias.

Redesigning work and decision-making processes are key. “For example, a transparent, clear system to monitor and evaluate performance that focuses on results-based metrics, discussed in relation to the autonomy-alignment component, helps mitigate bias in performance appraisal and rewards.”

The trust-building strategies discussed for the relationship component and team communication charters can also help to mitigate the perception that employees who are out of sight are not working as hard as those on-site.

To help managers make fair decisions, Spotify compares promotion rates and pay increases between employees each compensation cycle, and flags outliers, if any.

Margaret E Ward is chief executive of Clear Eye, a leadership consultancy. margaret@cleareye.ie

]]>Anchiy<![CDATA[Markets welcome US midterm results but too early to say if they will curb Trump]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/05/markets-welcome-us-midterm-results-but-too-early-to-say-if-they-will-curb-trump/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/05/markets-welcome-us-midterm-results-but-too-early-to-say-if-they-will-curb-trump/Thu, 05 Nov 2026 05:20:00 +0000Businesses and investors are going to take quite some time to work out the impact of the seismic result in the US midterm elections. Initially, after some wobbles overnight in the Far East, markets decided to take a positive view. In the US there was some relief that the scale of the Democratic win means president Donald Trump could not dispute the result.

Analysts, always looking for the bright side, also pointed out that previous periods when Congress was controlled by one side and the White House by the other led to policy gridlock and predictable policy, which suited markets quite well.

But the economic and market implications of what happened are going to take time to unwind. The result could lead Trump to rethink his tariff policy and his war aims in the Gulf – both of which have pushed up inflation. But we don’t know yet.

Trump has shown that he can bypass the need for Congressional approval on tariffs and buy time if the courts rule against him. And the president remains in control of foreign policy. Investors betting on a more benign world may be looking through rose-tinted glasses.

And then there is the AI question. The initial overnight wobbles in Far Eastern markets sprang from concerns of greater AI regulation as Democrats took over Congress, perhaps inhibiting the extraordinary investment boom which has driven US economic growth and Wall Street revenue higher.

Midterm drubbing could prompt Trump backlash abroad

Data centres linked to AI were also an issue locally in many areas, with voters objecting to the impact on electricity and water and the lack of local spin-off benefits.

It would be a step too far to call this a vote “against AI”, but this political factor is worth watching, nonetheless. The bromance between the tech bros and the White House could start to cool. And the data centre issue is now firmly on the political map.

In a logical world. the midterm vote would lead Trump to pull back on some of the polices that have fuelled inflation and, in some cases, favoured business. But logic is a scarce commodity in today’s White House.

]]>Matt Ramey<![CDATA[From photo to online shop in three minutes: Irish start-up harnesses AI ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/innovation/2026/11/05/from-photo-to-online-shop-in-three-minutes-irish-start-up-harnesses-ai/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/innovation/2026/11/05/from-photo-to-online-shop-in-three-minutes-irish-start-up-harnesses-ai/Thu, 05 Nov 2026 04:00:00 +0000Eamonn Grant got his first taste of the transformative power of technology when he was introduced to digital mapping as a geography student at UCD in the 1990s.

Digital mapping was in its infancy at the time, and Grant’s experience was to have a big influence on his subsequent career, using technology to push the boundaries in ecommerce and technology-enabled services.

Grant’s CV includes stints as head of ecommerce at Musgrave, European commercial director for Samsung Electronics and senior vice-president for corporate development at global ecommerce platform, ESW.

“Most ecommerce platforms and applications are designed as tools that people must operate,” he says. “They provide dashboards, reports or individual workflows, but employees still have to interpret the information, decide what to do and complete the work. RunCommerce is not Grant’s first start-up. Grant gives the example of a shopper looking at a product page online showing a jacket. Licensed betting businesses will have to contribute to a social impact fund that the GRAI aims to establish next year. The authority is working with the market’s bigger players on a self-exclusion system for people who fear they have a problem.

The ESRI published Patterns of Online and In-person Gambling in Ireland by Deirdre Robertson, Diarmaid Ó Ceallaigh, Shane Timmons and Pete Lunn, on Wednesday.

Kegs are stacked outside the pubs around the square. Restaurants are loading up on provisions.

Tourists gravitate towards Eyre Square, once an open ground used by market traders outside Galway’s medieval town gate, now enveloped by the city and its centrepiece.

Named after former mayor of Galway Edward Eyre, who donated the land to the city in 1710, the square is surrounded by historic and modern buildings.

Recent additions contrast sharply with the late Georgian and Victorian buildings, many of which struggle to find a use in modern Galway as they stand either vacant or underused.

The green park in the middle, owned by Galway City Council, was officially renamed John F Kennedy Memorial Park in 1965 to honour the US president who visited Galway months before he was assassinated in 1963.

The change never caught on. People never stopped referring to it as Eyre Square.

Property in the area has changed hands over the years. Based on a review of planning, company and Tailte Éireann (formerly the Land Registry) records, The Irish Times has pieced together who owns Eyre Square today.

Here are nearly all the landlords of Eyre Square. (Records did not exist for seven of the 47 addresses surrounding the plaza.)

The northeast side

1: There are some relative newcomers to Eyre Square, and two of them are the owners and occupiers of number one. In late 2023, the Richardson family, who operated a pub from the northeastern tip of the square for 70 years, sold their property to Tim and Wendy O’Connor for a reported €2.5 million. The O’Connors, who also own Dublin pubs O’Connors on Mount Street and Slattery’s in Rathmines, rebranded the venue from Richardsons to Jack J Foleys in early 2024.

2-3: A number of the city’s most frequented pubs, including Fibber Magees at number 3, are based on the northeast side of Galway’s plaza. Tailte Éireann records show Fahy Travel Limited, a travel agency controlled by Maura Fahy, owns the ground-floor commercial premises extending across numbers two and three. The records do not establish who owns the upper floors.

4-5: These buildings housing the Pick ‘N’ Pay store and Galway offices of Re/Max Property Experts and EBS are owned by Weleyre Holdings Limited, a company controlled by Padraic McHale and the late Martina McHale of the family behind Mayo machinery business McHale Engineering. The company first registered its ownership of number 4 in January 2023 when it took over the ownership from L & C Mulryan (Eyre Square) Limited, a company linked to local auctioneer Liam Mulryan. New land records filed also showed that the McHale family’s firm declared ownership of number 5, also known as Hardiman House, in April 2026.

7-9: Since 1862, O’Connell’s pub has traded from Eyre Square. It remained in the O’Connell family until 2006, when Maureen O’Connell nominated St Vincent de Paul as the main beneficiary in her will. The charity sold the venue to a syndicate of notable developers that included Michael Burke, Peter Gilhooly, Walter King and Tom Considine for €14 million. In 2013, property developers and Galway-born billionaires Luke and Brian Comer acquired the building housing O’Connell’s bar at number 8, Odeon House at number 7 and 9, occupied by Galway Luggage Storage, as part of a receivership sale. Based on land registry records, the Comer brothers’ firm Manna Property Company Limited co-owns these buildings with Weleyre Holdings Limited, a company controlled by Padraic McHale and the late Martina McHale, two of the family behind McHale Engineering. Manna Property Company Limited, which owns €20.6 million of property assets, and Weleyre Holdings Limited, with €13.9 million of investment property on its books, also co-own a number of properties just off Eyre Square, including An Púcán and 19 residential properties on St Patrick’s Avenue, often available for short-term letting.

10: Another property on this row that traded hands in recent years is number 10. Last year, Hession’s Londis opened on the ground floor of the building.

11: The building, occupied by Esquires Coffee, has been registered to owners Michael Burke and Rita Burke of Derrydonnell More, Athenry, Co Galway since May 2013.

12: This unit, occupied by car rental service Budget, is owned by R & M Property Limited, a company co-owned by Raymond and Mary McConn.

13: In addition to three other properties in the row, the Comer brothers’ property group also owns number 13, which houses the bar Thirteen on the Green. The property is controlled through Chateaugay Limited, which was registered as the owner of the property in September 2018. 16: Galway’s Ceannt station, built in 1851, doesn’t have a direct link on to Eyre Square, except for roadways beside The Hardiman that lead to a drop-off bay and car park, but Irish Rail does have an interest in a property facing on to the square. 18: At the southernmost corner of the square sits number 18, which was an AIB branch until 2021. The building is still owned by AIB. Goodbody Stockbrokers, acquired by the bank in 2021, has listed the upper floors of the building as its head office in Galway.

The southwest side

19: Many of Eyre Square’s pre-1900s buildings have been demolished in the past century, but number 19 is one of the survivors. 20: Eyre Square Centre takes up a relatively small part of the frontage of the square but the shopping centre, with 72 tenants, has a footprint almost the size of Eyre Square itself. Now it is managed by David Goddard’s firm Lanthorn, which acquired Davy’s real estate business in 2024.

21: Now used as offices by Colleran Auctioneers, this three-storey former house dating to the early 1800s is controlled by Independent Trustee Company Limited, which registered its ownership of the building in March 2026.

22: The property, registered to owner Mary Finnegan of Cartron, Oranmore, Co Galway, is used as offices by MacSweeney & Company Solicitors.

23: One of the oldest remaining buildings on Eyre Square, with origins in the early 1800s, number 23 was acquired in 2019 by Eyre Square Court Hotel Limited, a firm owned by the hoteliers Richard and Sandra Byrne, who are also behind the Salthill Hotel. 24: Formerly occupied by a Credit Union branch, number 24 was recently sold based on a listing from local real estate agents Mullery Auctioneers. Land registry records have not been updated to identify the new owners.

That building is owned by Gary and Robert Monroe, who run Monroe’s Tavern on Dominick Street.

32: Lil’ Bros Pizza, sitting on the edge of Eyre Square nearest Galway’s main shopping district, is another relative newcomer to the area. 33: The fragmented layout of Eyre Square is evident at its most northerly side, where more than a dozen properties are set back from the green area, including PTSB, which owns number 33 and trades from the premises.

35: The second-largest hotel on Eyre Square is the Imperial Hotel, which is based in number 35. The 83-bed property is run and owned by Kevin and Frank Flannery through the company Foxfield Inns. The Flannery family also run the Ashling Hotel in Dublin near Heuston Station.

36: Pat and Una McDonagh’s firm Atlantic Enterprises Limited, which is linked to the Galway-based restaurant group Supermac’s, owns number 36, where the McDonaghs’ flagship restaurant has traded for many years into early hours of the morning.

37: ADHD Tattoo and Card Factory both traded from the subdivided number 37. Planning records show that an entity called the O’Flaherty Group is the owner of the building.

38: Daybreak has traded from number 38 for many years. Two years ago, new filings with the land registry showed Glencree Stores Limited, a company controlled by Jason Henchy, is the owner the building.

39: No records exist to show the ownership of the property housing Ali’s Barbers.

40: Dunnes Stores, a long-time presence on Eyre Square, owns the unit it trades from. Planning records show the company, which also has a large store in Eyre Square Centre, also owns the building housing Golden Discs, but this latter property has no official number associated with its Eyre Square address.

41-42: Company filings show a firm called Community Newspapers Limited, a firm connected to the Galway Advertiser group, owns the buildings in which the local newspaper is based.

]]>Alan Betson<![CDATA[US dollar falls and stocks waiver as Democrats sweep to victory in midterm elections]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/11/04/oil-swings-after-two-day-decline-as-us-iran-talks-remain-mixed/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/markets/2026/11/04/oil-swings-after-two-day-decline-as-us-iran-talks-remain-mixed/Wed, 04 Nov 2026 07:05:01 +0000A Democratic Party sweep of the US Congress rippled across global markets, sending the dollar lower and boosting US bonds, while stocks steadied on bets the outcome will put the brakes on president Donald Trump’s agenda.

Futures for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 were little changed. Both had fallen earlier before buyers stepped in. The dollar weakened against all significant peers, while the yield on 10-year Treasuries fell five basis points to 4.92 per cent. Europe’s Stoxx 600 rose 0.4 per cent while a gauge for Asian equities wavered.

Investors initially saw a Democratic wave as a potential setback for stocks given the prospect of tighter regulatory scrutiny, particularly of high-growth technology and artificial intelligence companies. Treasuries, meanwhile, stand to benefit if political gridlock limits further tax cuts and government spending, easing concerns about federal borrowing.

Democrats scored victories in Republican strongholds across the country, flipping at least seven Senate seats and winning House races in districts Republicans easily carried in 2024.

Several news organisations projected that Democrats would win the House, while Decision Desk HQ projected they took the Senate. Trump said he could work with a House and Senate run by the opposition “if the Democrats want to work with me.”

“Political gridlock should reduce the likelihood of another significant fiscal expansion, while the accompanying decline in Treasury yields could ultimately provide some support to equities,” said Florian Ielpo at Lombard Odier Investment Managers.

“The fundamental backdrop has not suddenly changed, with US growth remaining solid.”

“The US midterms, like any significant political event, have created uncertainty, widening the disconnect between market valuations and fundamentals,” said George Efstathopoulos, a money manager at Fidelity International.

“I am now trimming defensive positions, including utilities, to buy technology stocks in Asia and elsewhere, while adding some exposure to India for diversification.”

Bond investors have been uneasy about the US’s fiscal trajectory, with the nation’s debt load at around $40 trillion (€35.16 trillion), and gridlock may reduce the risk of additional spending or tax cuts that would require more Treasury issuance.

“Democratic control of Congress will make it harder for the White House administration to pass significant partisan legislation,” David Chao, a global market strategist at Invesco Asset Management, wrote in a note. “Less fiscal stimulus could reduce upward pressure on US growth, inflation and Treasury yields.”

In currency markets, the New Zealand dollar was the biggest gainer among significant markets versus the dollar, rising 0.7 per cent, while the yen and euro both strengthened 0.4 per cent.

“The US dollar’s Achilles’ heel is being exposed,” with its fortunes tied to the AI boom, said David Forrester, a senior strategist at Credit Agricole CIB in Singapore. “A Democrat blue wave that stifles data centre buildouts and hobbles the AI boom would weigh on the US dollar.”

Bitcoin slipped as much as 2.8 per cent on concerns that a Democratic sweep could stall industry-backed legislation and bring tougher scrutiny of digital-asset firms. The cryptocurrency later erased all of its declines.

Meanwhile, Oil fluctuated after a two-day decline as traders weighed mixed signals on the trajectory of US-Iran peace talks.

Brent traded near $104 a barrel after swinging in a range of more than $6 on Tuesday. West Texas Intermediate was around $97. Arguably the best tank in the world, the German-made main battle tank was supposed to be a game changer when, after much hand-wringing, it was supplied to Ukraine in 2023 alongside similar behemoths: the British Challenger and the US Abrams. They were predicted to give Ukraine the upper hand over Russia on the battlefield.

They didn’t. What halted the advance of the Russian army and now enforces the stalemate on the battlefield is drones. Lots of them. Cheap and deadly. Made in Ukraine.

History is full of examples of unsuccessful generals who made the mistake of fighting the last war. Instead of adjusting to how the nature of conflict is being changed by technology, they just try to do what worked last time, only better. The Russians, who expected to roll over Ukraine in a couple of weeks based on their previous experience, are just the latest example.

Ireland should be careful not to fall into that trap. The Irish Army obviously needs vehicles but seems to have shaped its future role around turning itself into a conventional armoured brigade that can – don’t say it too loudly – fight alongside other European armies in the sort of battle groups that have been potentially rendered obsolete by the conflict in Ukraine.

The other task that is envisioned for the Army once it’s tooled up is deployment overseas on UN missions. There has not been a UN deployment authorised since 2011, and the mandate for Unifil – Ireland’s most significant deployment in Lebanon – is not being renewed when it runs out at the end of the year.

Not accepting the regrettable but real decline in the global role of the UN is also tantamount to fighting the last war.

The real elephant in the room is where are we going to find the soldiers to fight in these new tanks. The Defence Forces simply does not provide an attractive career for many. That might change. Driving tanks and going overseas are the sort of things that professional soldiers like doing.

Dangers on a train: Russia’s improved drones pose new threat to Ukrainian rail users

But the question that nobody seems to want to ask, however, is whether reshaping the Defence Forces around new armoured vehicles is really the most effective and economical way to defend our land and sea borders now that drones and missiles dominate the battlefield.

Paradoxically, the neglect of the Defence Forces over the years presents Ireland with a unique opportunity to skip a generation of military technology and create a force able to fulfil this goal at a cost that is realistic. And one that could attract the best and brightest engineering and technological talent.

‘Whatever Trump and Putin agree, we’ll fight the invaders’: Inside the dugouts powering Ukraine’s drone war

Our complete lack of a domestic arms industry means that, unlike our larger European partners, we are not trapped by history. Big countries end up locked into feeding their arms manufacturers in what former US president and D-Day commander Dwight Eisenhower dubbed the military-industrial complex.

This includes the French and hence their enthusiasm for selling us tanks. The cost will be enormous. As well as the upfront price, put at about €1 billion, we will be tied into a long-tailed maintenance contract with the French suppliers, which could bring the costs to many multiples of this.

Belgium bought 442 similar vehicles for €1.6 billion, but the lifetime cost is put at €14 billion, or €3.6 million per vehicle. It’s a lot of money for something that could be knocked out by a drone costing a couple of hundred euro.

The potential for marine drones to help police the 880,000sq km of seabed under Ireland’s jurisdiction, including vital submarine cables, is equally obvious for a Naval Service that faces real difficulties crewing its ships.

What adds to the paradox is that we already have a nascent drone industry, but seem determined to stamp it out. Manna Aero, the best-known Irish drone-maker, has abandoned attempts to set up a drone-based delivery service here, citing the lack of a national drone strategy. “It seems quite odd; it’s a very peculiar decision after only three months that a role is redundant. That sounds very strange to me.

As with software and AI today, the mass adoption of shorthand and typing changed work habits and roles. But not all workers benefited. As new technology sweeps away the last vestiges of these older office productivity tools, what can we learn about how they were applied and misapplied?

First, try not to be too optimistic.

By the 1880s, supercharged by the rapid spread of office work, the typewriter and shorthand – the 2,000-year-old technique of using written symbols to speed the recording and transcription of speech – had combined to create new job opportunities for many women.

Before office work expanded in the US and Europe, social norms confined most of them to traditional “female roles” such as teaching or domestic service. But shorthand and especially typing were marketed as particularly suited to the female mentality and physique. By 1900, three-quarters of shorthand typists in the US were women – hence the distress of male clerks. Their protests were in vain. By 1930, 95 per cent of the US profession were women.

Yet shorthand and typing were a double-edged sword. Given a chance to enter the workforce, some women thrived. For instance, many British suffragists and suffragettes were expert typists who used their office skills as levers of emancipation, for instance, to prepare, print and distribute leaflets.

Secretarial skills also helped the first women stockbrokers, journalists and publishers break into their professions. Others enjoyed secretarial work simply for the flexibility and cash it provided to develop other career paths.

But many shorthand typists were consigned to life under a very low glass ceiling, far removed from the rosy imaginings of the late 19th century’s women pioneers. The determination and sacrifices required to progress in full-time paid work were sometimes too great.

The second lesson is that the intervention of aggressive consultants, selling technology on grounds of efficiency, is often bad for the people at the sharp end of that implementation.

By the 1910s, “scientific managers”, inspired by consultant Frederick Winslow Taylor’s mechanistic push to make manufacturing more efficient, were putting speedometers on typewriters to assess productivity. One Taylor disciple, William Henry Leffingwell, author of 1917’s Scientific Office Management, obsessed over the best way secretaries should arrange a desk (“keeping stationery in desk drawers is [a] source of waste motion”), how long it should take to insert a sheet of paper in a typewriter (three one-hundredths of a minute), and whether it paid to take paper clips off correspondence before filing (it depends: it takes 10 minutes to remove one pound of clips, he calculated).

Leffingwell was naturally a big advocate of the typing pool, which grouped shorthand typists together rather than relying on “small groups of uncontrolled stenographers throughout the office who work only part of their time on letters and part on miscellaneous clerical tasks and, as is often the case, sit in absolute idleness at other times”.

Historian Lucienne Boyce, who worked as a temporary secretary in the 1970s, says: “The whole image of the typing pool was of a factory, and the women became instruments ... just as you keep workers down in a factory, by giving them a tiny bit of job to do.” Boyce later became a careers adviser and saw how rarely men were directed down the secretarial path.

This was a world where “bosses, almost always male, literally dictate to female clericals”, as academic Catherine Rankovic has put it. As the century progressed, the combination of complete control, a rigid focus on efficiency, and lower status sucked from the office what little autonomy and joy women had hoped they might achieve there. It created what sociologist Margery Davies called a “secretarial proletariat”.

Obstacles that stood in the way of these women included formal or informal marriage bars, inadequate or non-existent maternity leave or childcare options, and looming disparities between the pay and promotion opportunities offered to women, not to mention casual sexism and outright sexual harassment.

A third lesson is that the same forces that lead to the birth of one technology can also hasten its demise at the hands of the next wave of development. The earlier technology’s users are often the unwitting victims. The Dictaphone, the electric typewriter, the computer and the internet finally put paid to the typing pool and consigned shorthand dictation to the shredder of secretarial skills.

With the advent of the desktop personal computer, the typewriter became a “keyboard” and the association of typing with women’s work broke down. Executives started to realise the quickest route from the idea in their heads to the memo or letter was through their own fingertips. “Now computers have come along, and ‘typing’ is ‘keyboarding’. Suddenly, voila! Men can type,” Gloria Steinem, the feminist activist, said in a 2007 commencement address at her alma mater Smith College. “Gives you faith in men’s ability to change, doesn’t it?”

So the dream that many women nursed in the late 19th century – that innovations such as shorthand and typing would provide a route into the workplace and a launch platform for promotion – was, for many, a hollow one. Only in the 2020s did women managers start to outnumber secretaries in the list of most common roles for women in the US.

But there is a fourth, and more upbeat, lesson from the rise and fall of the secretarial proletariat. New technologies can create opportunities for a smaller number of workers to cultivate skills that enable them to shape better jobs for themselves.

Secretaries have morphed into high-value personal and executive assistants, for instance, increasingly sought after for their command of the newest office tools.

Rebecca Siciliano, managing director of agency Tiger Recruitment, says a lot of her clients “want someone [who] is AI and tech savvy”.

These assistants must provide the expert human touch needed to juggle diaries packed with virtual and in-person meetings, and to represent their boss inside and outside the business. They need to know when to delegate to bots the more mundane tasks of taking minutes or updating spreadsheets. The best command salaries of £85,000 annually, according to Siciliano. Some may rise to become chiefs of staff and operations managers.

Much has changed since Pierson made the case for women in the workplace. The manual typewriter is long gone in most offices. The smartphone and AI are eradicating the last remnants of need for written shorthand. And despite Tiger and its clients’ best efforts to broaden the pool of executive assistants, only a small minority are men.

Stanley said the National Planning Framework (NPF), which has set the strategic direction where and what type of development takes place, mean the State can only deliver around 25,000 to 30,000 own-door houses a year, which means the remainder will need to be apartments.

He added 85 per cent of zoned land has a density requirement that “necessitates some or all apartments within future developments”.

“There is also an important climate and infrastructure rationale behind this approach. The 2023 Climate Action Plan includes a target to reduce total vehicle-kilometres driven by 20 per cent by 2030.”

Last year, 12,047 of the 36,284 homes built were apartments, with 18,308 houses in new-build estates and the remaining 5,929 being one-off homes.

“The biggest resulting change in housing output will be the requirement to massively increase large-scale apartment output to meet land use stipulations,” Stanley said.

Corporate landlord says Ireland's housing shortage has led to profit surge

“Approximately 50 per cent of all new homes in the future will have to be apartments to comply with the objectives of the NPF. This means that unless the industry builds circa 25,000 to 30,000 apartments per year, there is little chance of achieving a total output of 50,000 to 60,000 homes per year.”

Research commissioned by the Department of Housing showed development costs for urban apartments in Dublin rose by more than €13,000 to €605,000 last year, while the price of a suburban apartment rose by 2 per cent to €559,000.

Developers have said the prices required to deliver apartments, and the lack of a viable exit from selling to individual owners or investors, has made many apartment projects unviable to build.

Stanley said the difficultly the industry faces making apartment schemes viable to build could impact the sector’s ability to scale home building up to the rate required to meet the 300,000 goal.

“With apartments forming part of the delivery sequence, a lack of a funding or viable exit for those apartments will have the knock-on effect of restricting or slowing down the delivery of houses and the wider development,” he said.

He added that the sector needs support from the State to make apartment delivery viable “while private capital remains more limited for this category of residential development”.

Opinion: Minister’s refusal to answer questions on house prices reveals confused state of housing policy

The State has set up the Croí Cónaithe (Cities) scheme, which was launched in 2022 to bridge the gap between how much it costs developers to build an apartment and the price owner-occupiers can afford to pay for apartments.

Cairn has sold more than 350 apartments that were built in its new Seven Mills development in Dublin 22 through this scheme at prices between €235,000 and €275,000 for one-bedroom units, while a 79.9sq m two-bedroom apartment costs about €375,000.

]]><![CDATA[Fish-and-chips chain Beshoffs gave EU staff better pay and hours, permit worker claims]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/fish-and-chips-chain-beshoffs-gave-eu-staff-better-pay-and-hours-permit-worker-claims/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/fish-and-chips-chain-beshoffs-gave-eu-staff-better-pay-and-hours-permit-worker-claims/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 17:21:10 +0000A Turkish worker has said she was discriminated against and made to feel like “rubbish” when her bosses at the Beshoffs fish-and-chips chain refused the annual leave she sought for her own wedding.

The employee, Zerha Fidan, has accused Beshoff Brothers’s operating company Glendalon Ltd of giving European Union nationals better pay, preferential shift allocations and priority for annual leave, in breach of the Employment Equality Act 1998.

She told the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) she could not quit her job as a counter assistant at its restaurant in Clontarf, Dublin 3, even after being denied leave for the wedding, because her residency entitlements in Ireland were tied to her employment.

Her lawyers argue she was discriminated against on the grounds of race, in breach of the Employment Equality Act – a claim being disputed by the restaurant group at the WRC.

Fidan started work at Beshoffs in November 2022, shortly after arriving in Ireland, and worked at various locations before being deployed at its Clontarf restaurant, she told the WRC last week.

Fidan’s evidence was that when the national minimum wage was raised to €12.70 at the start of 2024, she was kept on this rate until August that year, despite two colleagues – both EU nationals – at the shop getting a higher hourly rate.

She said the higher hourly pay for the other two workers was “hidden from me” and only disclosed “accidentally” by one of the women.

The business’s position was that one of the other workers was a supervisor, while the other performed the duties of a supervisor. However, Fidan said both were doing the same job as she was.

Fidan said she approached her manager in November 2024 after becoming engaged and asked for time off in September the following year. His response then, she said, was “Oh, you didn’t invite me.”

She wrote to her manager in February 2025 seeking four weeks off that September – a fortnight as annual leave and a fortnight as unpaid leave, she said.

There was no answer from the manager at that point, and she then wrote to the business’s general manager, Bridget Starbuck, asking about leave for September that year, she said.

Asked how she felt when Starbuck gave no reply, she said: “Rubbish. Who am I, of course?”

She said that having sought a day off for the sixth anniversary of her father’s death in March 2025, the roster was set so that she was required to work for 10 days straight.

This, she said, was “a punishment” for “talking about my salary, my wedding, and I wanted one Saturday off – you know, I am asking every day, every time”.

She said that after the 10-day run of shifts, she suffered a panic attack at work.

Fidan’s doctor placed her on medical leave after that, and suggested in June 2025 that the complainant could go back to work if there were reduced hours, flexibility on start and finish times, and a “calm” working environment, the hearing was told.

Starbuck had replied to the medical letter saying the business could not accommodate Fidan’s return to work on that basis “due to the nature of the role”.

The hearing was told a complaint was filed with the WRC after that.

The case stands adjourned and is not expected to resume before the new year.

]]>chang chang<![CDATA[Irish inflation hits 4% on back of energy prices]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/irish-inflation-hits-4-on-back-of-energy-prices/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/03/irish-inflation-hits-4-on-back-of-energy-prices/Tue, 03 Nov 2026 12:03:04 +0000Surging energy prices drove Irish inflation to a three-year high of 4 per cent in October, up from 3.8 per cent the previous month.

The latest readout of annualised price growth comes amid renewed US strikes on Iran and in advance of pivotal US midterm elections that could dictate the course of American foreign policy.

The Central Statistics Office’s Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices indicated that prices rose at an annualised rate of 4 per cent in the 12 months to October and by 0.5 per cent month-on-month.

The main driver was energy prices, which rose by 4.5 per cent in the month and were up by more than 18 per cent since October 2025.

Motorists have been the worst hit by the latest spike in oil prices, with petrol and diesel prices breaching €2 and €2.15 a litre respectively in many forecourts. Before the Iran crisis, both fuels averaged about €1.70 a litre.

The increase in food prices was more muted. They rose by 0.1 per cent month-on-month and by the same amount in annual terms.

There is typically a lag time before rising energy costs translate into higher food prices.

Eurostat will publish flash estimates of inflation from the euro zone as a whole on Wednesday.

They are likely to heavily influence the European Central Bank’s next move on interest rates, with markets anticipating another quarter-point rise in December.

The ECB paused its run of rate hikes at last week’s October meeting.

Frankfurt has raised rates twice in the past five months as it combats the surge in inflation from energy prices.

Although there is concern that euro zone inflation may soon climb above 4 per cent, double the ECB’s target rate, rising bond yields are acting as a counterweight, allowing the bank to pause its monetary tightening at least for now.

Kate English, chief economist at Deloitte Ireland, said: “The lag between fuel price increases and a more expensive food shop has not yet emerged in the latest inflation figures, with food prices increasing by 0.1 per cent in the last year.”

However, she cited research from the Economic and Social Research Institute that suggests there is typically an 8-10 month lag between increased energy prices and higher food prices.

“What is certain is that people are facing into a winter with much higher energy costs. While Ireland’s economy continues to demonstrate resilience, this will be of little comfort to people heating their home,” English said.

“This stems from continued conflict in the Gulf region, which is the driver of increased energy costs. This is the second time Ireland [and Europe] has been negatively impacted by energy prices stemming from a conflict in recent history, the first being the illegal invasion of Ukraine,” she said.

Polish political leaders have reacted to the results of Tuesday’s US midterm elections, in which the Democrats won control of both houses of Congress from President Donald Trump’s Republicans.

The outcome was welcomed by Poland’s ruling coalition, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk declaring that “democracy won”. The response was more muted from the right-wing opposition and the office of conservative President Karol Nawrocki, who is a Trump ally.

🚨 🇺🇸 Tusk gives Trump some great advice. But will the US president listen?

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk urged the US president to seek compromises after the Republicans' defeat and not to rely on vetoes as his main way of governing.

Trump had earlier threatened to become… pic.twitter.com/s3E6G5zIQT

— NEXTA (@nexta_tv) November 4, 2026

Tusk addressed the election results on Wednesday afternoon local time at a press conference alongside his Czech counterpart, Andrej Babiš. “Today, democracy won in America,” said a smiling Tusk. “I love democracy; it is a beautiful thing.”

“As President Donald Trump himself said just after the election, the Democrats did a good job, and I really could not agree more with him this time,” added Tusk. “I hope that the result will stabilise the situation also in our region.”

Although the United States remains Poland’s most important security partner, Tusk’s government – a broad, pro-EU coalition that ranges from left to centre right – has at times had uneasy relations with the Trump administration.

It has been critical of Trump’s conciliatory approach towards Russia, his often tough stance on Ukraine, as well as his pursuit of US control over Greenland.

 

Meanwhile, the head of the parliamentary caucus of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, Zbigniew Konwiński, told broadcaster Polsat News that “personally, I was happy with the Democrats’ victory”.

“We know how Donald Trump behaves, how volatile he is in his political declarations, how he can sometimes put Ukraine in a more difficult position than Russia, so I would rather look for the positives in what happened,” said Konwiński.

“If we look at recent years, the more Democrats, the stronger the Democrats, the better for Poland,” he added.

.@Konwinski_PO: Cieszę się z wygranej Demokratów w USA, bo to lepszy scenariusz dla Polski. @marcinfijolek pic.twitter.com/gJ3TnlMn0l

— Graffiti_PN (@Graffiti_PN) November 4, 2026

The speaker of Poland’s parliament, Włodzimierz Czarzasty, who is also the leader of one of KO’s junior coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), has clashed with the US ambassador to Poland twice this year over Czarzasty’s criticism of Trump.

Today, Czarzasty shared and commented on a social media post by Trump, published in the wake of the Democrats’ victory, in which the US president showed an image of his signature red cap with the word “VETO” on it.

“Where have I heard this before?” wrote Czarzasty, referring to the fact that Nawrocki has vetoed a record number of bills passed by parliament, where Tusk’s coalition has a majority.

Czarzasty then went on to list a series of characteristics that he suggested both Trump and Nawrocki share, including “arrogance”, “lack of respect for women”, a “suspicious past”, “transactional exploitation of their position”, and “admiration for politicians with fascist tendencies”.

Skąd ja to znam? Arogancja. Buta. Nieuzasadniona pewność siebie. Brak szacunku dla kobiet ( a to popchnę jakąś dwojga nazwisk, a to zakpię prymitywnie). Dziwna przeszłość. Instrumentalne traktowanie dziennikarzy. Pieniądze za spotkania. Transakcyjne wykorzystywanie funkcji.… pic.twitter.com/ryT2BMOZb2

— Włodzimierz Czarzasty 📚📖 (@wlodekczarzasty) November 4, 2026

Nawrocki has closely aligned himself with Trump. During last year’s Polish presidential election campaign, Trump invited Nawrocki for a private meeting at the White House. His then-homeland security secretary, Kristi Noem, visited Poland to endorse Nawrocki.

Nawrocki himself has not thus far commented on Tuesday’s midterm election results. However, Marcin Przydacz, the head of the president’s International Policy Bureau, did address the issue in a social media post.

“As predicted, in the US midterm elections voters decided on change,” wrote Przydacz. “Poland will continue its good cooperation with the US, because it is our ally, and collaboration is in our mutual interest.”

Przydacz also added that the results were “a reminder for Tusk” that “no government lasts forever”. In Poland, too, “the moment will come when voters will decide on change – and it might be quite soon”, added Przydacz, in a nod to next year’s Polish parliamentary elections.

Zgodnie z przewidywaniami w wyborach połówkowych w USA wyborcy zdecydowali o zmianie. Wcześniej wygrywali Republikanie, dziś Demokraci. Polska będzie kontynuować dobrą współpracę z USA, bo jest to nasz sojusznik, a kooperacja jest w naszym wspólnym interesie. O tym, kto sprawuje…

— Marcin Przydacz (@marcin_przydacz) November 4, 2026

Tusk’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, meanwhile, used the US election results to revive his long-running feud with Elon Musk, who is no longer part of the Trump administration but donated enormous amounts of money to support the Republicans agead of the midterms.

Last year, Musk and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio criticised Sikorski after he suggested that Musk had threatened Ukraine. In a post on his social media platform, X, Musk told Sikorski to “be quiet, small man”.

On Wednesday, Tusk shared a screenshot of a tweet he had published last year, after Musk left the Trump administration, in which Sikorski wrote: “See, big man, politics is harder than you thought.”

pic.twitter.com/r6h2B5WfWa

— Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) November 4, 2026

]]> International Commission of Jurists criticises takeover of Polish constitutional court https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/04/international-commission-of-jurists-criticises-takeover-of-polish-constitutional-court/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 11:05:52 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106374

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

The International Commission of Jurists (ICJ) has criticised the takeover of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) by a group of government-backed judges. It says that the move “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary”.

However, the ICJ, a Swiss-based NGO led by judges, lawyers and academics from around the world, also chastised Poland’s opposition-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, for his role in the crisis around the TK, in particular his refusal to swear in judges elected by parliament.

🚨#Poland’s constitutional crisis must be resolved through the rule of law. The ICJ urges all authorities to respect judicial independence, follow lawful procedures, and comply with European court rulings.

🔗More information: https://t.co/NWmca9mpUx

— ICJ (@ICJ_org) November 3, 2026

On Friday, eight judges who were elected to the TK this year by the government’s parliamentary majority effectively took over the tribunal. They announced that the chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański, had been suspended for failing to properly fulfil their duties.

Meanwhile, large numbers of riot police were deployed outside the court, holding back protesters, including opposition politicians, and preventing Święczkowski and Sochański from entering the grounds.

Święczkowski denounced the takeover of the court as an illegal “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the tribunal’s remaining six judges, who, like him, were appointed under the rule of the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which brought the TK under its political influence.

Nawrocki has likewise denounced the actions of the government-backed judges. In the early hours of Saturday, he dramatically forced his way into the court, where he clashed physically and verbally with the judges who had taken over the TK.

During a visit to the Constitutional Tribunal last night, President Nawrocki clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of the court.

The president is today seeking talks with political leaders to discuss the crisis https://t.co/7HmBnuIaDG

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 31, 2026

In a statement on Tuesday, the ICJ expressed regret that the latest developments have “deepened the crisis over the tribunal”. It called on Polish “state institutions to seek solutions…that comply fully with the rule of law, including the principle of the independence of the judiciary”.

The ICJ’s secretary-general, Santiago Canton, noted that Nawrocki has refused to swear in five of the eight TK judges elected by parliament this year. That “violates international standards and is contrary to the interim measures indicated by the European Court of Human Rights”, said Canton.

In May, the ECHR issued an interim order for all judges elected by parliament to be allowed to serve on the court. However, that has been ignored by Nawrocki and Święczkowski, who argued that the ECHR does not have the authority to make such a decision.

The ICJ also noted that the roots of the crisis at the TK date back a decade, to the time when the PiS government took actions – including unlawfully appointing judges to the tribunal – that rendered the court illegitimate.

 

“At the same time,” continued Canton, “the suspension of the president and vice-president of the tribunal without a fair and appropriate procedure established by law, carried out with the involvement of the police, contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary.”

In its statement, the ICJ added that “criminal and disciplinary proceedings must respect all the guarantees of a fair trial and must never be used as a means to change [a court’s] composition”.

Later on Tuesday, after the ICJ had issued its statement, the eight government-backed judges held their first general assembly, at which they moved forward with disciplinary proceedings against Święczkowski and Sochański.

The justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, has also submitted six requests to the TK to lift Święczkowski’s immunity from prosecution so that he can face charges for a range of alleged crimes relating to both his time as chief justice and his previous role as a senior prosecutor under the PiS government.

Skierowałem do Trybunału Konstytucyjnego kolejny, szósty już wniosek o uchylenie immunitetu Bogdanowi Święczkowskiemu, dołączając go do pięciu wniosków przekazanych w piątek. Dzisiejsza sprawa dotyczy zakupu systemu szpiegowskiego Hermes w czasie, gdy pełnił funkcję Prokuratora…

— Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 3, 2026

The takeover of the TK has also stirred controversy among Polish legal experts. The issue has even caused an unprecedented split at the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights (HFPC), a well-respected NGO.

On Saturday, the HFPC’s management board issued a statement, signed by its president, Maciej Nowicki, saying that it “sees no clear legal basis” for the actions taken on Friday by the government-backed judges to suspend Święczkowski and take control of the tribunal.

It warned that the situation “set a dangerous precedent” and “does not contribute to fixing the tribunal”. However, HFPC also made clear that the crisis at the court dates back a decade and reiterated its view that Nawrocki “has no right to block or invalidate the election [of judges] by parliament”.

Pełna treść stanowiska: https://t.co/OvJPpaGDel pic.twitter.com/2UpV2itgcd

— Helsińska Fundacja Praw Człowieka (@hfhrpl) October 31, 2026

That statement prompted six of the eight members of HFPC’s council – a separate body from the management board – to resign. Those to depart included a former chief justice of the TK, Andrzej Rzepliński, and a former deputy human rights commissioner, Hanna Machińska.

Machińska announced their resignation in a social media post. She said that the reason for her decision had been the management board’s statement, “with which I disagree”. Speaking later to broadcaster TVN, Machińska said that “we believe that the legal basis [for the TK takeover] was clearly defined”.

Poland’s government, including Prime Minister Donald Tusk, has also argued that the takeover of the tribunal was necessary to ensure that legally appointed judges can take up their seats and that the court’s legitimacy can be restored.

However, on Tuesday evening, Tusk shifted to a more conciliatory tone, offering to hold a one-on-one meeting with Nawrocki to discuss the crisis around the Constitutional Tribunal and “try to find solutions that will protect Poland from any political upheaval”.

]]> Disputed Polish constitutional court holds first meeting after takeover by government-backed judges https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/11/03/disputed-polish-constitutional-court-holds-first-meeting-after-takeover-by-government-backed-judges/ Tue, 03 Nov 2026 18:33:46 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=106353

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

The group of eight government-backed judges who last week took control of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) have held a meeting at which they made a number of key decisions, including moving forward with disciplinary proceedings against the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski.

However, the situation is mired in controversy and uncertainty. Święczkowski and the opposition-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, do not recognise the judges who are now claiming control of the court, describing their actions as a “coup d’état”.

Meanwhile, there are doubts as to whether today’s general assembly even had a valid quorum, given that the chief justice and six other judges appointed under the former government did not attend.

PILNE: Zgromadzenie Ogólne Sędziów TK przyjęło, że kworum to osiem osóbhttps://t.co/SYEf9Ead3L

— Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) November 3, 2026

The meeting was called by Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who on Friday declared that Święczkowski and the deputy chief justice, Bartłomiej Sochański, had been suspended for failing to fulfil their duties. Korwin-Piotrowska said that she herself, as the longest-serving judge on the court, was taking control.

Large numbers of riot police were deployed outside the court, holding back protesters, including opposition politicians, and preventing Święczkowski and Sochański from entering the court. However, Nawrocki himself did enter the premises, where he clashed physically and verbally with Korwin-Piotrowska.

For a general assembly of the TK to be valid, two thirds of the court’s judges need to be present. Normally, given that the tribunal has 15 positions, that would mean at least 10 judges being present.

However, only eight judges attended today’s meeting. They were all appointed to the TK by the government’s parliamentary majority this year. But Nawrocki has refused to swear in five of them, meaning that their legal status has become disputed.

 

The TK’s seven other judges, including Święczkowski and Sochański, were all appointed to the court under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under its political control, including by unlawfully appointing three judges.

None of them attended Tuesday’s general assembly. Nevertheless, the eight judges present at the meeting, which was broadcast live for the first time in the TK’s history, decided that a quorum had been reached.

They did so on the basis that three of the TK’s judges were not authorised to attend: Święczkowski and Sochański, because they are suspended, and Jarosław Wyrembak, because he inherited his position from one of PiS’s unlawfully appointed judges.

That meant only 12 judges were authorised to attend, and two thirds of that number is eight, meaning that a quorum had been reached.

Poland had the second-highest household electricity prices in the European Union in the first half of 2026 after adjusting for differences in the cost of living, new Eurostat data show. Prices in Poland were also among the fastest-rising in the bloc.

Poland’s relatively high electricity costs reflect the country’s continued reliance on coal, which results in EU charges for carbon emissions, and its taxes and levies, which make up the largest share of household electricity bills anywhere in the EU.

In nominal terms, Polish households paid €29.99 per 100 kilowatt-hours (kWh) for electricity in the first half of 2026. This was the seventh-highest price among the EU’s 27 member states and above the bloc-wide average of €28.32.

Ireland (€38.71 per 100 kWh) had the highest prices, followed by Germany (€36.18) and Belgium (€35.75). The lowest costs were recorded in Hungary (€11.39), Malta (€12.68) and Bulgaria (€13.41).

However, when adjusted for purchasing power standards (PPS), which account for differences in the cost of living, Poland ranked second in the EU, at 41.12 PPS per 100 kWh.

Only Romania had higher prices, at 46.89 PPS. The lowest prices when measured in PPS were recorded in Malta (13.75), Hungary (14.7) and Luxembourg (15.47).

Poland’s electricity prices, in PPS terms, rose by 10.7% compared with the second half of 2025, which was the second-biggest increase in the EU after Finland. They were also up 17.6% compared to the first half of 2025, the fourth-largest rise in the bloc.

 

One reason why electricity prices in Poland remain high is the country’s continued reliance on coal, which last year generated just over half of power, by far the highest proportion in the EU.

Almost all coal used in Polish power plants is mined domestically and is among the most expensive in the world to extract. Additionally, burning it also produces high carbon emissions, which power generators must pay for under the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS).

These costs contribute to the high taxes and levies included in household electricity bills, which accounted for 39% of the final price in Poland in the first half of 2026. This was the highest share in the EU, ahead of Germany (23.6%) and well above the bloc-wide average of 18.6%.

“In Poland, only one-third of our electricity generation is carbon-free. We have to pay for the rest – often dearly,” noted Polish energy journalist Jakub Wiech, commenting on the data.

Without taxes and levies, the nominal price of electricity in Poland would have been just under €16 per 100 kWh, below the EU average of €20.27.

However, Bartłomiej Orzeł of the Project Tempo think tank notes that electricity prices in Poland would, in fact, be even higher were it not for the huge state subsidies paid to support the unprofitable coal mining sector, which amount to billions of zloty a year but also shield end consumers from the full cost of extracting coal.

He told news website Interia that mines actually sell coal to power stations at a price below the cost of extraction.

Poland’s first-ever nest of Asian hornets, an invasive species seen as a particular threat because it preys on honeybees, has been eliminated. But scientists who have studied the colony say that it is likely more will be found next year.

Since arriving in France in 2004, Asian hornets, which are indigenous to Southeast Asia, have gradually spread to other European countries.

The first confirmed nest to be found in Poland was sighted in a tree in the village of Wielka Wieś near Kraków in mid-October, with individual hornets also being spotted at the apiary of the city’s AGH University of Science and Technology.

The nest was removed last week and sent to be studied by a team of scientists at Wrocław University of Environmental and Life Sciences, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP).

Paweł Migdał, from the university’s faculty of biology and animal science, told PAP that the nest was “fairly large” considering the Polish climate, containing around 1,000 workers and several dozen queens and males.

The scientists’ assessment of the nest revealed that it contained eggs and larvae, indicating that the hornets inhabiting it were still feeding, he added.

“I think we’ll find more of these nests,” Migdał told PAP. “They’re often built in the treetops, which means they’re invisible until the leaves fall in the autumn.”

Young queens had already left the nest to establish new ones after overwintering, and have greater chances of surviving the longer and warmer the Polish autumn is, he explained. They seek shelter in warm, dry places, such as underground or in storage areas.

 

With queens measuring 30mm and males about 24mm, Asian hornets, also known as the yellow-legged hornet, are smaller than the European variety, and no more dangerous to humans than European hornets or wasps.

The major concern over their arrival relates to their tendency to seek out beehives and prey on honeybees.

“Besides killing honeybees, their presence also causes bees in apiaries to stop working,” explained Migdał. “With the European hornet, the bees recognise the threat but, in a sense, continue working. However, the yellow-legged hornet presents a completely new threat to them.”

The number of bee colonies in Poland has risen 54% over the last decade to reach two million, thanks in part to a state programme supporting beekeepers.

Bees' value to the ecosystem as pollinators is estimated to be worth 5bn zloty (€1.1bn) https://t.co/ElISOc2o2T

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 30, 2022

The scale of the species’ invasiveness is shown by the fact that it releases an average of 150 young queens from its nest, and sometimes even 500 – each of which can potentially create its own nest – while European hornets release just 50, Migdał pointed out.

The location of the first nest found in Poland surprised scientists as the closest previously known was in Opava, around 150 km away in the Czech Republic. The hornets therefore probably travelled in a vehicle, although Migdał noted a potential concern that other populations might be found between the two sites.

President Karol Nawrocki has clashed physically and verbally with judges involved in an attempt to take control of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK). Afterwards, the president announced that he would hold a series of meetings with political leaders on Saturday afternoon to discuss the crisis.

However, it remains unclear to what extent the government, which is in conflict with the opposition-aligned Nawrocki and is backing the judges seeking to control the court, will engage in that process. Meanwhile, the court itself remains surrounded by riot police and anti-government protesters.

pic.twitter.com/Gk4bPH1pJU

— Maciej Berek (@MaciejBerek) October 31, 2026

On Friday, Nawrocki had been flying to Senegal for a state visit when the crisis at the court broke out. He ordered his plane to turn around in midair and return to Warsaw.

At around 1 a.m. on Saturday morning, Maciej Berek, a close associate of Prime Minister Donald Tusk who was recently chosen as a new TK judge, shared videos showing Nawrocki entering the TK building amid a confrontation at its doors.

The president was heard asking judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who is leading the attempt to take control of the court, to move out of his way and could be seen pushing his way past her.

pic.twitter.com/sni7uvIVke

— Maciej Berek (@MaciejBerek) October 30, 2026

Afterwards, presidential aide Marcin Przydacz claimed that Korwin-Piotrowska and another judge, Krystian Markiewicz, had “breached the inviolability of the head of state”.

Berek denied this and said that it was the president who “barged into judge Korwin-Piotrowska with great force”.

Subsequently, a further film showed Nawrocki, after he had entered the building, in a verbal confrontation with Korwin-Piotrowska and others, in which he can be heard telling them, “you are not Constitutional Tribunal judges”.

The conflict stems from a years-long crisis around the TK. Since the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Tusk – came to power in 2023, it has refused to recognise the court’s legitimacy.

That is because three of its judges were unlawfully appointed under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under political control. It also regards the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Świeczkowski, as illegitimate.

As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench.

 

That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its nominees in theory now have a majority on the court.

However, under Polish law, although new TK judges are chosen by parliament, they must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of those eight new judges, including Korwin-Piotrowska, Markiewicz and Berek.

Those five judges arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies in parliament and submitted their oaths to the president’s office. However, Święczkowski, who before being appointed as a TK judge had served in the former PiS government, refused to accept those five judges on the court.

Poland has introduced its first fast-track zones for renewable energy projects as the coal-dependent country seeks to speed up its transition to cleaner sources of electricity.

The regional assembly in Wielkopolska province, western Poland, this week approved plans covering 105.4 hectares across four municipalities, where investors will be able to develop solar farms under simplified planning and environmental procedures.

The environment ministry estimates that the changes, introduced under an EU directive, could reduce project preparation times from three to four years down to just one or two years.
