Under the scheme, planning and much of the environmental assessment will be completed before investors apply for permits, allowing projects to move forward more quickly.

Environmental authorities will also have a maximum of 45 days to review projects with a capacity of at least 150 kW. Industry representatives told energy Świat OZE, a renewable energy news service, that obtaining an environmental decision can currently take up to 150 days.

The newly designated areas, known as Accelerated Renewable Energy Development Zones (OPRO), will be located in the municipalities of Złotów, Lwówek, Rawicz and Słupca. Together, they have an estimated technical potential of 66-80 megawatts of solar capacity, depending on the arrangement of the panels.

Maria Niewitała-Rej, a climate and energy policy analyst at the Reform Institute, a Warsaw-based think tank, told the Dziennik Gazeta Prawna newspaper that while “the scale of the Wielkopolska plan is modest, the adoption of the first resolutions is a step in the right direction”.

 

The creation of accelerated renewable energy development zones stems from the EU’s revised Renewable Energy Directive (RED III), which requires member states to designate areas where renewable energy projects can be developed more quickly.

Under the directive, permitting procedures in these zones should take no longer than 12 months for onshore projects and 24 months for offshore projects.

EU rules required the first zones to be designated by 21 February 2026, making Poland’s adoption several months late.

The Church Fund, originally established in 1950 to compensate religious communities for property seized by the communist authorities, provides state subsidies for the health insurance contributions of clergy, for religious organisations’ charitable activities, and for the renovation of religious buildings.

It now supports all legally recognised religious denominations in Poland, including those that did not lose property at the time. Last year, the state spent 275.7 million zloty on the Church Fund. This year it has budgeted 272.6 million zloty.

Most of this money is then used to cover 80% of clergy members’ social security contributions. Under the bill proposed by The Left, churches would pay half of the contributions, with clergy covering the other half.

For regular workers, such contributions are funded jointly by employees and their employers, Anna Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s parliamentary caucus, pointed out, as quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We are introducing the same arrangement for priests and members of the clergy.”

At least 17.5bn zloty in state funds went to religious bodies from 2021-23, with over 95% going to Catholic organisations, the state auditor has found.

An exception is made in the bill for members of enclosed religious orders and missionaries, who would have their contributions paid in full by their churches. The cost of maintaining historic churches would be covered by the National Fund for the Protection of Monuments, Żukowska explained.

Włodzimierz Czarzasty, who is the leader of The Left as well as the speaker of the Sejm, the more powerful chamber in the Polish parliament, said the party did not oppose religion but wanted clergy to be treated equally under the law.

“I would like to remind my coalition partners: our coalition agreement includes a commitment to work toward establishing the principles of a secular state in Poland,” he said, speaking alongside Żukowska. “Our patience is running out”.

 

Ahead of the 2023 election, both the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk and The Left pledged to abolish the Church Fund, while the centre-right Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) proposed replacing state funding with voluntary taxpayer contributions. PSL had no equivalent formal party-wide pledge.

In 2024, after the coalition came to power, Tusk announced plans to reform the fund and appointed a government working group led by the PSL leader and deputy prime minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. The group’s work has since stalled.

Kosiniak-Kamysz yesterday dismissed The Left’s proposal, saying it has “not the slightest chance of support in parliament”. His party, the second largest in the coalition with 32 of 239 MPs, sees the existing fund as an inexpensive form of compensation and will oppose abolishing it, he vowed.

Instead, taxpayers should be able to allocate part of their taxes to a religious institution of their choice, a system used in several European countries, to “let the Polish people themselves decide whether or not they want to contribute,” he said, quoted by broadcaster Polsat News.

Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński, a member of Tusk’s Civic Coalition (KO), said that he supported reform, but criticised The Left for submitting the bill without consulting its coalition partners.

A sharp acceleration in bulk purchase annuities stopped M&G from sliding into net outflows in the third quarter, as asset management demand slowed.

The investment manager generated net inflows of £1.8bn in the third quarter, remaining flat from the prior year, with the majority recorded by its Life channel.

The segment, which handles personal insurance and bulk purchase annuities (BPA), delivered £1.1bn of net inflows.  Its Prufund option generated over £100m of net inflows, supported by its launch on Scottish Widows’ platform.

The group has now lifted its full year guidance for the BPA sales to £2.5bn, which chief executive Andrea Rossi said demonstrated the “success in reigniting” the business and shifting group focus back to the pension risk transfer market.

“In a volatile external environment, we continued to grow and make good progress against our strategic objectives,” said Rossi.

“The inflows we generated, reflect the resilience of our business model, and the attractiveness and diversification of our offering.”

M&G asset management arm struggles

The FTSE 100 group’s asset management arm failed to keep pace with the wider business, after an uptick in client exits and a downturn in its private market fundraising damaged inflows.

Net inflows in the channel fell 53 per cent from the prior year to £0.7bn, with wholesale asset management reporting the sharpest decline.

Inflows tumbled to £100m from £700m, while client redemptions also spiked to £5.1bn.

Its higher-margin private market division also saw inflows dry up, tumbling 87.5 per cent to £0.1bn. Public markets accounted “for the majority of net inflows” at £600m, M&G said.

Total assets under management and administration (AUMA) also slipped over the period, falling to £385bn from £387bn the prior quarter.

Despite the growth in BPA solutions, the life channel recorded the largest fall in AUMA, decreasing to £194bn. The investment giant blamed the decline on “small adverse market movements” offsetting further growth.

Asset management’s AUMA remained broadly flat at £355bn, after new client money offset losses from market headwinds.

BP has offloaded around a third of its stake in Norwegian oil and gas company Aker BP marking a major cash injection as it seeks to bring down its debt pile. The FTSE 100 energy giant told markets on Thursday it had sold a five per cent stake in Aker for around NOK9.83bn (£785m). BP [...]]]>

BP has offloaded around a third of its stake in Norwegian oil and gas company Aker BP marking a major cash injection as it seeks to bring down its debt pile.

The FTSE 100 energy giant told markets on Thursday it had sold a five per cent stake in Aker for around NOK9.83bn (£785m).

BP still owns around 68.7m of the remaining shares, leaving it with a holding just shy of 11 per cent. The sale was completed at a price of 311 crowns, marking a 12 per cent discount to Aker’s closing price on the Oslo bourse on Wednesday.

“In recent months, [Aker BP] has further increased its value through a combination of its strong performance and the favourable macro environment,” BP boss Meg O’Neil said.

“We believe now is the right time for us to realize part of this value to further strengthen BP’s balance sheet, our first priority as we build a simpler, stronger, more valuable BP.”

The firm raised its full-year asset sale target by $1bn to roughly $9bn.

BP to release new strategy

Last month, the firm reported earnings of $8.5bn (£6.3bn) for the third quarter, a near-quadrupling compared to the same period last year. It follows the surge in oil prices from the US-Iran war, which have left energy giants reaping mammoth profit windfalls.

BP has halved its debt over the past year to $13.9bn. It is set to be cut by a further $6bn following proceeds collected from the sale of lubricants business Castrol.

In December, BP is expected to present its new long-term strategy after O’Neil took the reins this year, replacing Murray Auchincloss who had just two years in the post.

In September, the group also appointed Ian Tyler as its new chair who had been serving as interim chair since 26 May. Tyler joined BP as a non-executive director in April 2025.

He replaced Albert Manifold, who was stripped of his roles as chair and director of the oil major in May after taking over in July 2025.

The ousting was reported to have been due to his “volcanic” temper towards colleagues. Manifold has disputed the characterisation of his conduct.

]]> 2474725Samuel Norman Samuel Norman AI ‘godfather’ takes aim at Altman, Musk and Zuckerberg over ‘dangerous’ tech dominance https://www.cityam.com/ai-godfather-takes-aim-at-altman-musk-and-zuckerberg-over-dangerous-tech-dominance/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 07:55:29 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2474582

The ‘godfather of AI’ has warned the UK’s growing dependence on a handful of American tech giants is “very dangerous”, taking aim at Silicon Valley’s most powerful executives and questioning whether they can be trusted to control the technology. Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel Prize-winning scientist whose research helped lay the foundations for modern artificial intelligence, [...]]]>

The ‘godfather of AI’ has warned the UK’s growing dependence on a handful of American tech giants is “very dangerous”, taking aim at Silicon Valley’s most powerful executives and questioning whether they can be trusted to control the technology.

Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel Prize-winning scientist whose research helped lay the foundations for modern artificial intelligence, told City AM the concentration of AI development in the hands of a few American firms was particularly concerning given the people running them.

“I think it’s particularly dangerous because of the character of some of the people involved, like Altman, Musk and Zuckerberg. I wouldn’t buy a used car from any of them”.

The swipe at OpenAI boss Sam Altman, Tesla, SpaceX and xAi chief Elon Musk and Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg comes as their companies pour billions into increasingly powerful systems, while governments struggle to establish how they should be regulated.

Hinton also took aim at OpenAI boss Sam Altman over the company’s failed boardroom coup in 2023, which saw co-founder Ilya Sutskever help orchestrate the chief executive’s short-lived removal.

“Ilya has a strong moral compass. He’s a brilliant scientist. He’s not so strong on political manipulation. Sam is the exact opposite”, Hinton said.

He admitted he too would have fired Altman, although joked he would have waited until after a funding round to do so.

Hinton, who left Google in 2023 to speak more openly about AI safety, also dismissed the idea of a the idea of a “kill switch” that could cut countries off from AI systems they rely on.

“When AI is that smart, it’ll be very good at persuasion. So even if you have someone who’s meant to turn it off if it misbehaves, it’ll be able to persuade them not to”.

Two months ago, the UK government rejected calls from MPs and peers for an emergency AI shutdown mechanism, arguing that blocking access to models domestically would not prevent their development or misuse overseas.

Britain faces an uphill AI battle

Hinton was equally dismissive of Britain’s prospects of becoming a major force in the global AI race.

“The UK sort of tries to position itself as very important in AI. I don’t think it’s going to be”, he said when asked about Britain’s role in international AI governance.

The assessment is unlikely to please ministers, who have spent the past year trying to position Britain as a leading destination for AI investment while reducing its dependence on Big Tech.

The government has committed £500m to a Sovereign AI Fund, topped up with another £60m in last week’s Budget, to back domestic developers and strengthen the UK’s tech independence.

But the government’s own AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, warned that the country risked becoming a “high-value AI customer” rather than a developer of the tech shaping its economy.

The concern is that British businesses and public services could become increasingly reliant on AI models and infrastructure controlled by companies overseas, leaving them exposed to foreign policy decisions and commercial restrictions.

Meanwhile, UKAI has warned that without a coherent national strategy, Britain risks becoming a “vassal state” dependent on these firms.

Hinton’s verdict suggests the gap between the UK’s ambitions and the financial willpower of American AI behemoths may be harder to close than ministers would like.

Silicon Valley’s race for profits

The Nobel laureate also warned that competition between governments and the tech sector was pushing AI development forward far faster than efforts to make it safe.

“What’s happening at present is there’s just this competition between countries and between companies to make it smarter and smarter and smarter, in the hopes that you can replace lots of workers and get lots of money”, he said.

“That’s what’s driving it. And this is the future of humanity that’s on the line”.

Hinton, who won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics for his pioneering work on neural networks, said he had brought forward his own estimate of when AI could surpass human intelligence”.

“I used to say 10 to 20 years; now I say 10. It’s always getting closer”.

He added that researchers were devoting too little time and attention to making sure intelligent systems would act in humanity’s interests.

“We’re going to have to share the planet with something smarter than us. What would we like the other aspects of that being to be, other than its intelligence?

“And we’re hardly doing any work on that – it’s crazy”.

Hinton also called for developers to face legal liability when their AI systems cause harm.

“If people produce AI models that do bad things, somebody should be held to account”, he said.

Despite his concerns, he acknowledged AI’s potential to increase productivity and accelerate scientific breakthroughs, including the development of better batteries and new materials.

But he questioned who would ultimately benefit from the wealth it generates.

“Sam Altman and Elon Musk talk about radical abundance for all of us. They don’t talk about exactly how that wealth is going to be distributed”, he said.

But organic growth, which strips out currency volatility and the [...]]]>

Diageo recorded sluggish sales growth in the first quarter of its financial year as the drinks giant faced “competitive pressure” in its top markets.

The FTSE 100 group, which owns Guinness, Johnnie Walker and Tanqueray, recorded net sales up 1.2 per cent year-on-year at $4.9bn. But organic growth, which strips out currency volatility and the sale of East African Breweries to Asahi, came in at 0.6 per cent higher.

Sale volumes were also a touch lower falling 0.1 per cent for the July to September period. 

This was led by a drop in north America, which makes up 36 per cent of the group’s business. US sales dropped 3.7 per cent and volume fell by the same amount.

“In north America, we continue to focus on making our offer more competitive, and whilst this remains our biggest challenge, clear actions are underway,” Diageo boss Sir Dave Lewis said.

Sales of the group’s premium brands Don Julio and Casamigos plunged double digits in north America, while tequila broadly was down double-digit in Mexico. This was partially offset by double-digit growth in beer in the region and ready-to-drink canned cocktails.

Chris Beauchamp ,chief market analyst at IG, said: “Turnarounds are tricky things to spot in real time, but Diageo appears to be in the midst of one. The share price seems to have effectively bottomed out, while the fundamentals are picking up too.

“Admittedly the north American business isn’t helping, but with everywhere else now contributing to performance it seems that Diageo has recaptured market confidence.”

Hot UK weather troubles Diageo beer sales

In Europe, Middle East and Africa (EMEA), which accounts for 26 per cent of the group’s business, organic sales grew 2.4 per cent driven by a 4.4 per cent rise in volumes.

Diageo sold 4.4 per cent more bottles in Europe, but earned two per cent less per bottle due to deliberate price cuts and promotions.

Beer sales saw low-single-digit growth in EMEA despite Guinness rising double-digits in Africa and Central Europe.

Diageo said this partly offset by low-single-digit decline in Britain and Ireland “due to unusually hotter weather and competitive pressure”.

Lewis took the reins at Diageo at the beginning of 2026 and quickly implemented a turnaround plan telling shareholders there was “hard work ahead” to boost sales.

The drinks giant shed around 2,000 jobs before the plan was formally kicked off with total headcount falling six per cent to 27,938 according to its annual report.

The group reported a three per cent dip in sales to $19.6bn in the year to end June, with profit tumbling by more than a fifth to just under $2bn.

But Lewis, who earned the name ‘Drastic Dave’ for his infamous turnaround effort at Tesco, vowed to deliver as much as $850m in cost savings.

Asos has returned to profit despite the cyber attack that rocked the fast-fashion seller last month, as its boss insisted the incident was “not a big thing”. The London-listed retailer said its decision to pause some marketing and customer-related activity in the aftermath of the incident resulted in a “short-term disruption” to trading, estimated at [...]]]>

Asos has returned to profit despite the cyber attack that rocked the fast-fashion seller last month, as its boss insisted the incident was “not a big thing”.

The London-listed retailer said its decision to pause some marketing and customer-related activity in the aftermath of the incident resulted in a “short-term disruption” to trading, estimated at between two and four per cent of the group’s gross merchandise value (GMV) in October.

The group typically generates £200m in GMV each month, valuing the impact of lost sales due to the incident at between £4m and £8m. Chief executive José Antonio Ramos said he is confident the group’s turnaround efforts have not been derailed by the attack.

He told reporters on Thursday: “We’re confident that this [impact] is going to dilute over time. So I don’t think that it is such a big thing, to be honest.”

Ramos has been leading turnaround efforts to reduce the retailer’s stock, simplify its supply chain and boost its margins since taking charge in June 2022.

Investors have been buoyed by the group’s use of artificial intelligence to get ahead of fashion trends, harking back to its original purpose as a destination for clothing inspired by celebrity looks.

Asos swung back into the black in the year to the end of August, posting a £24.4m pre-tax profit, compared to last year’s £282m loss. The group’s £46.4m adjusted loss before tax was better than the £61m forecast by analysts, and revenue dipped nine per cent to £2.2bn in line with market expectations.

Ramos said the fast-fashion seller has made “strategic pivot towards growth, building on the progress made through our transformation to date”.

The chief executive pointed to the group’s eight per cent GMV growth in womenswear in the second half of the year, though he said the firm’s menswear category “is still in recovery”. 

Asos ‘confident’ of better cyber defences

Ramos said Asos will ramp up its use of AI with a new ‘Stylist’ tool. “Imagine a store that is different for every customer, every time they visit, built around their own wardrobe and style, and shared with the friends, stylists and creators they love,” he said.

Last month, Asos’s share price dropped 12 per cent after a previously unknown group claimed they had hacked into the firm’s systems and gained access to personal details of its customers.

The hackers obtained an employee’s login information by posing as a trusted contact, the company later said, though it assured shoppers that their payment details had not been accessed.

Asos told shareholders on Thursday that its sales have not been affected in the long-term by the incident, with growth broadly flat in recent weeks despite the disruption caused by the attack. 

Ramos said: “We are confident that we are in a significantly better position now to avoid that this happens again. Obviously it’s impossible to say what is going to happen in the future, but we are confident that we have taken the right measures, in our collaboration with cyber experts.”

]]> 2474558Felix Armstrong Felix Armstrong BT slashes workforce as Talktalk takeover adds to turnaround challenge https://www.cityam.com/bt-slashes-workforce-as-talktalk-takeover-adds-to-turnaround-challenge/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 07:30:01 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2474688

BT has cut its workforce by 11 per cent as boss Allison Kirkby presses ahead with an overhaul of the telecoms giant, just weeks after rescuing struggling rival Talktalk from administration. The cost-cutting drive helped push pre-tax profits up 12 per cent to £1.1bn in the six months to September, despite revenue growing just one [...]]]>

BT has cut its workforce by 11 per cent as boss Allison Kirkby presses ahead with an overhaul of the telecoms giant, just weeks after rescuing struggling rival Talktalk from administration.

The cost-cutting drive helped push pre-tax profits up 12 per cent to £1.1bn in the six months to September, despite revenue growing just one per cent to £8.8bn.

The former state monopoly said its workforce, including contractors, had shrunk to 90,000 over the past year, helping deliver £312m in annual savings as it looks to simplify the business and cut costs.

The reductions form part of a wider restructuring plan that will see BT’s workforce fall to between 65,000 and 70,000 by 2030, excluding its international operations.

But while the cuts have helped boost profits, BT’s finances remain under pressure. Cash left over after running and investing in the business plunged 59 per cent to £236m, while its debt pile grew by £1bn to £21bn.

The results come as BT takes on the task of integrating TalkTalk’s consumer and wholesale businesses, which it rescued from administration last month after the struggling broadband provider failed to find a buyer.

The deal is expected to cost BT around £400m this financial year, with the company now responsible for services used by 2.5m TalkTalk customers.

“Our UK-centric strategy and transformation is clearly delivering with £312m of annualised savings achieved in the first half, as we continue to simplify and modernise”, Kirkby said.

Broadband rivals under pressure

BT’s broadband infrastructure arm Openreach reported record demand for its full-fibre network, with more than 10m homes and businesses connected by October.

The milestone comes as Britain’s broadband market faces mounting pressure from fierce competition and the heavy debts accumulated by companies racing to build rival fibre networks.

Virgin Media O2, which is grappling with a £22bn debt pile, is reportedly in talks to use Openreach’s network to serve new customers while shelving plans to upgrade parts of its own infrastructure.

The potential tie-up would mark a significant shift for BT’s biggest broadband rival, which has spent years investing in its own network to compete with Openreach.

BT has also struggled to hold on to customers. Openreach lost 366,000 broadband lines during the first half and expects to lose around 800,000 over the full year.

Meanwhile, its consumer broadband business reported a three per cent fall in average revenue per customer as competition continued to weigh on prices.

Kirkby said BT was making progress despite the challenging market, with more customers taking up its faster broadband services.

The company maintained its full-year forecasts, including around £2bn in cash left over after running and investing in the business, excluding the impact of the TalkTalk acquisition.

BT also increased its interim dividend by two per cent to 2.5p per share.

]]> 2474688Saskia Koopman Saskia Koopman I thought chairing Sussex Cricket would mean a quiet off-season. I was wrong https://www.cityam.com/i-thought-chairing-sussex-cricket-would-mean-a-quiet-off-season-i-was-wrong/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 07:00:00 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2474486

Ed Warner on the deluge of work that is triggered by the end of cricket’s County Championship, from recruitment and sponsorship to strategic planning for a possible fall in media rights revenue. The sun never sets on modern day cricket. Just ask the Australian squad, five matches into a 21-Test stretch across 12 months and [...]]]>

Ed Warner on the deluge of work that is triggered by the end of cricket’s County Championship, from recruitment and sponsorship to strategic planning for a possible fall in media rights revenue.

The sun never sets on modern day cricket. Just ask the Australian squad, five matches into a 21-Test stretch across 12 months and under the cosh from both national media and past players. Fancy a swift cricket fix this weekend? There’s a clutch of matches in the Abu Dhabi T10 tournament that starts on Saturday. You’ll find them in the UK on Premier Sports.

I had thought that my first off-season as a county chair would be an opportunity to de-stress, but was swiftly disabused of the notion. If anything, the workload stepped up once stumps were pulled for the final time in the English summer (or more accurately, early autumn), and Sussex’s players scattered on holidays, international duty or overseas employment.

As a fan, the end of the domestic season is an opportunity for other sporting interests to crowd in. As an administrator, autumn is the season of hellos and goodbyes, recruitment interviews, sponsor and membership renewals, budgeting and strategic planning. It is as if a deluge of work has been held back by the activity of cricket itself. Only once that necessary focus on the sport is removed can preparations for the next season begin in earnest.

As has been well reported, including here, Sussex Cricket is operating under “special measures” imposed by the England and Wales Cricket Board as a result of past poor financial management and governance failings. While this has added to the list of essential tasks that are dominating our diaries right now, a trawl of specialist cricket media and announcements from other counties reveals that we are far from alone in having to reshape our leadership and playing roster. The merry-go-round of talent is spinning faster than ever, the money in global franchise cricket proving its accelerator.

Just this week we welcomed new men’s head coach Matt Walker to his first day of work at our County Ground. The first members of his squad will arrive back for fitness conditioning work in a couple of weeks. We were also delighted to announce the appointment of our new CEO, Beth Barrett-Wild, who has most recently spent 13 years at the ECB in leadership roles in women’s cricket, including as tournament director at this summer’s ICC Women’s T20 World Cup. The response to Beth from within cricket and sport more widely has been phenomenally positive. In between, we appointed five new directors, completing a refresh of the board that began earlier in the year.

“The opportunity to lead and help shape the future of the oldest professional cricket club in the world is something eight-year-old Beth could only have dreamt of.”

Beth Barrett-Wild on her appointment as Sussex Cricket CEO

In the next couple of days we will hopefully go public with the hiring of a new director of cricket. Next up after that, a couple of player signings and a high-profile former cricketer to be nominated to our members as Sussex Cricket’s next president.

All of this activity is taking place against the backdrop of movements elsewhere across the sport as well as rumours and misdirections. It may be that the growing propensity of many news outlets to report on overseas matches from UK sofas rather than sending correspondents abroad has increased the gossip quotient. Idle hands and minds and all that. Or, just as likely, editor demands for 24hr rolling updates. I confess it’s fun and frustrating in equal measure to be in the maelstrom.

The strategic planning at all first class counties, and the ECB itself as the sport’s national ruling body, is currently dominated by talk of the next round of TV rights deals, both here and internationally. The strong sense is that values will likely be flat at best, with a very real risk that they will be down. If so, the financial consequences would be felt throughout cricket.

The biggest single contributor to the ECB’s revenues is broadcast income. Remember, unlike the FA in football and the RFU in rugby, the ECB does not own its own ground and all the income opportunities that come with ownership of Wembley and Twickenham. If the Indian TV market softens on cricket, that’s less money for the International Cricket Council, and hence less to be distributed by it to the ECB. If Sky TV in turn were to bid less for domestic cricket rights, that’s less income again for the ECB.

Forget next year’s Ashes and all the talk of steep ticket prices, the only years in which the ECB turns a profit are when India play a Test series here. All down to TV revenue.

One link down the chain, payments from the ECB represent the biggest single element of Sussex’s income, as is the case for most of our county counterparts. You’ll appreciate, then, that there is an urgency about our search both for new commercial income and for different ways to monetise the use of our ground – after all, cricket is only played there around 50 times a year.

We need, too, to explore ways to inject fresh capital into our business while preserving the precious engagement with our members – both individuals and local clubs – who are our owners. Buy what is in effect a season ticket and you become an owner of Sussex Cricket, which is a fantastic protection for our heritage that stretches back to 1839, but can also be a constraint to investment. Too early to say what if anything we might want to propose on this front, but we can’t not have the debate given the imperative to be financially self-sustaining in a world of high inflation and possibly lower income trickling down from the sport’s Indian TV mothership.

For now, though, it’s diaries at the ready for the release of the 2027 fixture calendar later this month. Hope to see you in Hove in April and beyond!

Fight for the right to party

No doubt LA28 will be the brashest, noisiest Olympics and Paralympics yet. I’m intrigued in that context by a Sky News report that the US Olympic and Paralympic Committee has engaged advisors to try and sell a stake in Team USA’s commercial rights. 

Smart timing and a bold move if true – one which perhaps could only work in the massive American market. It may be too late for any fresh funds raised to boost medal prospects for 2028, but we should expect enormous US success on home soil regardless. And it might help Team USA put a lock on future medal tables. Over to you Team GB.

Seven nation army

If Andy Burnham wants a sense of the challenge in mounting a successful bid to host the 2040 Olympics and Paralympics in the north of England, he need only reflect on the list of seven nations that have formally expressed an interest in hosting the 2036 Games: Germany, Hungary, India, Qatar, South Africa, South Korea, Turkey.

The International Olympic Committee will conclude its choice of host in early 2029. Whichever countries get close but fall just short may well reload for 2040. My money remains on 2048 for Great Britain, 100 years on from the second London Olympics.

    As Ukraine’s domestic defence-tech sector has rapidly scaled through wartime innovation and decentralized procurement, the military relationship between the West and Ukraine is evolving into a symbiotic exchange, says Tom Bailey

    When Russian tanks streamed over Ukraine’s border in 2022, Western military aid was vital for Ukraine’s heroic defence. But as the war has ground on, Ukraine is increasingly becoming reliant upon its own locally developed and produced technology and weapons. In April this year, the Ukrainian government noted that over 50 per cent of weapons used on the frontline were Ukrainian-made. Ukraine’s Defence Procurement Agency reported that 95 per cent of the drones it procured were Ukrainian-made. 

    This was largely achieved through the necessity of war. In the early days of the war, civilian volunteers were adapting commercially available drones for military use, often working directly with frontline units. Since then, Ukraine’s government has initiated reforms and policies that have led to the number of Ukrainian defence-tech companies growing from 10 in 2022 to 1,500 by 2025.

    These companies have been able to develop and adapt their technologies in real-world conditions, with soldiers reporting back on the effectiveness of different weapons. An interesting attempt to harness this is through the launch of the Brave1 marketplace. Units within Ukraine’s military earn “points” for verified successful strikes or missions, with more awarded for higher value categories. These points are then used by the unit to buy military equipment, including drones, from a list of approved vendors. Drones deemed the highest performing by those whose lives are on the line are likely to receive more orders. Around 600,000 drones have been ordered via the market-place since the start of the year.

    The benefits of the marketplace

    This “marketplace”, however, goes beyond providing a real-time feedback loop. Rather than relying upon government officials to determine which drone should be bought from which supplier in which quantity, Ukraine has decentralised these decisions. As often happens in centralised systems, those at the top may have inadequate information or not appreciate certain nuances in all situations or environments. Better, at least in some instances, to trust those on the ground, risking their lives, to choose which drone will best serve their specific mission. At a recent Brave1 event I attended in London, this marketplace was directly contrasted with the almost centrally planned way military procurement often works – a comparison that resonates in a country trying to shake off its Soviet legacy.  

    This marketplace approach also lowers the barriers to entry for smaller companies looking to sell their drones. Globally, smaller defence manufacturers often struggle to secure big government contracts without first showing their ability to manufacture at scale. Yet without those contracts, scaling production can be difficult. Ukraine has found an innovative way around this problem. 

    Despite Rheinmetall’s CEO once dismissing Ukraine’s drone industry as “housewives” with 3-D printers in the kitchen, there is growing interest among global defence companies in partnering with or acquiring Ukrainian defence-tech companies

    So, despite Rheinmetall’s CEO once dismissing Ukraine’s drone industry as “housewives” with 3-D printers in the kitchen, there is growing interest among global defence companies in partnering with or acquiring Ukrainian defence-tech companies. According to the Kyiv School of Economics, at least 180 defence-industry partnerships have been initiated between Ukrainian and foreign companies since the war began.

    Earlier this year, Ukrainian drone company General Cherry signed a letter of intent with Finnish defence company Patria to manufacture drones. General Cherry has consistently topped Ukraine’s rankings tables for verified battlefield strikes. Another drone company, Skyfall, has partnered with Airbus to develop air defence technologies. Nasdaq-listed Swarmer, which provides AI-software for drones, is currently in the process of acquiring Ratel Robotics, a Ukrainian firm which produces unmanned ground vehicles. Draganfly, a Canadian-drone maker, has made an investment in DoD Solution, an Estonian-Ukrainian drone software company. 

    So while at the beginning of the war, Ukraine depended heavily on Western weapons, as Europe confronts its own geopolitical vulnerability, it is starting to find itself depending on Ukrainian ones. The defence relationship between the West and Ukraine is becoming symbiotic.

    Just after 8pm last Saturday, it struck me that every single person on the Northern line train to Tooting was not just in a Halloween costume, but in an elaborate Halloween costume. We’re not talking about low-effort zombie boys with muscle-revealing t-shirt rips, or girls dressed as scary bunnies. 

    Instead, the carriage was full of high effort, expensive and self-consciously un-flattering garb. Costumes that wouldn’t have looked out of place at Maya Jama’s Halloween party. This weekend, the ascendant TV star underwent a full transformation, helped by an extensive team, to become the spitting image of Olympic gold medalist and national treasure Mo Farah. Jama proved that a step-change is complete: People are willing to put major effort, imagination and funds into dressing up for Halloween. 

    And I mention Maya Jama because she is becoming a fully-fledged national treasure herself, following a barnstorming run on Celebrity Traitors. The game show format rivals Strictly and the World Cup with 10m+ viewership figures straight out of the 20th century. Surely, no media watcher a decade ago could have predicted that an elevated parlour game could so totally capture the public imagination. 

    But, perversely, the strength of our finest TV format reveals a weakness in our economy: Brits are indulging in a world of pretend. The seemingly unending economic good times of the 2000s gave us a taste for the glossless, ultra-realism of Big Brother. Now, with an economy on the brink of calamity, we want precisely the opposite. 

    Britain descends into fantasy-land

    It’s a pattern that crops up over time. At the close of the 1970s, that decade of high inflation with so many parallels to now, Brits could look to Rocky Horror and Adam and the Ants, whose vivid colours could distract from power cuts and rubbish piling up outside. The Winter of Discontent spurred on the birth of Punk and New Wave in its wake.

    A little further back, London had a particular costume moment in the mid 18th century, as the city was gripped by the devastating “gin craze” that would ultimately halve its birth rate. The ‘Masquerade Mania’ centred around subversive, cross-class gatherings in big London venues, slammed by cultural critics for drunkenness and degeneracy. 

    Back to 2026, and that cultural mishmash of masquerade and mischief is firmly back in. My colleague Anna wrote a great dispatch from a Renaissance Faire, where the open displays of ‘Furry’ sub-culture could not overshadow the truly mainstream status of high fantasy at its climactic masked ball – powered by the unquestionable goldmine that is ‘Romantasy’. 

    And I have spent an unnerving chunk of the last year delving into the commercial success surrounding our current fantasy boom, from Dungeons and Dragons to a trading card convention that spanned much of the Excel Centre. It means that I will be on the Comic Con press email list forever, but more importantly signals that there is serious money in escapism.

    And that’s serious money that isn’t necessarily being spent on house deposits, or invested in the FTSE 100. It’s a phenomenon that Leonard Lauder, the former chair of Estee Lauder, dubbed the ‘Lipstick Effect’. When the expected ladder of purchases – a holiday, a car, a property – is suddenly kicked away by deflated wages and poor growth, dopamine boosting luxuries are put on the menu. 

    We are doom-spending

    The impulse to spend is a strange kind of commercial self-soothing, which has fueled an experience economy peddling £300 concert tickets to a generation of forever renters. Glastonbury tickets sold out in 40 minutes in the year that prices breached £400. 

    The effect is magnified in the US, which just delivered a comprehensive rebuke to its unpopular President. Just because consumer confidence is low, it doesn’t necessarily put a lid on frivolous consumer spending. And booming consumer spend does nothing to stem inflation.

    We’ve seen this all over the place. Apple has set an iPhone sales record this year, even with the price of its latest models starting well in advance of £1,100 (with its foldable Duo starting at a mind-boggling £1,999). This was, in part, helped by consistent warnings from the press that prices would go up even more for consumers who waited too long to upgrade their phones. 

    But Halloween costumes are, surely, the ultimate example of this effect: Elaborate, one-use, unrepeatable. While the pressure to meet social media body image ideals is well-chronicled, who complains of the peer pressure to go all in on Halloween? One social media creator spent hours with make up artists perfecting her Halloween look, an uncanny Jeremy Clarkson. And the clip of her, flanked by Hammond and May, striding down the Top Gear test track has scored more than 16m views on Instagram. 

    Britain is enchanted by make-believe, and the root cause is fairly prosaic. It’s all very well to get stuck into London 2012 in a world of zero interest rates and solid wage growth, or to boogie to Britpop at the End of History. But now, in a zombie economy, it is not surprising that the public are keener to play in the world of the undead. And our Halloween parties mark the eve of an economic winter.

    Entrepreneurship is no longer a niche career choice, but a mainstream route into work for a generation being written out of traditional employment, writes Steve Hare

    The government has rightly recognised that young people are finding it harder to get onto the first rung of the traditional career ladder, and have thrown around a number of measures to solve it. But they would do well to acknowledge that entrepreneurship is just as legitimate a route into the workplace, and it’s one young people are taking up by themselves.  

    The Chancellor’s Autumn Budget did contain encouraging steps for young people hoping to start a business in England. The announcement of a Young Entrepreneurs Allowance will help cover living costs for young people in their first year of running a business, sending signals that this government is pro-entrepreneurial activity. But more could be done. Young people are not just in need of economic help, but would also benefit from mentoring with practical guidance, or a youth version of ‘Help to Grow’ that could provide the digital skills and AI capabilities needed to turn an idea into a viable business.

    Helping young people into employment through apprenticeships, graduate programmes and other routes remains essential. But we should be giving just as much attention to those who want to create a job for themselves. Starting a business is a legitimate route into work, and successful businesses can go on to create jobs for others. Indeed, analysis from economics consultancy Cebr suggests that helping even five per cent of these young people move into self-employment could create almost £4bn of additional economic value by 2029.

    Youth self-employment is at record highs

    Our research highlights that young people aren’t waiting around anymore. Youth self-employment has reached its highest level in a decade, with 27,500 more under-25s working for themselves than in 2022. Technology, particularly AI, has the potential to make that route both more accessible and affordable by providing access to capabilities that would previously have required specialist expertise. 

    People like Olivia Regan, 23, for example, who launched her Solihull-based cleaning company in 2024 after leaving school without GCSEs. Her business now supports a network of freelancers, with monthly revenues reaching £10,000. Olivia uses AI tools to set pricing, generate marketing ideas and identify new customers.

    Christina Davis, 25, founder of a Newcastle-based growth marketing business, took a different route. Having qualified as a doctor, she built an online audience as a hobby during the pandemic. Christina began running her marketing business full-time in January 2026, and within three months, she had matched her previous salary. She now serves clients around the world, using AI to help identify leads and analyse marketing performance.

    Their businesses are very different, but both show what young people can achieve when they have the opportunity to put their ideas into practice and run with it. Technology can help make starting and running a business easier, but the ambition and hard work still come from the individual. 

    It’s clear that a new generation is ready to turn its ideas and ambition into businesses. The challenge now is to give more young people the confidence and support to take the self-employment route, and to recognise entrepreneurship as an important part of the answer to the UK’s youth employment crisis.

    Steve Hare is CEO at Sage

    Britain can lead on AI, but only if its firms can get the power to build it, write Grant Shapps and James Marks 

    One of us runs an AI business in London and is asked every few weeks by investors when he’s moving to America. The other spent years in government, including as defence secretary, worrying about what happens when a country relies on infrastructure it doesn’t control. We’ve reached the same conclusion from different directions. Britain’s AI ambitions are stalling because British firms can’t get the computing power they need on fair terms. 

    Compute is the processing power AI runs on. It is becoming as fundamental to the economy as electricity, and as strategically important as energy security. Last week’s Budget showed the government is finally waking up to understand this. The new British Data Centre Covenant offers priority grid access to developers who invest in jobs, local communities and water. There’s £500m for AI safety and security, and £140m to back British AI companies. 

    The direction is right, but the investment landscape is less forgiving. Last month Microsoft walked away from a planned AI data centre in Essex because it couldn’t secure power in time. More than 70GW of data centre projects are queuing for the grid, against roughly 5GW the system operator expects to connect by 2030. Businesses pay almost double what they did for electricity in 2019. Investors notice these things, and capital is mobile.

    This is a resilience question as much as an economic one. A country whose hospitals, banks and defence systems increasingly run on AI cannot afford to have its most innovative companies priced out of the compute they need, or to rely on a handful of overseas providers for capacity it cannot secure at home. 

    Five companies now hold an estimated 71 per cent of the world’s AI compute, and four of them plan to spend around $725bn on infrastructure this year. Whoever controls compute increasingly shapes who can build AI, where, and on what terms.

    Keeping sensitive data on British soil is welcome, but it means little if British firms can’t get that capacity on fair terms. Often they can’t. Compute is bought in an opaque market, listed prices rarely match what’s paid, quotes expire before finance signs them off and the biggest buyers get the best deals. A British start-up is negotiating against the world’s largest companies.

    That’s what’s at stake. If only the biggest players get a fair price, Britain’s AI firms will build on someone else’s terms, or leave. Every founder who moves to San Francisco takes the jobs, tax and know-how with them.

    Britain must seize the opportunity in front of us. This technology can help deliver the much-needed economic growth and sovereignty Britain needs in an increasingly volatile world. Growth on this scale, however, does not come without consequences. AI is already having profound effects on ecosystems and workforces across the globe, and the companies driving that change need to take responsibility for those consequences before they become impossible to reverse.

    Government announcements won’t fix this alone, and industry doesn’t need to wait to be told what to do. The Covenant sets a floor: build here, and give back to the communities that host you. The whole industry should meet that standard. If you help build something this powerful, you share responsibility for what it does.

    That’s why Canopy is committing a share of its profit to a new founders’ initiative, and why in January we’ll be at Davos working with others to do the same. The early focus is on four areas: the communities that host AI’s infrastructure, so they share the benefits as well as the costs; workers whose jobs AI is changing; young people who lack access to AI and computing education; and independent research on AI’s real footprint.

    Responsible growth doesn’t slow investment. It makes infrastructure secure and trusted by the communities that host it. EY found firms with stronger responsible AI practices were more likely to report gains of 80 per cent across efficiency and innovation.

    Britain has the universities, the talent and the capital markets to lead. What it needs now is a compute market that works for everyone, not just the biggest players, and an industry ready to take responsibility for the future it’s building.

    We want that future built in Britain. Let’s make it easier for firms to stay.

    Sir Grant Shapps is a former secretary of state for defence and secretary of state for energy. James Marks is the founder and CEO of Canopy

    If you are old enough to remember 70s London you will have heard of Big Biba, the fashion retailer that expanded into a huge, seven-storey department store on Kensington High Street in 1974.

    The opening of Big Biba mesmerised Londoners: the shopping experience was unlike anything else. The walls were adorned with groovy patterns while decadent displays and massive art-deco statues intersected the aisles. There was an enormous neon-lit restaurant, the “rainbow room”, which quickly became stuffed with A-list celebs, and above that stood the capital’s biggest roof garden, policed by a troop of pink flamingos, who strutted around its perimeter. It was part-department store, part-Disneyland.

    I, alas, am too young to remember Biba, but I’m enthralled by all the photos I have found of it online. Among my favourites is one taken in the food hall, which, remarkably, made canned food look glamorous. The hall housed huge shelving units, each six foot high, designed to resemble what they were selling: a giant can of Heinz beans, an enormous tin of sardines.

    Punters flocked to Kensington in their millions. But despite its enormous initial fame, Big Biba would go on to last barely more than a year before shutting its doors (the building now houses an M&S, H&M, a luxury gym and the newsroom of the Daily Mail).

    And as Biba fell out of fashion, so too has Britain’s love for tinned food. As a rough estimate to how well-stocked our pantries are with non-perishables, I had a peruse through the government’s family food statistics dating back to the 1970s.

    Taking together the eight categories I looked at – canned beans, fruit, peas, beef, potatoes, tomatoes and beans – there is a clear trend: our consumption of canned stuff has declined sharply in favour of fresh alternatives.

    The total amount purchased per person per week across these eight categories peaked at just over 450 grams in 1976, and has almost halved over the past half-century.

    The decline is particularly acute for canned peas (down 90 per cent) and tinned fruit (down 85 per cent), while sales of soup (down 47 per cent) and beans (down 18 per cent) have fallen more modestly.

    But two areas buck the trend: canned tomatoes, sales of which have more than doubled, and tinned fish, which has grown just as fast. That is in part, I think, because innovative retailers have found a way to add a Biba-like touch of glamour to these foodstuffs.

    While a can of potatoes is about as chic as a Noel Edmonds autobiography, followers of foodie fashion are willing to pay eye-watering amounts for tinned fish. A high-end can of anchovies retails for as much as £50, and white tuna £60. The website The Tinned Fish Market offers gift subscriptions for £325.

    Last week Andy Burnham told Brits we need to stock up on at least three days’ worth of tinned food, to prepare us for a crisis. Might this trigger a resurgence in premium tinned products across the board, a la anchovies? Can it create a new market for those who want to live out the last days of the apocalypse with a culinary climax? I think our supermarkets are leaving money on the table.

    Investors cut their exposure to equities last month, turning to bonds and money market funds, as UK-focused funds suffered another wave of withdrawals.

    UK investors withdrew £1bn from equity funds in October, up from £858m the prior month, marking the sixteenth month of outflows in the last seventeen, according to the latest fund flow index from Calastone.

    It also marked the ninth largest month on record for outflows. Since the start of the year equities have suffered outflows of around £6.8bn.

    UK equity funds shed £815m, a sharp uptick from September’s £708m of withdrawals. Since the start of the year outflows have reached £5.3bn.

    Buyers step back

    But Calastone said the rise in equity fund outflows reflected a sharp fall in buying compared to an increase in selling, as sell orders fell just 0.3 per cent month on month.

    Meanwhile, daily trading figures did not indicate a swell of activity in the lead up to this year’s Autumn Budget which had previously been recorded under Healey’s predecessor.

    “In a welcome change from recent form, the Budget left little immediate trace,” said Edward Glyn head of global markets at Calastone.

    “Moreover, because October’s higher outflow was driven by a lack of buyers, not an increase in selling, it does not suggest a repeat of investors rushing to crystallise gains ahead of a feared capital gains tax increase.”

    But amid wider outflows, emerging market equities stood out once more, attracting £131m, as investors continue to seek opportunities away from concentrated Western markets.

    Despite a slight decrease from the £133m of inflows last month, the sector is the only one to attract new money across each of the last three months.

    The gloom in the domestic market was felt across the Atlantic, as North American outflows accelerated to £164m, a further £40m loss from September.

    Global funds lost £229m, while European and Japanese sector-focused funds also reported net selling.

    Passive funds slump as money market shine

    Passive funds also reported their first negative month since August 2023, losing £44m, indicating that the pullback from equities goes beyond pressure on active managers. Active funds saw outflows of £1.4bn.

    In contrast, investors continued to pile into “safe-haven” money market funds, adding £516m, the strongest inflows seen since the Budget-related November 2025 surge.

    Glyn credited the enthusiasm to “a continuing appetite to keep capital readily available” amid ongoing geopolitical and market uncertainty.

    Investors also added more to bond funds, but inflows slowed to £302m from £655m last month.

Most people protect their digital lives with a handful of passwords they've memorized—a security practice so common it's become catastrophic.]]>

For about five months, a browser extension sat quietly on the home computers of 154 people and watched them log in.

The researchers never saw a password. Everything was hashed on the machine before it went anywhere, leaving them with the shape of each one: its length, its mix of characters, the site it was typed into, and whether the same string had appeared before.

Very often, it had.

What 154 people actually typed

Sarah Pearman and her co-authors at Carnegie Mellon University presented the results at a 2017 computer security conference, having followed each participant for an average of 147 days. Those people logged in across 26 web domains apiece and covered the lot with fewer than 10 distinct passwords.

Roughly 60 per cent of those distinct passwords were recycled, either typed identically on another site or built around a chunk of four or more characters lifted from one the same person used elsewhere.

Banking got no special treatment. Around 85 per cent of the passwords on financial sites appeared elsewhere too, and nearly all of that crossover ran into unrelated categories, so the login for a savings account was also the login for a shoe shop.

What partial reuse looks like up close

Mostly it looks like adding a character.

Among passwords that shared a substring with another, the most common gap between the two was a single character. Digits were the strongest predictor in the Carnegie Mellon model, multiplying the odds of reuse by more than twelve. The authors’ own explanation is that a password with a number in it satisfies more websites’ fussy signup rules, so it travels further.

The tidy minority had barely any accounts

Ten participants mostly built something new for each site, which sounds like a win for good habits until you look at what they were doing online. With one exception, every one of them entered passwords on eight domains or fewer, and they were active on their computers on only 17 per cent of the days they spent enrolled.

The heavy users went the other way. Ninety-four participants, the largest cluster by far, both copied passwords outright and modified them, and they averaged 32 online accounts each. Discipline held up fine at eight accounts and collapsed at thirty.

The password manager result, with a handbrake

Only 19 of the 154 participants had a password manager installed, and the study found no measurable effect on either reuse or strength.

That result deserves caution. One paper is one paper, the subgroup is tiny, and the software could not tell whether people were generating random strings or merely parking passwords they had invented themselves. Rick Wash and colleagues at Michigan State University, who watched 134 participants over six weeks, found each password being reused on 1.7 to 3.4 websites. Their study did not measure partial reuse at all, so the higher figure out of Pittsburgh partly reflects counting a habit nobody had counted before.

Why a recycled password is worth money

Somewhere there is a text file with an old forum password in it, sitting in a folder alongside a few hundred million others. Troy Hunt, the Australian security researcher behind the breach notification service Have I Been Pwned, has documented the trade in combo lists, which are exactly that: vast dumps of email and password pairs scraped out of past breaches. Cheap automated tools fire them at unrelated websites until one opens. Defending against it is awkward, because a successful run looks identical to a customer logging in correctly.

One shared string, and the breach at a defunct hobby forum becomes a problem at an email provider.

The rules that encouraged this have been withdrawn

In 2025, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology finalised revision 4 of its digital identity guidelines, and the password section reads like a quiet apology. Websites must stop demanding mixtures of character types, and they must stop forcing periodic changes unless there is evidence of compromise. Password managers and autofill have to be allowed, and every new password gets checked against blocklists of strings already known to have leaked.

Each of those requirements targets the behaviour the extension recorded: a handful of memorable strings, nudged sideways by a digit, stretched across an entire online life.

The standard now assumes a machine is doing the remembering. Anyone who ever stuck a “1” on the end to get past a signup form was just covering the shift until it arrived.

]]> A telemarketer refused to keep his webcam on for nine hours a day while working from home and was fired the next day — a Dutch court ruled the demand invaded his privacy and ordered his employer to pay him roughly €75,000 https://siliconcanals.com/d-a-telemarketer-refused-to-keep-his-webcam-on-for-nine-hours-a-day-while-working-from-home-and-was-fired-the-next-day-a-dutch-court-ruled-the-demand-invaded-his-privacy-and-ordered-his-employ/ Tue, 22 Sep 2026 14:15:27 +0000 https://siliconcanals.com/?p=109737

A Dutch court sided with a worker who refused constant video surveillance, forcing his employer to pay damages—a warning shot across the evolving battle over remote work monitoring.]]>

A camera that stayed switched off cost a Florida software company about 75,000 euros.

It belonged to a telemarketer working from the small Dutch town of Diessen, employed since January 2019 by Chetu, an American software firm that at the time ran a Dutch office in Rijswijk. On 23 August 2022 he was told to join something called the Corrective Action Program, which meant staying logged in for his whole shift, sharing his screen and leaving his laptop camera on. He shared the screen. The camera stayed dark.

His objection was brief and entirely unlegalistic. Court filings quoted by The Register record him saying he was not comfortable being monitored for nine hours a day, calling it “an invasion of my privacy” and noting that his laptop activity was already visible to management.

Two more instructions followed, each firmer than the last. On 26 August he was dismissed on the spot, the stated reasons being refusal to work and insubordination.

Three days from the first instruction to the sack.

What the company argued

Chetu’s case, set out in the published judgment of the Court of Zeeland-West-Brabant, was that watching a remote worker through a webcam is no different from a manager walking past a desk. Performance software already sat on the man’s laptop, and that was not considered enough. Chetu wanted to see him working.

Nobody from the company turned up to make the argument in person, as TechCrunch noted, so it went undefended.

What the judge decided

Ruling on 28 September 2022, the subdistrict judge in Tilburg found that ordering an employee to keep a camera running for a full shift conflicted with his right to respect for private life, and that nothing had been offered to justify it. An unreasonable instruction cannot be unreasonably refused, so there had been no refusal to work and no grounds for summary dismissal.

Data protection law dropped out early. On the understanding that no footage would be recorded, stored or used for anything, the judge treated the monitoring as falling outside data processing altogether, and tested it directly against Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, alongside Strasbourg case law holding that filming staff at work, covert or not, is a serious intrusion into private life. Had the images been kept, the analysis would have looked quite different.

One much-quoted line deserves care. Coverage including a report in Fortune presented the claim that all-day camera tracking is disproportionate and not allowed in the Netherlands as a finding of the court. In the Dutch record it sits among the employee’s own submissions. What the judge actually held was narrower, and sufficient: this instruction, to this man, in his own home, breached Article 8 with no justification advanced.

Why the sum was so large

Almost none of the money was a penalty for the privacy breach. The largest slice, 50,000 euros, was a billijke vergoeding, an equitable award Dutch judges reserve for employers whose conduct in ending a job has been seriously culpable, with a wrongful summary dismissal among the standard triggers, as the Amsterdam employment firm Workx Advocaten explains. Privacy is why the sacking failed. The sacking is what got billed.

Around that sat roughly 8,375 euros for ignoring the notice period, close to 9,500 euros in statutory transition payment, more than 2,700 euros in unpaid wages, 23 days of untaken leave, the 8 per cent holiday allowance and some 585 euros in costs, all itemised by NL Times. His non-compete clause was lifted as well, leaving him free to walk to a competitor.

How common all-day camera rules are

Is this a bizarre one-off or a policy plenty of people are quietly living with? A survey of 1,000 business leaders at mostly remote companies, commissioned by ResumeBuilder in March 2023, found 37 per cent required staff to sit on a live video feed, and that 93 per cent of those firms had somebody monitoring it, usually for four hours or more a day.

The same survey found 73 per cent had dismissed workers on the strength of monitoring data, and 69 per cent had lost staff who would not accept it.

One survey is one survey. It polled American executives, it relied on self-reporting, and executives describing their own management habits are not a neutral instrument. Treat it as a temperature reading rather than a census.

Where the line actually falls

Whatever this settles, it settles in one jurisdiction, on one set of facts, at the lowest rung of the court system. Article 8 offers nothing in Florida, where employment is generally at will and can end without a stated reason, subject to the usual exceptions for discrimination, retaliation and whatever a contract says.

What the case supplies is a price tag on a boundary that remote-work policy has been drifting across without much thought: supervising the work is one thing, keeping a lens open in somebody’s house for the length of a shift is another. A Dutch judge has now looked at that question once, and the employer left lighter.

The idealised 90-to-9-minute ratio implies about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging; early access is planned for the first half of 2027.

Agility Robotics has unveiled Digit 5, the fifth generation of its bipedal warehouse robot, and the headline change is the safety cage — specifically, its absence. Earlier Digit models, like most industrial robots, operated inside fenced cells to keep people out of reach. Digit 5 is designed to work in the open, using sensors and a separate safety controller that can make it stop, back away or drop into a seated position when a person gets close, according to the company’s hardware rundown from The Robot Report.

The robot stands 5 feet 11 inches tall and weighs 284 pounds, roughly the mass of two adult humans packed into a torso, legs and a pair of articulated arms. That weight matters less as a curiosity than as context for what follows: a machine that heavy needs a battery system that can be recharged fast enough to stay useful across a full shift, and Agility has built its pitch to investors and warehouse customers around exactly that number.

The 90-minute run, nine-minute charge math

Digit 5 runs for about 90 minutes on a charge and returns to full power in roughly 9 minutes, a figure Agility frames as a 10-to-1 run-to-charge ratio, up from the 2-to-1 ratio it says the previous Digit 4 managed, per the company’s own announcement. In practical terms, that means a robot could in theory swap onto a charger for the length of a coffee break and be back on the floor before a human coworker finishes one.

The idealised arithmetic gives each 99-minute cycle 90 minutes of runtime and nine minutes of charging. Repeating that ratio across 24 hours yields about 21.8 hours of runtime and 2.2 hours of charging before allowing for maintenance, handoffs or faults. That is the basis for the company’s more conservative claim that Digit 5 can deliver more than 20 productive hours in a 24-hour day.

Agility is measuring two things and projecting a third. The 90-minute runtime and 9-minute recharge are specifications the company attaches to Digit 5’s battery hardware. The “more than 20 productive hours” figure is a company calculation built from those two hardware numbers, assuming charging cycles that fit cleanly around a robot’s task queue — no downtime, faults or maintenance stops of the kind that show up in real operations. Agility has not published an independent customer-floor validation of a Digit 5 working day yet.

Independent reporting on the launch has generally repeated the 20-hour figure as Agility’s claim rather than as a verified outcome. IEEE Spectrum’s Evan Ackerman, reviewing Digit 5, raised a broader doubt about Agility’s underlying assumption that the robot can function as what he called “a more or less effortless drop-in replacement for human labor,” noting he was not sure that had happened yet with any robot, anywhere. Alongside the battery changes, Agility increased what Digit 5 can physically do. Both changes target the same use case Agility has pursued since the original Digit: moving totes, boxes and cases between conveyors, shelving and pallets in warehouses and distribution centers, work currently done by human “pickers” and “stockers.”

How Digit 5 compares with Boston Dynamics’ Atlas

Agility is not the only company chasing this category, and the comparison is not entirely favorable to Digit 5 on paper. Boston Dynamics’ electric Atlas, per the same Forbes report, is rated to carry up to 66 pounds, reach 7.5 feet and run for about four hours on a hot-swappable battery pack that can be physically pulled and replaced rather than recharged in place. On payload and reach, Atlas currently claims an edge. Digit 5’s advantage is charging speed and, by extension, uptime: a fixed nine-minute recharge cycle is a different operational model than swapping battery packs, and it is the piece Agility is betting its productivity math on.

Orders, a SPAC, and a company still losing money

The timing of the announcement lines up with a corporate transition. Agility disclosed more than $300 million in multi-year customer orders for Digit 5, a figure the company itself qualifies as subject to unspecified contractual milestones being met, and it disclosed the number days after filing paperwork for a SPAC merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a deal valued at roughly $2.5 billion. Regulatory filings tied to that merger show a company still far from commercial scale: Agility net sales and losses came to $1.78 million in 2025, up from $310,000 in 2024, against an operating loss of $140.2 million that roughly doubled year over year, and an auditor’s note flagging “substantial doubt” about its ability to continue as a going concern absent further financing.

That financial picture is the backdrop against which the hardware claims should be read; it doesn’t make them false. A company preparing to go public via SPAC has a direct financial incentive to publish its most favorable operating math right before that listing, and the $300 million order figure and 20-hour productivity claim are doing real work in that narrative, alongside more grounded facts, like Amazon’s $1.05 million purchase of five Digit units — a completed transaction, not a pipeline projection.

What 2027 actually promises customers

Agility says early customer access to Digit 5 is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with general availability, aimed at manufacturing, warehouse and distribution operators, following by the end of that year. The company also plans to extend sales into the European Union and United Kingdom alongside its existing North American base, pending regulatory approval in those markets. Those dates put Digit 5’s actual commercial debut several months out from this week’s unveiling, and every performance figure attached to the robot right now, from its 90-minute runtime to its 20-hour workday, is a specification and a projection. Still, this has not yet been measured on a customer floor.

Markus Villig was 19 in 2013, fresh out of high school in Tallinn, and frustrated with how hard it was to get a reliable taxi in his own city. He borrowed €5,000 from his family to build a first version of an app, then did the unglamorous part himself: walking up to taxi drivers on the street in Tallinn and persuading them, one at a time, to sign up. Revenue kept climbing through all of it. Profit didn’t.

Operating profit told a similar story of a company just crossing the line, at €19.5 million, reversed from the prior year’s €87.7 million loss. A margin that thin is not really a statement about profitability so much as a statement about intent. Estonia’s population stood at 1,360,745 at the start of 2026, according to Statistics Estonia. That is smaller than many single cities. Out of it has come ten companies that reached a billion-dollar valuation at some point in their history, among them Skype, Wise, Bolt, Pipedrive, Playtech and Veriff, according to Invest in Estonia’s own tally.

Using CB Insights’ underlying company data alongside that population figure, a figure Invest in Estonia and outlets including Fintech Baltic put at roughly 7.1 unicorns per million residents, based on Invest in Estonia’s cumulative count of companies that have ever reached $1B — not a live ranking CB Insights itself publishes, second only to Liechtenstein and more than three times the United States’ rate of about 2.2 per million.

That per-capita figure is a calculation built on CB Insights’ data, not a ranking CB Insights itself publishes, and it is worth reading as a proxy for the ecosystem’s density rather than a formal league table.

The tiger leap that came before the unicorns

This density didn’t happen by accident, and it didn’t start with a startup. In 1996, five years after regaining independence from the Soviet Union, Estonia launched a state programme called Tiigrihüpe, or Tiger Leap, championed by future president Toomas Hendrik Ilves and education minister Jaak Aaviksoo. Its goal was blunt: wire the country’s schools for computers and the internet as a deliberate act of catching up. It worked faster than almost anyone expected.

The rollout was rapid but not instantaneous. Education Estonia says all schools had computers by 2000 and all were connected to the internet by 2001. Two decades later, in 2014, the government extended the same instinct outward with e-Residency, a digital identity scheme that lets people anywhere in the world register and run an Estonian company online, without granting them any right to actually live there. Neither programme produced a unicorn by itself. What they produced was a population that treated computers as ordinary tools a generation before most of Europe did, and a legal and administrative system built to let a small number of people start companies with very little friction.

Skype itself has since been folded into Microsoft and no longer exists as a standalone business, but it left something behind in Tallinn that the other nine companies on the list arguably needed first: a generation of engineers and early employees who had already helped build something that scaled to hundreds of millions of users, and who knew, from direct experience, that it could be done from Estonia rather than London or Silicon Valley.

According to the company’s own account of its founding, on Wise’s own history page, the two of them started by simply swapping money directly with each other every month, at the real mid-market exchange rate, to avoid their banks’ fees and markups. That pattern, alumni from one successful company seeding the next, is common in tech clusters generally, but it is unusually visible in a country as small as Estonia, where the total pool of experienced software engineers was never large to begin with, and where a handful of Skype veterans and their networks touch a disproportionate share of what came after. It wasn’t only talent that recirculated. Toivo Annus, one of Skype’s founding engineers who led its engineering team until the eBay sale, went on to co-found Ambient Sound Investments with three other early Skype engineers in 2003, a private investment firm that has since backed more than 50 early-stage ventures, according to documented accounts of his career. Annus died in 2020, but the firm he helped start is still one of the more active early-stage investors operating out of Tallinn, another channel through which Skype’s original payout kept funding whatever came next.

The ecosystem underneath those ten companies is larger and more active than the unicorn count alone suggests. A per-capita unicorn count says nothing about how many of those companies are still worth a billion dollars today, still headquartered in Estonia, or profitable. Playtech moved its primary listing to London years ago. Skype no longer trades as an independent business at all. What the figure does capture, reliably, is how much outsized technology output a small population has produced relative to its size, whatever has happened to any individual company since, and how much of that output traces back to a single, now-defunct voice-calling app and the state’s own earlier bet on wiring its classrooms. For a country with fewer people than a mid-sized American county, that is the more durable claim.

The part of Vinted’s model that isn’t obvious from the outside is that listing and selling on the platform costs a seller nothing.
