]]>

Korean researchers have developed a beetle-like soft robot. Source: KAIST

When we hear the word “robot,” we still conjure up images of mechanical figures from old science fiction films. However, reality has long since evolved: We’re surrounded by smart vacuum cleaners, voice assistants, and even four-legged machines that mimic dogs. But what are these robotic animals?

They’re not just battery-powered toys. They’re complex electronic devices, infused with elements of artificial intelligence, that replicate the appearance and behavior of real or imaginary creatures.

These devices contain sensors, speakers, motors, and processor modules that analyze external signals. They’re controlled via mobile apps. Digital pets can make distinctive sounds, respond to signs of affection, answer to their names, and display a range of emotions—from delight to fear, from satisfaction to fatigue.

Manufacturers employ a variety of engineering approaches when creating these devices. Let’s look at some interesting examples.

Microrobot beetle and its relatives

A microrobot beetle might seem like a fun little gadget. But leading research centers such as the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) are working on developing similar insects (see image above).

So why are robot ants, robot beetles, and robot bees being created? The answer lies in solving practical and even humanitarian problems.

Cyborg cockroaches: Rescuers from under the ruins

In the spring of 2022, a tragedy occurred in the city of Changsha, China—a six-story building collapsed. Dozens of people were trapped under the rubble. Many remained missing for nearly six days.

Rescue efforts were hampered by piles of rubble and collapsed floors. Ultimately, 53 people died, and only 10 were rescued. In such operations, every minute is precious. Rescuers use thermal imaging cameras and comb through the rubble, but this takes precious time.

But what if cockroaches come to the rescue? These insects are fast and can penetrate even the tiniest cracks, allowing them to quickly survey the disaster area. But how can they be made to search for people? A team at Nanyang Technological University (NTU) in Singapore said it has found a solution by transforming a Madagascar cockroach into a cyborg.

A miniature backpack containing a microcomputer is attached to the insect’s back. It contains sensors that detect dangerous gas concentrations, as well as an infrared camera with a thermal imager, allowing it to detect bodies under the rubble. To prevent the insects from scattering randomly, but rather to remain confined to a specific area, the scientists have developed a remote control system.

Electrodes and a microchip are attached to the cockroach’s body. An electrical impulse to the right side causes the insect to move to the left, and vice versa. When both electrodes are activated, the cockroach accelerates and runs straight.

This cyborg can operate for long periods in rubble: the microcomputer is powered by solar panels. One individual can survey an area of up to 100 sq. m (1,076.3 sq. ft.). The operator controls the movement and monitors the signals from the sensors.

However, there’s a catch: to fully survey a large building, about 500 of these cockroaches are required, meaning 500 operators. And although the cyborg will indicate the location of the victim, it won’t be able to extract them—that’s a task for humans.

Robot ants: Strength in miniature

Stanford University engineers created mechanical ants capable of moving loads 2,000 times their own mass. For a human, this is the equivalent of moving a 150-ton whale.

Just four of these tiny animals can transport an adult, and a whole group can lift a concrete slab or rebar. This phenomenal lifting capacity was achieved thanks to a gecko-inspired paw design that provides a secure grip on any surface.

A special coating of microscopic rubber hairs creates a bio-stimulated adhesive effect: When the rope is taut, the robot adheres and releases when it is loosened.

However, this high performance requires a lot of energy. The battery can run out at critical moments, so in industrial settings, these ants are connected to a cable and used as towing vehicles.

Snake-like robot: Underwater repairman

Animal robots are capable of not only eliminating the consequences of disasters but also preventing them. Norwegian developers have created a 5 m (16.4 ft.) robotic snake for servicing underwater oil pipelines. It inspects pipelines, transmits images to a dispatcher, and, if a defect is detected, repairs it.

Equipped with manipulators at both ends, the snake can replace valves and clean deposits from pipes. These devices can operate at depths of up to 500 m (1,640.4 ft.) for up to six months, recharging at special stations.

Robot crab: Underground explorer

University of California, Berkeley, engineers developed a robotic crab for underground exploration. Using fabric scoops on its claws, it burrows into the ground, collects samples, and analyzes the soil. Equipped with sensors and a manipulator, it can determine the suitability of a site.

These robotic animals could be used in construction or agriculture, detecting pollution. In the future, such crabs are even planned for use on the Moon. Scientists are currently working on improving the design so that the robot can dig deeper.

More recently, open-source crab platforms are helping developers innovate locomotion.

Robot falcons: Airfield guardians

Mechanical falcons, developed at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands, are already in service in Canada and Germany. They frighten real birds away from runways, preventing collisions that could lead to plane crashes.

Unlike acoustic cannons, which birds quickly become accustomed to, robotic predators exploit natural fear—they not only mimic predators but also pursue live birds, demonstrating dominance.

Robot bee: Space scout

A miniature robotic bee, the size of a pinhead, was created at Harvard University. Although it can theoretically pollinate plants, its true purpose is reconnaissance. Sensors mimic the vision and antennae of insects and transmit a three-dimensional image to the operator.

This micro-reconnaissance vehicle can fly, swim, and dive. It runs on solar batteries, consuming only 120 milliwatts—less than a light bulb. Scientists are confident that these bees will be useful for exploring Martian canals, lunar craters, and even the toxic clouds of Venus.

A variety of zoomorphic robots emerges

Today, numerous robots mimic the behavior of a wide variety of animals. Their advantage is the ability to move horizontally and vertically, navigate obstacles, and penetrate hard-to-reach places.

Unlike real animals or people, they do not require food or water, making them suitable assistants in deserts, mountains, and the exploration of other planets. They could be indispensable in rescue operations and scientific research.

For example, MIT scientists created Mini Cheetah—a platform used to test algorithms for guide robots and jumping machines. Chinese engineers have developed an insect-sized model that has the properties of spiders and cockroaches. Another robotic cheetah from DARPA reached speeds of up to 18 mph.

A flexible robot, modeled after the Caenorhabditis elegans roundworm, was capable of navigating around obstacles. Gecko Robotics has commercially deployed systems equipped with suction cups for vertical movement and can operate in hazardous environments.

Submit your innovation now!

Quadrupeds follow dogs as human companions

Some four-legged robots can travel over 30 km (18.6 mi.) without recharging and carry loads of up to 180 kg (396.8 lb.). They can transport the injured and recognize voice commands.

Three years ago, Moscow State University unveiled the first such robot in Eastern Europe, costing approximately 1.5 million rubles. The Unitree Robotics A1 model, weighing 15 kg (33 lb.), was controlled by powerful electric motors. It was even tested at a zoo to observe the animals’ reactions.

After testing, the design was modified, improving access to the internal subsystems. The robot is controlled by a joystick and connected to cameras and lidar for navigation. Its basic gait is a trot, and its speed is 3.5 km/h. The dog can change its gait, shake a paw, stand up, and lie down.

Unitree introduced the As2 companion earlier this year.

Animal-inspired robots evolve

Although today there are robotic kangaroos, insects, and reptiles, the dog was the first and most common prototype. This is due to the animal’s familiarity as a human assistant. The mechanics of canine movement (walking, running, jumping) proved optimal for engineering solutions. Robo-dogs range in size from a mastiff to a Labrador.

The predecessor is considered to be Phony Pony, a Californian robot from the late 1960s. It didn’t resemble an animal much, but it already had articulated supports, sensors, and motors, becoming the forerunner of all quadrupeds.

Companion animal robots offer therapy and care

Interacting with animals can reduces stress and anxiety. There’s even pet therapy. Pets are especially beneficial for the elderly with dementia, children with mental health issues, and hospital patients.

However, live animals require care, and they are often prohibited in medical facilities. That’s where companion robots come in.

New Zealand scientists have proven that interacting with them is just as beneficial as interacting with real animals. They are hypoallergenic, don’t require food or walking, and their behavior is predictable.

Joy for All

These realistic cats and dogs from Joy for All are covered in soft fur. Cats open their mouths, blink, groom themselves, and roll over when petted. Dogs bark in response to voices, respond to hugs, and their “heartbeat” changes. They fall asleep in the dark. Touch and light sensors are built into the body.

Scientists at Brown University worked on software to transform them into assistants for the elderly. The robotic animals can remind them to take their medications and find their glasses or keys.

Jenny by Tomobot

Tomobot has designed its realistic golden Labrador puppy for the elderly and children with autism. It does not walk to avoid creating a hazard. Jenny senses touch, responds to commands (called “voice”), wags its tail, whines, and snores in its sleep.

The robotic animal contains 50 sensors, 10 motors (seven in its face), and microphones. An app allows users to name the dog and update its settings.

PARO — a harp seal

This robot animal is listed in the Guinness Book of World Records as “the most therapeutic.” Developed in Japan, it promotes relaxation and positive emotions.

The seal pup is covered in sensory whiskers and tactile sensors, moves its paws, makes sounds, recognizes its name, and responds to affection. If ignored, it cries. The charger is shaped like a pacifier, and when removed, PARO makes a disgruntled squeak. Its personality changes depending on how it’s handled.

Aibo by Sony

This sophisticated puppy featured a camera, sensors, and 22 axes of motion. Its eyes are two OLED screens. Thanks to cloud technology, aibo remembered events, developed its personality, and learned.

This robotic dog could play, bark at strangers, patrol a route, and send photos to its owner, although this was primarily for entertainment purposes. Sony discontinued sales of Aibo in June of this year, demonstrating some of the challenges with developing robots for the consumer market.

Robotic animals could become part of our lives

Robot animals are increasingly becoming a part of our lives as therapists, assistants, and friends. They are purchased for children, the elderly, and people with allergies or restrictions on pets.

In Japan, where the problem of an aging population is particularly acute, these devices have long been part of the care system. Europe and the U.S. are also actively investigating them for hospitals and nursing homes, accelerating development. Electronic animals are not just toys, but an important tool for care and rescue.

Krosheva covers topics such as digitalization, IT, the modern economy, and transhumanism. She loves computers and cyberpunk, having graduated from a technical college before graduating from the Faculty of Journalism.

Autonomous drone inspection provider Percepto this week launched Axion, a hardware-agnostic physical AI platform that marks the company’s shift to a software-first strategy. The company said it allows critical infrastructure operators to analyze data from any third-party drone or sensor network to prevent equipment failures before they escalate.

Founded in 2014, Percepto said its initial team built the technology needed for scale. The company asserted that its new management has decades of independent experience with growth across robotics, sensors, the Internet of Things (IoT), physical AI, and cybersecurity.

Percepto is based in Modi’in, Israel, with U.S. headquarters in Austin, Texas.

New executives pivot Percepto to software-first strategy

Julien Bellanger recently took the the helm from longtime CEO Dor Abuhasira alongside new revenue and marketing leadership. Percepto said the executive shifts signal its strategic pivot from a hardware-centric autonomous drone maker to a software-first physical AI provider.

“When I looked at Percepto, I saw a company that had already done the hardest part: fully autonomous drones flying real missions every day at some of the most demanding industrial sites in the country,” Bellanger told The Robot Report. “With AIM [Autonomous Inspection & Monitoring] and Axion, we’re taking that operational intelligence beyond our own fleet and opening it to the entire industry.”

The company plans to continue selling, deploying, and supporting its current product line of drones and drone docks. At the same time, manufacturing will be located onshore in the U.S. to support the American Drone Dominance Initiatives.

Submit your innovation now!

Axion extends inspection workflows

Percepto said it has designed the Axion platform to add value to inspection workflows across mission-critical operations, including upstream oil and gas, power transmission and distribution, and most downstream processing facilities.

With Axion, Percepto said it expects to work across the entire industry and to help business grow with AIM’s capabilities. The company is using compliance waivers to control and autonomously fly in one-to-many configurations. Axion will ingest all data sources and provide actionable insights with more than 160 AI models, it claimed.

“The infrastructure powering our economy should benefit from the same advances in AI that are transforming the digital world,” said Bellanger. “Our vision is to provide operators with a trusted understanding of what is happening across their infrastructure, with the foresight to protect the people and operations that depend on it.”

“Axion is the first step in this next chapter, opening our technology to more operators and putting their existing inspection investments to work toward that goal,” he added. “From Day 1, a team can bring the inspection data it already has and see which assets need attention first.”

Available as a software-as-a-service offering, Axion organizes inspection data by asset and applies AI that interprets equipment condition in context. It ingests data from supported third-party drone platforms, fixed and mobile sensors, and existing inspection archives, so operators are not tied to a single hardware provider.

Percept said that Axion can identify a downed wire by its relationship to surrounding components or evaluate a thermal anomaly against expected asset behavior and environmental conditions. Each finding is backed by inspection history and expert validation, giving teams confidence in what needs attention.

In addition, Percepto asserted that Axion enables users to query the corpus of inspection data using plain-language queries. It said its large language model (LLM) enables users to quickly get to the answers that they are seeking and exposes the valuable signals contained in the inspection data.

]]> Sequoia Capital, one of Silicon Valley’s oldest and most prominent venture capital firms, has closed its London office as part of a broader restructuring.

In an announcement titled “The Sequoia of Tomorrow”, the firm outlined several sweeping changes and confirmed that it has raised €8.89 billion ($10 billion) in new funds. The biggest announcement is that it no longer sees the need for a physical European presence. While the firm is exiting Europe, three of its four London-based partners have decided to remain in Europe rather than relocate to California.

“We are closing our London office, which means several people will be leaving Sequoia.  This is not about the team – they are excellent. We simply don’t see the need for a local presence. We believe that Europe will continue to produce outlier founders and companies, and that we can continue to provide world class support from our home base in the Bay Area,” the firm said.

Despite being offered the opportunity to move to San Francisco, three of Sequoia’s four London-based partners – Luciana Lixandru, Julien Bek, and George Robson – have opted to remain in Europe. Anas Biad is the only London-based partner who has confirmed he will relocate to the United States and remain with Sequoia.

Lixandru joined Sequoia in 2020 as its first European partner and has backed companies such as Trade Republic, Pennylane, and Rillet. “My conviction on Europe hasn’t moved, and neither am I; when given the opportunity to move to San Francisco, I chose to stay here and focus on this wonderful, imperfect ecosystem.  Europe is where my family is, and where I want to build,” she wrote on LinkedIn.

She further confirmed that she will remain a Sequoia partner, continue serving on portfolio company boards, and also invest personally in the next generation of European founders.

Bek, who spent a decade investing in European founders through Sequoia, backing companies including Revolut, Miro, Attio, and Dust, added that he is already thinking about what the next decade in European venture could look like.

“My heart is in Europe, and I’ve decided to stay here. I’ll continue supporting the founders I work with and serving on my boards,” he said.

The closure of Sequoia’s London office follows a similar move by fellow US VC giant Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), which shuttered its London office in early 2025, less than two years after opening its first international outpost in the UK.

After roughly 20 years of expansion, during which it built multiple businesses across geographies, Sequoia says it is now pulling back to focus on what it does best: high-conviction, highly selective venture capital investing.

As part of this restructuring, the firm has decided to simplify the structure of the Sequoia Capital Fund, sunset its batch accelerator Arc and Scouts programmes, and streamline both its operational and investing teams. It is also eliminating the distinction between its Early and Growth stages, consolidating into one team under a single mission. The firm is also doing away with its Monday partner meeting cycle.

“Founders operate 24/7, and so do we.  Founders shouldn’t have to adhere to our process – we will do our best to adhere to yours,” the firm added.

European founders have already weathered a16z’s exit and now need to prepare for a phase where Sequoia may be hard to reach, especially without a local partner to back them. While the firm has insisted it can keep backing European companies from its Bay Area base, the attention will be on the UK partners who decided to stay, and the European tech ecosystem will watch their next move closely.

]]> FluoRok, an Oxford-based chemical manufacturing startup that has developed a patented process to produce fluorochemicals without using highly hazardous hydrogen fluoride (HF), has secured a €26.64 million ($30 million) Series A financing round.

The round was led by Orano Ventures Fund/Supernova Invest, with participation from investor Bidra Innovation Ventures. Existing backers Oxford Science Enterprises, BGF, GGF, Volta Energy Technologies, and the University of Oxford also participated in the round.

“We back companies whose technologies support a sovereign, sustainable industrial transition. FluoRok has already shown its process works at pilot scale, and taking hydrogen fluoride out of fluorochemical production tackles a safety and supply problem the whole industry shares. We are pleased to join a strong group of investors supporting the team as it moves to industrial scale,” said Florian de Beauchaine, Investment Manager, Orano Venture Fund/Supernova Invest.

FluoRok says its Series A funding round exceeded its original target and included several angel investors, smaller partners such as EverQuest Capital Partners, CPI Enterprises, and WS Investment, as well as approximately €1.15 million ($1.3 million) in grant funding from Innovate UK through its Investor Partnerships programme.

Founded in 2022, FluoRok is a University of Oxford spin-out developing a patented manufacturing platform that bypasses the conventional HF-based process used to produce fluorochemicals entirely. Conventional fluorochemical production has relied on a 250-year-old process that depends on HF, one of the most hazardous chemicals in industrial use, and high-purity fluorspar predominantly sourced from China, creating safety, supply, and cost risks.

FluoRok bypasses this process by relying on mechanical activation combined with base chemistry to unlock fluorine from lower-grade mineral sources and even fluoride-containing industrial waste streams, under controllable conditions. The process runs on off-the-shelf industrial equipment, which makes it faster and easier to scale.

The company targets critical end markets including pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and lithium-ion battery manufacturing, sectors where fluorochemicals are indispensable but supply remains heavily concentrated and hazard-prone.

Dr. Gabriele Pupo, founder and CEO, FluoRok, said, ”We are thrilled to welcome new investors on our journey to fundamentally change how the world makes fluorochemicals, with safer chemistry and better economics.”

“Closing another oversubscribed round, backed by both new and existing investors from around the world, is a testament to the strength of our technology, the incredible commercial traction and the speed of execution of the FluoRok team. This funding will ensure FluoRok can swiftly move from start-up to scale-up and take a further step towards becoming a large-scale industrial manufacturer,” he added.

FluoRok says it has completed pilot qualifications and established strong commercial traction with key customers, with products being validated by more than ten partners across eight countries and three continents.

The Series A funding round builds on the €12.43 million ($14 million) secured in previous rounds and more than €11.54 million ($13 million) in UK and European public funding to date. It plans to use the new capital to transition from startup to industrial scale, including building demonstrator facilities for its reagents and battery electrolyte salts, expanding its team, and deepening its commercial partnerships.

The company also plans to scale its platform for next-generation battery products such as LiFSI and FEC, and for a waste-to-value stream that transforms fluorinated polymer waste, over 25,000 tonnes of which is incinerated annually in Europe alone, into high-value chemical intermediates.

]]> EU-Startups has received exclusive investment data directly from our partners at the European Innovation Council (EIC), revealing the ten companies that secured the largest EIC Fund commitments during the first three quarters of the year.

From quantum computing and nuclear fusion to biotechnology and space technology, the total 85 investments made by the EIC in 2026 offer a closer look at where European public investment is flowing – with the top 10 representing the forefront of European innovation.

We’ve ranked the companies by their total EIC Fund commitments signed between January and September 2026, combining multiple investments in the same company and outlining EIC contributions from larger funding rounds involving other investors. Here are the ten biggest recipients so far!

The European Champions

€34.5 million

EnduroSat (Bulgaria): Founded in 2015 by Raycho Raychev, EnduroSat is a Bulgarian SpaceTech company making satellite technology accessible and affordable. €33.3 million

The company is working to make renewable energy available when solar and wind production cannot meet demand. Its EIC commitments total €33.3 million across two investments signed in June and August 2026.

EU-Startups covered Reverion’s €154.2 million Series B round in September 2026, which included participation from the EIC Fund alongside Kembara, Allianz, KfW Capital and other investors.

€30 million

Pasqal (France): Founded in 2019, Paris-based Pasqal develops quantum computers powered by neutral atoms manipulated using lasers. Its technology aims to tackle complex calculations in areas such as materials science, optimisation and pharmaceutical research. The company was co-founded by a team including Alain Aspect, the 2022 Nobel Prize winner in Physics.

Pasqal secured an EIC Fund investment of almost €30 million on 30 January 2026, when it was still a privately held quantum computing scaleup. The company subsequently went public on Nasdaq in August 2026, marking a significant milestone in its growth.

Focused Energy (Germany): Founded in 2021, Darmstadt-based Focused Energy is working to turn nuclear fusion into a commercially viable electricity source. The company uses powerful lasers to compress and heat fuel, pursuing a fusion process that could eventually generate electricity without the carbon emissions associated with fossil fuels.

The German-American startup secured an EIC commitment of almost €30 million in May 2026. That same month, it announced a €213 million ($240 million) Series A, with investors including RWE, SPRIND, Prime Movers Lab and the EIC Fund. €25 million

€20 million

]]> Women TechEU is a European Union initiative that supports the growth of women-led DeepTech startups across Europe. Between 2026 and 2028, the programme aims to support 160 startups through grants of €75,000 each, alongside mentoring, training, expert guidance, networking, and opportunities to connect with investors and other European funding programmes.

To extend this support beyond the programme itself, Women TechEU has created the Allies network, bringing together organisations that want to help women-led DeepTech startups grow. The network includes investors, technology companies, innovation organisations, media partners, EU projects, and public institutions.

Who are the Women TechEU Allies?

The Women TechEU Allies network brings together organisations from across Europe that can offer startups valuable connections, expertise, resources, and visibility.

Its members include investors such as Alma Angels, Antler, and Playfair Capital, which help connect startups with investment opportunities and funding networks.

Technology companies and ecosystem organisations such as Microsoft, FundingBox, Women in Tech, the Western Balkan Startup Alliance, allWomen, Impulse4Women, and WomenTechIceland contribute through mentoring, knowledge sharing, and access to entrepreneurial communities.

Media and event partners, including TechBBQ, Web Summit, and Wolves Summit, help increase the visibility of women-led DeepTech startups. European initiatives such as EIT Deep Tech Talent, PQreact, and Ready2Scale also participate, supporting collaboration and access to additional opportunities.

Together, these organisations help create a stronger network of support for women entrepreneurs across Europe.

What does being an ally involve?

Becoming a Women TechEU ally means joining this network and contributing to the growth of women-led DeepTech startups.

Allies can support startups in different ways, including offering mentoring, sharing business and funding opportunities, making introductions to investors or corporate partners, and promoting women-led innovations through their networks.

In return, Allies gain access to the Women TechEU Partner-Hub, an online platform where startups, investors, companies, and other ecosystem organisations can connect and collaborate.

Through the Partner-Hub and the wider network, Allies can:

  • Connect with women-led DeepTech startups and other European innovation stakeholders.
  • Participate in investment events, corporate challenges, meetups, and networking activities.
  • Receive a dedicated ally badge on their Partner-Hub profile.
  • Gain visibility through Women TechEU’s website and social media channels.
  • Receive a communications pack to help promote Women TechEU within their own networks.

How to become a Women TechEU ally

Joining the Allies network is a straightforward process.

First, interested organisations register on the Women TechEU Partner-Hub, the programme’s online networking platform. During registration, they simply select the option indicating that they would like to become an ally.

Within one week, the Women TechEU Helpdesk team contacts them with further information and a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU). This is a document that sets out the collaboration between Women TechEU and the organisation.

Once both parties sign the MoU, the organisation officially becomes a Women TechEU ally and can take part in the network’s activities.

The Partner-Hub therefore serves two purposes: it is where organisations express their interest in becoming Allies, and it is also the online space they use to connect with startups and other members of the Women TechEU community.

By joining the Allies network, organisations can contribute their expertise, connections, and resources to help more women-led DeepTech startups access opportunities and grow across Europe.

]]> When Ireland’s Government recently announced Budget 2027, it focused on addressing a problem that has beset Ireland’s startup community for decades.

A €1 billion Ireland Strategic Investment Fund (ISIF) scaling programme would seek to provide startups with greater access to growth capital. The need was made particularly stark after, in 2025, the Department of Enterprise grimly projected a €1.1 billion equity-financing gap for Irish enterprises by 2030.

The Budget recognised a problem that startups here have known about for years: Ireland is excellent at getting businesses started, but too many founders struggle to raise the money they need to scale and expand. 

Ireland’s scale-up funding gap

This is particularly the case for those seeking Series B investment and beyond. In fact, a 2026 survey from Scale Ireland shows that three-quarters of Irish startup founders find it difficult or very difficult to attract private capital.

Their response tends to be one of two options: sell to a foreign acquirer or move to bigger markets like the UK or US where there is a much larger pool of investors. And why wouldn’t they? It makes sense for the survival and growth of their company.

It does, however, raise a bigger question for Ireland: how do we help more companies grow internationally while keeping their roots here? 

Turning investment promises into action

The new ISIF programme is aimed at addressing the right issue, but its impact will depend on how it works in practice. What companies can access it, how will the money be deployed and on what terms, and how much process will founders have to navigate? These are the important questions that need to be answered with tangible solutions.

The proposed €1 billion is exciting, but only if the timing and application are right. In 2025, the European Commission revealed that Ireland performed below the EU average for innovation-friendly regulation, highlighting the need for better and clearer support infrastructures. Therefore, it is crucial to know if capital will be available at the point when a company needs it.

Budget 2027 also extends existing startup and small business investment schemes. Again, this is most welcome but also sort of a non-announcement. Of course we want these schemes to continue, but the extension does not address the underlying problems. In reality, processes remain complex, funds are slow to be administered and it is unclear who qualifies.

The Capital Gains Tax reduction from 33% to 31% is another positive signal. But a two-point reduction on its own is unlikely to close the scale-up funding gap. The wider goal should be to encourage more investment in Irish companies and give founders the confidence to reinvest in growth.

Growth requires more than capital

Founders need practical improvements: less time spent navigating national requirements, clearer processes and a more straightforward path to customers and investors in other member states. Europe has the scale to be a powerful growth market; it needs to work more like one.

Capital is vital, but it is not the only ingredient required for a growing company. Founders also need customers, experienced people, local knowledge and trusted connections. Starting a business can be lonely. A supportive community can help founders find advice, collaborators and opportunities through the conversations that happen when people spend time together.

Ireland has built a strong base of entrepreneurs and international connections. According to the European Commission, Ireland sits 7th of 27 EU member states on the European Startup and Scaleup Scoreboard, highlighting the potential in our competitive startup environment.

Helping Irish startups scale from home

The next task is to build the conditions that help more of those businesses raise later-stage capital and reach international markets from here. The Budget’s announcements are a start. Their success will be measured by whether companies can use the supports in time, whether private investment follows and whether more Irish businesses can scale without having to leave to do so.

Delivery Hero’s €7.5 Billion Founder Factory

The findings come from a report by Delivery Hero and startup data platform Dealroom.co, which identified 150 startups founded by alumni of Delivery Hero’s European brands, collectively valued at an estimated €7.5 billion.

The post Boeing 787 and 747 fuel tank inspections ordered by FAA after safety concerns over potential ignition risk appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 2 min read
  • FAA orders fuel tank inspections on selected Boeing 787s and 747s over potential ignition source concerns.
  • Dreamliner checks follow evidence some fuel tank sealant inspections were missed during production.
  • No aircraft groundings ordered; affected airlines must inspect and repair aircraft where necessary.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has ordered inspections on dozens of Boeing 787 Dreamliners and Boeing 747s after identifying conditions that could allow an ignition source to develop inside a fuel tank during a lightning strike.

The US aviation regulator has issued two airworthiness directives (ADs) covering 60 US-registered Boeing 787s and 31 Boeing 747s. This requires airlines to carry out inspections and, where necessary, repairs.

In its order affecting the Boeing 787, the FAA warned that the issue, ‘if not addressed, could result in development of an ignition source within the fuel tank volume and a risk of a fuel tank explosion during a lightning strike event.’

The directives take effect on 7 December 2026.

Dreamliner inspection order follows production concerns

The FAA said the issue on certain Boeing 787-8, 787-9 and 787-10 aircraft stems from reports that some sealant installations inside the centre wing fuel tank did not undergo the required visual and adhesion checks during production.

In other words, the FAA is concerned that potential sealant defects may not have been detected because the required inspections were not completed.

Airlines will now be required to inspect the sealant in affected areas of the aircraft, looking for defects, inadequate adhesion and surface depressions before carrying out any necessary repairs.

The FAA stressed that the directive is limited to a specific group of aircraft and not the wider 787 fleet. In fact, the FAA said it had confirmed that the required inspections are now being carried out during production on aircraft outside the scope of the order.

The regulator estimates the checks will take around 34 work-hours per aircraft and cost approximately $2,890 per jet.

Separate issue affects Boeing 747s

A second FAA directive targets certain Boeing 747-400 and 747-8 aircraft. This time, the concern centres on pumps located in the aircraft’s tail fuel tank.

According to the FAA, wear inside the pump assembly could expose metal surfaces and create a potential ignition source in the presence of fuel vapours.

The agency is replacing an earlier requirement for a one-off inspection with repeated checks designed to monitor the condition of the components over time.

Around 31 US-registered aircraft are affected, with each inspection cycle expected to cost airlines about $1,530 per aircraft.

What have the airlines said?

Boeing and American Airlines both sought clarification during the consultation process. Boeing successfully argued for airlines to be allowed to use existing approved repair procedures, while American Airlines asked for further detail on the inspection requirements.

The FAA has not grounded any aircraft as part of either directive.

]]> Rare USAF RC-135U Combat Sent spy plane lands in UK amid Iran tensions https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/usaf-rc-135u-combat-sent-uk-iran-tensions/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 15:35:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55659 The Combat Sent gathers detailed intelligence on foreign military radars, helping the US develop ways to detect and defeat them. Its latest flight has prompted speculation about a Middle East deployment.

The post Rare USAF RC-135U Combat Sent spy plane lands in UK amid Iran tensions appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 3 min read
  • One of only two USAF RC-135U Combat Sent aircraft has been tracked heading toward RAF Mildenhall.
  • The aircraft gathers detailed radar intelligence to help develop countermeasures against foreign military systems.
  • A Middle East deployment remains unconfirmed, and the flight alone does not indicate imminent strikes on Iran.

One of the US Air Force’s two RC-135U Combat Sent reconnaissance aircraft has been tracked crossing the Atlantic toward the UK, drawing attention to a rare aircraft that helps American forces understand how an adversary’s air defences work.

The aircraft, serial number 64-14849, was identified by flight trackers using the callsign COBRA49 on 4 November. Its eastbound journey prompted suggestions that it could be heading toward the Middle East amid uncertainty over further US military action against Iran.

The aircraft has since landed at RAF Mildenhall in the UK, a well-used jumping-off point for US military flights to the Middle East. However, its onward deployment remains unknown for the time being.

RC-135U Combat Sent tracked flying to RAF Mildenhall

Flight-tracking reports indicate that the aircraft left Offutt Air Force Base in Nebraska on November 3 and stopped at Pease Air National Guard Base in New Hampshire before continuing across the Atlantic the following morning.

Open-source tracking from ADSBexchange shows the aircraft leaving Offutt at 23:45 on 3 November, arriving at Pease a couple of hours later. It departed Pease at 06:51 on 4 November and landed at RAF Mildenhall at 13:33.

The arrival of the aircraft in the UK doesn’t guarantee deployment to the CENTCOM area. However, British military bases were extensively used during Operation Midnight Hammer as a stopping point on the way to the Middle East.

18 hours, 125 aircraft: Inside Operation Midnight Hammer and the US strategy to strike Iran undetected 18 hours, 125 aircraft: Inside Operation Midnight Hammer and the US strategy to strike Iran undetected

What is the RC-135U Combat Sent?

The Combat Sent is a highly specialised electronic intelligence aircraft. The US Air Force lists just two in its inventory, both assigned to the 55th Wing at Offutt.

Its mission is to locate, identify, and examine radar emissions from foreign military systems on land, at sea and in the air. The information supports senior US decision-makers, military commanders and intelligence analysts.

The aircraft’s value lies in the detail it collects. Detecting a radar establishes that a system is transmitting; studying its signals helps analysts determine its operating characteristics and capabilities.

According to Air Combat Command, Combat Sent’s precision collection equipment can gather multiple signals of interest. This information feeds national databases and detailed technical analysis to support the development of equipment and techniques to detect, warn of or defeat foreign electronic systems.

Externally, distinctive antenna arrays around its chin, wingtips and extended tail help distinguish the RC-135U. Inside, its crew includes electronic warfare officers, airborne systems engineers and mission specialists. Aerial refuelling extends its reach beyond its published 4,000 nm range.

Does the Combat Sent flight signal further US strikes on Iran?

The movement comes amid renewed scrutiny of US military flights associated with the Middle East.

As Aerospace Global News reported earlier, C-17 transport flights to Israel and reports of diplomatic warnings have fueled speculation about a wider campaign against Iran following the November 3 midterm elections.

Those flights do not establish what cargo was aboard or whether an offensive has been authorised. Limited US strikes have already continued, making the question really about whether Washington will escalate to a more sustained campaign.

President Donald Trump has also played down the prospect of immediate escalation. In an interview with the Financial Times, he said the US had no immediate plans to strike Iran, while maintaining that American forces were “locked and loaded” if required.

Combat Sent would be a valuable intelligence asset wherever detailed knowledge of foreign radar systems is required. But the Air Force explicitly describes it as a platform used worldwide in both peacetime and contingency operations.

Its rarity makes the flight noteworthy. Its presence alone does not establish that another attack on Iran is approaching.

]]>
In Brief 4 min read
  • Embraer is in talks with IndiGo for up to 150 regional jets, potentially one of its biggest commercial orders.
  • The deal could significantly expand Embraer's presence in India, supporting routes connecting smaller cities and regional markets.
  • A firm agreement would strengthen Embraer's record order backlog and boost E-Jet visibility across the fast-growing Asian aviation market.

Brazilian aircraft manufacturer Embraer could be on the verge of securing one of the largest commercial aircraft orders in its history, following reports that Indian airline IndiGo is in discussions to purchase up to 150 regional jets.

According to a Reuters report published on 4 November, IndiGo is in early-stage negotiations to acquire 100 Embraer aircraft, with options for a further 50. Although an agreement has yet to be finalised, the potential deal represents a significant opportunity for Embraer as it seeks to expand its international commercial aviation business.

The discussions also underline the growing importance of regional aircraft in a global aviation market increasingly characterised by airline fleet expansion, network diversification and demand for more efficient operations.

IndiGo negotiations could transform Embraer’s Indian presence

IndiGo, India’s largest airline, is considering the acquisition as part of its wider fleet and network expansion strategy.

With a rapidly growing domestic aviation market, India represents an attractive opportunity for Embraer, particularly as airlines look to connect smaller cities and develop routes that may not justify the use of larger narrowbody aircraft.

The proposed order has not yet been allocated to a specific aircraft type, with Embraer’s E175, E190-E2 and E195-E2 families all potentially relevant to the discussions.

These aircraft offer seating capacities ranging from approximately 88 to 146 passengers, depending on the model and configuration. Deliveries would be expected to begin no earlier than 2030, should the negotiations result in a firm contract.

For Embraer, the significance extends beyond the potential aircraft sales. The company currently has a relatively limited commercial aviation footprint in India, where Star Air is its only airline customer operating Embraer regional jets.

The manufacturer has already been strengthening its Indian industrial relationships, including a January 2026 partnership with Adani Defence & Aerospace to explore regional aircraft manufacturing and supply-chain opportunities.

Embraer’s latest commercial aircraft orders worldwide

The potential IndiGo agreement comes amid a particularly strong period of commercial activity for Embraer. Its third-quarter 2026 results, announced on 23 October, revealed a commercial aviation order backlog worth $15.8 billion, representing a 5% increase quarter-on-quarter.

In July, Abra Group placed a firm order for 20 E195-E2 aircraft, with options for another 10 and purchase rights for 15 more. The potential transaction could therefore reach 45 aircraft.

Also in July, Japanese aviation group ANA Holdings ordered eight additional E190-E2 aircraft, increasing its total firm orders for the type to 23.

The same month, Binter added five E195-E2 aircraft to its fleet commitments and secured purchase rights for a further four, while Luxair converted three existing purchase rights into firm orders and secured another purchase right, bringing its total order book to nine aircraft.

During the third quarter of 2026, Embraer secured 36 firm orders for its E2-family aircraft, alongside 30 additional purchase rights and options. These transactions contributed to 72 firm E2-family orders during the first nine months of 2026.

Earlier in 2026, Embraer also secured important business from European and North American customers. Finnair announced a fleet agreement for up to 46 E195-E2 aircraft, while aircraft lessor Azorra placed an order for 15 E195-E2 jets during the second quarter.

These transactions demonstrate the appeal of the E2 family to both airline operators and aircraft leasing companies.

A growing worldwide order backlog

Embraer’s overall order backlog reached a record $35.7 billion at the end of the third quarter of 2026, an increase of 14% compared with the same period last year.

Commercial aviation accounted for $15.8 billion of this total, while Executive Aviation contributed $8.2 billion. Defence and Security recorded a backlog of $6.1 billion, reflecting growing international interest in its military aircraft programmes.

The figures demonstrate that Embraer’s growth is not dependent on a single aircraft category or geographical market. Its commercial jets, business aircraft and defence platforms are all contributing to a substantial international order book.

What the IndiGo deal could mean for Embraer

An agreement with IndiGo would represent a major strategic breakthrough for Embraer in one of the world’s fastest-growing aviation markets.

For IndiGo, regional jets could provide additional flexibility, allowing the airline to serve smaller cities, increase frequencies and develop routes where larger Airbus A320-family aircraft may not be the most commercially appropriate option.

For Embraer, the opportunity is potentially even greater. A successful agreement could establish a substantial new customer relationship, increase the visibility of its E-Jet family in Asia and create opportunities for future aircraft sales, maintenance and support services.

Although the negotiations remain preliminary, the proposed 100-aircraft order, with options for another 50, would be an important milestone for the Brazilian manufacturer.

With a record $35.7 billion backlog, 72 firm E2-family orders during the first nine months of 2026 and new business from airlines across Europe, Asia and the Americas, Embraer is enjoying considerable commercial momentum.

The potential IndiGo agreement could provide another significant boost, particularly if it develops into a firm order covering 150 aircraft.

For the regional aviation sector, the message is clear, in that airlines are increasingly recognising the value of appropriately sized aircraft as they balance capacity, operating economics and network expansion. Embraer appears well positioned to benefit from that trend.

]]> How NASA astronauts vote from space: Three ISS crew members cast ballots in US midterm elections https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/how-nasa-astronauts-vote-from-space/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 14:36:00 +0000 https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/?p=55604 Nearly 30 years after the first American voted from space, NASA astronaut Anil Menon offers a glimpse of how democracy works 400 kilometres above Earth.

The post How NASA astronauts vote from space: Three ISS crew members cast ballots in US midterm elections appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 5 min read
  • Three NASA astronauts cast electronic ballots from the ISS during the 2026 US midterm elections.
  • Space voting began in 1997 when astronaut David Wolf became the first American to vote from orbit.
  • Encrypted ballots travel via NASA's satellite network to county election officials on Earth.

There was no queue, polling official or ballot box when NASA astronaut Anil Menon voted in the US midterm elections on Tuesday. His polling booth was a small compartment aboard the International Space Station, orbiting Earth at roughly 28,000 kilometres per hour.

Menon was one of three American astronauts who cast their ballots from space on 3 November, using an electronic voting system that allows eligible crew members to participate in elections without returning to Earth.

The other two were NASA astronauts Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins.

“Yes, you can even vote from space!” Menon wrote in a social media post. “All three US crew members had the privilege of voting from space station. We filled out an electronic ballot and sent it securely to the election officials.”

Yes, you can even vote from space! All three US crew members had the privilege of voting from space station. We filled out an electronic ballot and sent it securely to the election officials. https://t.co/hJCExQ2nKr

— Anil Menon (@astro_anil) November 3, 2026

The astronaut also shared a short video showing how he voted, offering a rare glimpse of an everyday civic responsibility being carried out in an extraordinary setting.

Wearing an “I voted” sticker, Menon showed viewers the personal crew compartment he had used as his polling booth.

“Inside of it is my computer, where I was able to fill out an electronic form and send it to Harris County so I could vote today,” he explained.

The process took place hundreds of kilometres above the United States, but the ballot was destined for the same election authorities responsible for votes cast by residents of Harris County, Texas.

It was a small personal moment in a mission devoted largely to scientific research, spacecraft operations and maintaining the orbiting laboratory.

The first ballot from space

Voting from space is not a new privilege. Its origins go back to 1997, when American astronauts began spending extended periods aboard Russia’s Mir space station.

At the time, astronauts assigned to long-duration missions faced a problem that most voters never encounter. They could be away from Earth for months, with no practical means of visiting a polling station or returning an absentee ballot through ordinary postal services.

Texas lawmakers addressed the issue by passing legislation allowing eligible residents travelling in space to vote while in orbit.

The connection with Texas was important. NASA’s Johnson Space Center, the principal training and mission-control facility for American astronauts, is in Houston. Many astronauts live in the surrounding area.

The legislation provided a way for those residents to exercise their voting rights even when their work took them far beyond the planet.

Later that year, NASA astronaut David Wolf became the first American to cast a ballot from space.

Wolf was aboard Mir, the Russian station that preceded the International Space Station as a major destination for long-duration human spaceflight.

His vote established a precedent that has continued through successive generations of astronauts.

When the ISS began supporting a permanent human presence in November 2000, the same basic principle carried over: an astronaut’s absence from Earth should not prevent participation in an election.

How does a ballot travel from space to Earth?

Although the voting process appears simple from the astronaut’s perspective, delivering the ballot requires several stages of communication.

The astronaut first arranges to vote absentee, working with the election authorities in the county where they are registered.

As with other Americans who are away from home, astronauts can use a Federal Post Card Application to request an absentee ballot. Election officials prepare an electronic ballot, which is made available to the astronaut through NASA’s communications systems.

The astronaut accesses the ballot using individual credentials, makes the selections and sends the completed document back to Earth.

NASA says the process is supported by its Space Communications and Navigation programme, known as SCaN.

The ballot travels through the agency’s Near Space Network, which provides communication and navigation services for spacecraft operating relatively close to Earth.

From the ISS, the electronic document is transmitted through NASA’s Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System.

These satellites allow the space station to exchange information with ground facilities without having to wait until it passes directly over a particular receiving station.

The ballot is relayed to a ground antenna at NASA’s White Sands Test Facility in New Mexico. It then travels to Mission Control at Johnson Space Center in Houston before being forwarded to the appropriate county election official.

Security is an essential part of the arrangement.

NASA says the ballot is encrypted and accessible only to the astronaut and the county clerk, protecting the confidentiality and integrity of the vote during transmission.

The system does not mean astronauts can simply vote in any election by sending an email from orbit. They must meet the normal eligibility requirements and complete the necessary absentee-voting arrangements.

The difference is that their ballot travels through a spacecraft communications network rather than a postal system.

A tradition that has continued for decades

Several NASA astronauts have exercised their voting rights during missions since Wolf’s pioneering ballot in 1997.

Kate Rubins voted from the International Space Station during the 2016 presidential election and again in 2020.

During the 2020 election, Rubins was photographed beside a makeshift voting booth aboard the station.

The photograph captured an unusual contrast: an American election being observed from a spacecraft surrounded by scientific equipment, cables and the machinery needed to sustain human life in orbit.

The Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum later highlighted her experience as an example of how astronauts remain connected with ordinary life while living and working far from home.

More recently, NASA astronauts Loral O’Hara and Jasmin Moghbeli cast electronic absentee ballots from the station in March 2024 while registered as Texas voters.

Their completed ballots were transmitted to Mission Control and passed to local election officials.

Menon’s vote in the 2026 midterms continues that tradition, but his video offers a more personal look at the process.

Instead of focusing on the communications infrastructure or the legislation behind the system, he showed viewers the place where he sat to make his choices.

The voting booth was simply his room aboard the station.

Three votes from the same spacecraft

Menon arrived at the ISS in July aboard a Russian Soyuz spacecraft.

Delaney and Watkins joined the orbiting laboratory in October on SpaceX‘s Crew-13 mission.

Their election-day participation meant all three American crew members aboard the station were able to vote despite being away from their home country.

  • Organisers say the relocation provides greater certainty and helps secure the military airshow's long-term future.
  • The move follows RIAT 2026's cancellation and supports continued fundraising for the RAF Charitable Trust's STEM programmes.

Organisers have confirmed that the Royal International Air Tattoo (RIAT) will relocate to MOD Boscombe Down in Wiltshire from 2027, ending a relationship with RAF Fairford that stretches back more than four decades.

The first edition at the new venue will take place from 16-18 July 2027.

Why is the Royal International Air Tattoo leaving RAF Fairford?

According to Royal Air Force Charitable Trust Enterprises (RAFCTE), the decision to relocate was taken following a review of the event’s future operating requirements.

The organisation said Boscombe Down will provide greater certainty for exhibitors, participating air forces, volunteers and visitors while helping protect the long-term future of the show.

“This decision follows a comprehensive review of the show’s future operating requirements and has been taken to protect, strengthen and secure the long-term future of RIAT,” an RAFCTE spokesperson said.

What does the move mean for airshow visitors?

The announcement marks one of the biggest changes in the event’s modern history. Since establishing itself at RAF Fairford, RIAT has grown into one of the most important fixtures on the global airshow calendar.

“Every generation of RIAT has had its defining moments, and I believe this is one of them,” said RAFCTE Chief Executive Gavin Gager.

“The decision to move RIAT to Boscombe Down is about much more than a new location. It is about securing the future of the world’s greatest military airshow and the charitable impact it generates for future generations.”

Boscombe Down’s airshow history

Although best known internationally as a centre for military flight testing and aircraft evaluation, Boscombe Down has previously hosted major aviation events. The airfield welcomed the Battle of Britain Airshow in 1990 and Air Tournament International in 1992, both organised by the Air Tattoo’s predecessor organisation.

Its aviation heritage made it a natural candidate as organisers evaluated options for the future of the event.

The Royal International Air Tattoo is also the main fundraising event for the Royal Air Force Charitable Trust.

“What excites me most is not simply the move itself, but what it makes possible,” said Gager. “Every year RIAT brings people together through a shared passion for aviation, while generating vital funding that enables the Royal Air Force Charitable Trust to inspire hundreds of thousands of young people through STEM engagement.”

The post NTSB finds Learjet 60 wreckage miles from site of fatal Florida crash appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 3 min read
  • NTSB recovered three Learjet 60 elevator sections up to 3.8 miles from the crash site, confirming in-flight separation before impact.
  • Investigators are assessing whether tail failure caused loss of control or resulted from overspeed and aerodynamic forces during descent.
  • Weather, icing, turbulence, maintenance records, cockpit communications and eyewitness footage remain central to the ongoing investigation.

Investigators have recovered parts of a Learjet 60‘s tail up to 3.8 miles from the site of Sunday’s fatal crash in Florida, confirming that sections of the aircraft separated before impact.

The Learjet 60, operated by Aurora Aviation under the Upper Jets name, crashed in Palm Beach County on Sunday, November 1, killing all nine people aboard.

The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) disclosed the discovery during its 3 November press briefing as investigators continued examining the aircraft’s rapid descent near West Palm Beach.

The aircraft departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas at approximately 10:37 am Eastern Time, bound for North Eleuthera in the Bahamas.

Investigators recovered most of the aircraft’s left elevator, a movable control surface on the horizontal tail that controls pitch, in three pieces between 1.3 and 3.8 miles from the main crash site.

“Certainly it tells us that at least some components, some pieces of the aircraft, important pieces of the aircraft, separated before the impact,” NTSB board member Tom Chapman said. “What that means exactly in terms of what caused the aircraft to lose control, or whether the loss of this piece was a result of the forces on the aircraft, we don’t know yet.”

He described the discovery as a “very significant bit of evidence.”

Investigators confirm tail components separated in flight

Asked whether the elevator could have broken away when the aircraft struck the ground, Chapman said, “The distance from the site indicates that it separated before impact.” 

“It seems implausible that it would have been a result of the impact. It would have separated before the impact.”

Investigators are examining whether losing the elevator contributed to the aircraft’s loss of control or whether forces acting on the aircraft during its descent caused the component to break away.

“Those are the two likely possibilities that we’ll want to examine,” Chapman said.

The NTSB has not determined when the elevator separated or whether the aircraft was already descending uncontrollably when it happened.

Asked whether excessive descent speed could have caused the aircraft to break apart, Chapman said: “That is certainly one possibility.”

He cautioned that the elevator might not have remained effective at the aircraft’s speed, even if it had remained attached.

Learjet crew reported turbulence, icing and overspeed

According to the NTSB’s first briefing, the crew reported moderate turbulence and manageable icing while flying at 35,000ft. The pilots requested permission to climb to 37,000ft after encountering precipitation. Less than 30 seconds after receiving clearance, the crew reported a descent, followed by a mayday call.

The crew then reported the aircraft was overspeed and descending. Later communications indicated a rapid loss of altitude. The aircraft crashed at approximately 12:51 pm.

The NTSB has not established whether the reported icing, turbulence or overspeed caused the loss of control.

“Weather is certainly a key focus of the investigation,” Chapman said.

Weather remains a focus of the investigation

Asked whether investigators had examined the aircraft’s maintenance history, including the condition of its weather radar, Chapman said that work was ongoing and there was insufficient information to draw any conclusions.

Investigators are also examining crew qualifications, aircraft maintenance records and operational information.

The NTSB has received dashcam footage and multiple eyewitness accounts that could help establish the aircraft’s condition during its final moments.

The NTSB say they expect to start investigating the crash crater today. Chapman told the press conference an unstable utility pole had been removed and added, “NTSB is working with local public works teams to begin water removal from the impact crater so our investigation in and around the crater can begin. We believe that will begin tomorrow [Wednesday] in terms of being able to access the crater.”

The investigation is still in its early stages, and the NTSB has not yet identified a probable cause of the tragic accident.

The post Avolon finalises order for 140 Boeing 737 MAX 10 jets appeared first on AGN.

]]>
In Brief 4 min read
  • Avolon finalised a record order for 140 Boeing 737-10 jets, taking its Boeing backlog above 240 aircraft.
  • The deal reflects strong demand for larger, fuel-efficient narrowbodies as airlines expand and renew fleets.
  • Boeing’s newly certified 737-10 is set to enter service soon, offering higher capacity and lower per-seat costs.

Aircraft leasing company Avolon has finalised an order for 140 Boeing 737 MAX 10 aircraft, marking the largest 737 MAX purchase by a lessor to date and significantly expanding its portfolio of next-generation single-aisle jets.

Announced on November 4 by Boeing and Avolon in Seattle, the agreement brings Avolon’s total backlog of unfilled Boeing 737 orders to more than 240 aircraft.

The deal further strengthens the company’s position in the global aircraft leasing market and reflects growing demand for fuel-efficient, higher-capacity narrowbody aircraft.

Record-breaking order strengthens Avolon’s Boeing partnership

According to the leasing firm, the 140-aircraft agreement represents “a major commitment to the Boeing 737 MAX family and provides Avolon with additional capacity to meet the evolving requirements of airline customers worldwide.”

Demand for the largest member of the 737 MAX family has increased considerably throughout 2026. Aircraft lessors have placed firm orders for more than 230 Boeing 737-10 aircraft during the year, approximately five times the total lessor backlog for the largest 737 MAX variant at the end of 2025.

For Avolon, the order provides an opportunity to capitalise on demand for larger single-aisle aircraft while benefiting from the operational flexibility of the Boeing 737 family.

Avolon CEO Andy Cronin said the agreement reflects continued demand for new-technology aircraft and strengthens the company’s long-term delivery pipeline.

He highlighted the 737 MAX 10’s combination of competitive operating economics and increased passenger capacity, noting that the aircraft is well positioned to support airline growth and fleet renewal throughout the next decade.

Cronin also emphasised the importance of Avolon’s longstanding relationship with Boeing, describing the latest agreement as another step in strengthening the partnership.

Boeing highlights the benefits of the 737 MAX family

Boeing welcomed Avolon’s expanded commitment to the 737 MAX programme, highlighting the benefits the aircraft family offers airlines seeking to modernise their fleets.

Brad McMullen, Boeing’s Senior Vice President of Commercial Sales and Marketing, said Avolon’s growing and diversified 737 MAX portfolio would help airline customers introduce aircraft that reduce emissions and operating costs while improving route economics. He also pointed to the importance of fuel-efficient aircraft as airlines prepare for continued growth in global passenger traffic.

With strong long-term travel demand anticipated, Boeing believes lessors will play an important role in helping airlines access modern single-aisle aircraft capable of operating across a wide range of route networks.

Boeing 737 MAX 10: Capacity, range and operating economics

The Boeing 737 MAX 10 is the largest aircraft in the 737 MAX family and has been developed to provide airlines with additional passenger capacity while retaining the operational advantages of a single-aisle aircraft.

According to Boeing, the aircraft offers the best per-seat economics of any single-aisle aircraft. Key specifications include a passenger capacity of up to 230 passengers and a maximum range of approximately 3,100 nautical miles (5,740 kilometres).

Its additional seating capacity makes the 737 MAX 10 particularly attractive to airlines operating high-demand short- and medium-haul routes. The aircraft’s economics also provide operators with opportunities to increase capacity without moving into the widebody market.

For aircraft lessors such as Avolon, the 737 MAX 10 offers an opportunity to meet airline demand for larger narrowbody aircraft while maintaining exposure to one of the world’s most widely operated commercial aircraft families.

Growing demand for single-aisle aircraft

The order comes amid expectations of sustained growth in global air travel. Passenger traffic is projected to increase by approximately 4% annually over the next 20 years, encouraging aircraft lessors to expand and diversify their single-aisle portfolios.

The Boeing 737 remains a cornerstone of the global aircraft leasing industry, accounting for approximately 30% of all financed aircraft. Across the lessor market, orders for the 737 MAX family have now exceeded 1,450 aircraft, representing approximately 20% of Boeing’s total backlog.

These figures underline the importance of the 737 MAX programme to the leasing sector and demonstrate the continued appetite for modern, fuel-efficient narrowbody aircraft.

Avolon’s latest agreement positions the company to support airline fleet expansion and replacement requirements over the coming years, while further strengthening its relationship with one of the world’s leading commercial aircraft manufacturers.

The Boeing 737 MAX 10 nears entry into service

The Boeing 737 MAX 10 is the fourth and largest member of Boeing’s 737 MAX family. Its development was launched in 2017 in response to airline demand for a higher-capacity narrowbody aircraft capable of competing more directly with the Airbus A321neo and to replace the Boeing 757.

Although the aircraft shares much of its design and technology with the other 737 MAX variants, the MAX 10 incorporates modifications to accommodate its longer fuselage and increased passenger capacity.

One of the most significant certification considerations has been the aircraft’s updated landing gear design. The 737-10 features a semi-levered main landing gear arrangement designed to provide the necessary ground clearance during take-off despite its longer fuselage.

The aircraft’s certification programme also involved extensive flight testing and regulatory evaluation, including assessments of handling characteristics, systems integration, performance, and compliance with applicable airworthiness requirements.

The Boeing 737 MAX 10 was eventually certified on October 20, paving the way for its entry into service with several airlines. WestJet, Ryanair, Alaska Airlines, Delta Air Lines, and United Airlines are all preparing for Boeing’s largest 737 MAX variant, with WestJet likely to be the first recipient.

]]> Investigators from the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) say they expect to start investigating the crash crater where the Learjet 60 crashed.

The plane came down in Florida on 1 November, killing the two crew members and seven passengers onboard.

Speaking at a press conference last night (3 November) NTSB board member Tom Chapman said crews were preparing the site so investigators could begin work in and around the crater.

“NTSB is working with local public works teams to begin water removal from the impact crater so our investigation in and around the crater can begin,” he said. “We believe that will begin tomorrow [Wednesday] in terms of being able to access the crater.”

Chapman said the removal of an unstable utility pole had been an important step in making the area safe to examine.

“A key step was the removal of an unstable utility pole this morning and that took quite a bit of work. That helps us now access the crater and begin to stabilise it.”

“Challenging” impact site

Investigators believe important evidence remains at the site despite the difficult conditions.

Asked whether critical components, including flight recorders, could still be recovered from the crater, Chapman said: “I feel confident that they’re going to find the evidence that they need within that crater despite the challenges.

“I feel confident they’re going to find what they need to help put together what happened here and why it happened.”

The briefing also disclosed that a large section of the aircraft’s left elevator was recovered up to a few miles from the impact site, highlighting the wide debris field investigators are working to document.

Learjet 60 crash: Was a black box on board, and could it survive the impact? Learjet 60 crash: Was a black box on board, and could it survive the impact?

The investigation has also been complicated by weather and by the severity of the impact. Chapman said much of the wreckage recovered so far consists of very small fragments.

“You’ve seen the video, you know, with the force of that impact,” he said. “Even the elements of the aircraft that are in the crater are very likely in smaller pieces.

“So we don’t know exactly what all we have yet, but that’s part of the investigation very early here. It’s a big puzzle to try to put together.”

Investigators reviewing dashcam footage and eyewitness accounts

Investigators spent much of Tuesday collecting and documenting wreckage, while also gathering information from people who witnessed the accident.

“Witnesses have been quite helpful and we’ve now received dashcam footage and multiple eyewitness accounts that will help us better understand the condition of the aircraft and the circumstances of the crash,” Chapman said.

Florida Learjet victims named

The passengers have been named as entrepreneur Adam Robinson, 44, his wife Helen Sharp, 40, their two children Emma, four, and Charlie, two. Also onboard was the family’s nanny Anita Maria Cetina and two family friends Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr.

The pilot has been identified as Jeff Gregory, 55, from Pennsylvania and the co-pilot as Nathalia Gadelha, 20.

Left elevator found miles from crash site

The NTSB revealed that a large portion of the aircraft’s left elevator was found a few miles from the main impact site.

Investigators have not indicated what significance the discovery may have, but the location of the component will form part of the wider investigation into the aircraft’s condition before the crash.

Chapman urged anyone who finds suspected wreckage not to touch or move it, and instead contact the NTSB or local authorities so it can be properly documented and recovered.

The NTSB has not released any preliminary findings and said the investigation remains in its early stages.

]]>
In Brief 3 min read
  • US military flights to Israel and reported diplomatic warnings have fueled speculation about renewed major strikes on Iran, but Trump has not confirmed a decision.
  • C-17 movements may indicate additional air defense deployments, although flight-tracking data alone cannot establish their cargo or purpose.
  • Limited US strikes have continued, making the key question whether Washington will escalate to a sustained air campaign.

US military transport flights to Israel have fueled speculation that Washington could launch a new wave of major strikes against Iran following the November 3 midterm elections. However, the aircraft movements alone do not establish that an offensive is imminent.

Reports of diplomatic warnings and possible air defence deployments have added to expectations of an escalation. President Donald Trump has not confirmed a decision to authorise a wider campaign, and limited US strikes have already continued during the standoff.

US C-17 flights to Israel draw attention

Flight trackers have reported a series of US Air Force C-17 transport movements from Biggs Army Airfield, near Fort Bliss in Texas, to Israel’s Ovda Air Base.

In a November 3 update, open-source aircraft tracker Armchair Admiral reported that a second group of C-17s was heading to Ovda. The tracker said this would bring the total to 16 once the latest group completed its flights.

The movements followed eight missions to Ovda the previous week. Armchair Admiral suggested that the activity could indicate preparations for another Patriot surface-to-air missile deployment.

#USAF United States Air Force Operation Epic Fury 3 November – 1100z Movements from Biggs Army Airfield / Fort Bliss are continuing. A second group of C-17s that began positioning to Biggs are now also en route to Ovda Air Base in Israel, which should bring the total to sixteen once this group is complete. Additionally, we have a flight from Pope Army Airfield to Ali Al Salem Air Base. In the opposite direction, two C-17s have flown from Ali Al Salem Air Base to Davis-Monthan Air Force Base. @MATA_osint @DefenceGeek @sipjack1776 @TheIntelFrog @Andyyyyrrrr @vcdgf555 @sentdefender @Osinttechnical @Faytuks @Andyyyyrrrr

— Armchair Admiral 🇬🇧 (@ArmchairAdml) November 3, 2026

That remains an interpretation of the flight activity. Public tracking data can reveal aircraft routes and movements, but does not establish what cargo is aboard or why it is being transported.

Additional air defences could help protect against retaliation during a wider campaign. Their deployment would not, by itself, confirm that a decision to launch that campaign had been made.

The tracker also reported flights elsewhere in the region, including a movement from Pope Army Airfield to Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait and two C-17 flights from Ali Al Salem to Davis-Monthan Air Force Base in Arizona.

Reports point to possible US escalation after midterms

On October 29, the Associated Press reported that US officials had told several Middle Eastern countries and regional allies to prepare for potential renewed military action against Iran after the midterm elections.

The BBC also reported intensified mediation efforts aimed at preventing a return to all-out war after the November 3 vote.

Trump, however, has said he is in “no rush” to resume strikes.

Warnings to allies and military preparations can indicate that Washington is keeping its options open. They do not establish that the president has authorised an operation or settled on its timing and scale.

81 US aircraft lost or damaged in Iran war: The real cost to US airpower 81 US aircraft lost or damaged in Iran war: The real cost to US airpower

Limited strikes continue amid uncertainty over wider campaign

The question is whether the US will expand its operations into a sustained air campaign.

On November 3, the BBC reported US strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran claimed to have shot down a US MQ-9 Reaper drone, although Air & Space Forces Magazine quoted US officials as saying no aircraft had been lost.

Those attacks were more limited in scope than Operation Epic Fury, the earlier US-Israeli air campaign against Iran.

A renewed offensive could involve different targets, levels of force and durations. Preparations for one possible course of action do not mean it will necessarily proceed.

For now, the reported C-17 movements add to the picture of continuing US military activity in the region. They leave the central questions unanswered: whether a wider campaign will be authorised, when it might begin and what it would seek to achieve.
